modules.doc:
velt/cli: command-line argument parsing (Node's `util.parseArgs` rules, commander-style API).

Build a parser, then parse an argv array (usually `args()` from std/process):

  const p = new ArgParser("tool", "Does things")
    .flag("verbose", { short: "v", help: "Chatty output" })
    .option("out", { short: "o", default: "out.txt", help: "Output file" })
    .positional("input", "File to read");
  const a = p.parse(args());
  if (a.flag("help")) { console.log(p.help()); return; }

Builder methods change the parser and return it, so they chain (`p.flag(...)` alone also works).
Accepted syntax: `--name`, `--name=value`, `--name value`, `--no-name` (flag set to false),
`-v`, `-abc` (short flags clustered), `-o value` / `-ovalue` (short option, value attached or
next), `--` (everything after is positional) and `-` (a positional). An option's value is
taken verbatim even if it starts with `-`. Repeated options keep every value (`getAll`).
Every parser has `-h, --help`.
docs/std/cli.md.
modules.summary: velt/cli: command-line argument parsing (Node's `util.parseArgs` rules, commander-style API).

broken invariant: keys in order and inside their node's range, node fill, the leaf chain, each

modules.doc:
velt/collections (internal): the smallest and the largest key of a `Pool`
(velt/collections/btree/pool), internal.

A node at the edge of the tree (the root, and the first and last node of each level) lacks a
separator on one side, so the separators alone would give it no prefix: for keys that all
share a long beginning (`user/…`, paths, URLs) its words would all be equal and every search
would compare whole keys there. The smallest and the largest key stand in for the separators
those nodes lack (`Pool.prefixFor`). That holds for keys between them, so every operation first
places its key against them (`edgeOrder`): a lookup of a key outside answers at once, and an
insert of one makes it the new smallest or largest first, giving the nodes along that edge
their prefix again (`noteEdges`). A delete of the smallest or the largest leaves the edge
prefixes as they are: a range that narrows keeps them true, if shorter than they could be.
modules.summary: velt/collections (internal): the smallest and the largest key of a `Pool` (velt/collections/btree/pool), internal.

exports.name: edgeOrder
exports.signature: function edgeOrder<K extends Comparable<K>, V>(p: Pool<K, V>, t: K, win: Window): i64
exports.doc:
Where `t` (window `win`) lies against the smallest and the largest key: -1 below the smallest,
1 above the largest, 0 between them (or when the map is empty, or keys have no words: no prefix
to keep true). The windows settle it unless they tie.
exports.summary: Where `t` (window `win`) lies against the smallest and the largest key: -1 below the smallest, 1 above the largest, 0 between them (or when the map is empty, or keys have no words: no prefix to keep true).

exports.name: noteEdges

exports.doc:
Before `key` goes in: makes it the smallest or the largest key when it is outside them (the
first key both), and gives the nodes along that edge their prefixes for the wider range.
exports.summary: Before `key` goes in: makes it the smallest or the largest key when it is outside them (the first key both), and gives the nodes along that edge their prefixes for the wider range.

modules.doc:
velt/collections (internal): `InlineKey`, the order-preserving bytes of a key that
`BTreeMap` keeps beside its keys, a few per key, to search nodes without reading the keys.

A key's encoding is a byte string that orders as the keys do: for keys `a < b`, `a`'s bytes
are at most `b`'s in byte order. Numbers encode big-endian (signed ones with the sign bit
flipped), `bool` as one byte, and strings as their CESU-8 bytes, the order of `<` on
strings. Shorter encodings read as zero past their end. Other comparable types get the
blanket implementation, which has no encoding (`hasInlineKey()` is false): the map compares
their keys in full. A type with an order of its own implements `InlineKey` with an `extend`
block (or `implements InlineKey`) to get the fast search.
modules.summary: velt/collections (internal): `InlineKey`, the order-preserving bytes of a key that `BTreeMap` keeps beside its keys, a few per key, to search nodes without reading the keys.

exports.name: string
exports.doc:
Strings: their CESU-8 bytes (each UTF-16 code unit as UTF-8 would write it), whose byte order is
the order of the code units, `<` on strings. A string keeps its text as WTF-8, the same bytes
but for a character past U+FFFF (four bytes, from F0), which CESU-8 writes as its two
surrogates; so up to the first such byte the encoding is read where the string keeps it, two
ASCII characters to a word. Past one it is decoded (`cesuBytes`).
exports.summary: Strings: their CESU-8 bytes (each UTF-16 code unit as UTF-8 would write it), whose byte order is the order of the code units, `<` on strings.

modules.doc:
velt/collections (internal): inserts into a `Pool` (velt/collections/btree/pool), internal.

An entry goes into the leaf its key belongs to; a full leaf moves entries to a sibling with
room (`shiftToSibling`), and only when both are full splits in two, the new leaf going right
of it under a separator, which may split the parent in turn, up to a new root. Moving entries
to a sibling instead of splitting keeps leaves fuller (B*-trees): about 85% instead of 70%
for random keys, so fewer leaves, less memory and fewer cache lines per entry.
modules.summary: velt/collections (internal): inserts into a `Pool` (velt/collections/btree/pool), internal.

exports.name: insert
exports.signature: function insert<K extends Comparable<K>, V>(p: Pool<K, V>, key: K, value: V)
exports.doc: Stores `value` under `key` in `p`, replacing the value already there.
exports.summary: Stores `value` under `key` in `p`, replacing the value already there.

modules.doc:
velt/collections (internal): entries of a leaf of a `Pool` (velt/collections/btree/pool),
internal.

A leaf keeps its keys and values in physical slots `0 .. n` in the order they came, its words
by physical slot too, and its rank order apart (`Pool.leafOrder`: rank → slot). An insert
appends at slot `n` and inserts the slot into the order; a delete moves the last slot into the
hole. So neither moves the other entries: an insert touches one key and one value line where
a sorted leaf would shift (and so read) every key and value after the new one. A search needs
no order: words below the target's give its rank, words equal to it give the slots of the
keys to compare. What works on ranks (walks, ranges, splits, merges) reads the order; entries
move between leaves by rank (`moveRanks`), so no leaf is ever sorted.
modules.summary: velt/collections (internal): entries of a leaf of a `Pool` (velt/collections/btree/pool), internal.

exports.name: moveRanks
exports.signature: function moveRanks<K extends Comparable<K>, V>(p: Pool<K, V>, from: u32, lo: usize, k: usize, to: u32, before: bool)
exports.doc:
Moves the entries of `from`'s ranks `lo .. lo + k` (its smallest when `lo` is 0, else its
largest) to `to`, all of whose keys are above them (`before`) or below them: into `to`'s free
slots from its count up, at its ranks `0 .. k` or after its own. The entries of `from` left in
slots past its new count move into the holes, so its slots stay `0 .. n - k`. Nothing else
moves: no leaf is put in rank order. Words follow their keys, at each leaf's present prefix;
a caller whose change of separators changes a prefix refreshes that leaf.

modules.doc:
velt/collections (internal): `Line`, the 32 `u16` words of a B-tree node, internal.

A line is 64 bytes, four `u16x8` vectors: slots 0 to 30 hold a word per key (two bytes of the
key's encoding past the node's prefix, `EMPTY` past the last key) and slot 31 (`HEAD`) the
node's header, its count in the low 5 bits and its prefix (in bytes) above them. An array of lines
keeps each one in one cache line (an array buffer of elements that are whole lines is
line-aligned), so a node's search reads one line.
modules.summary: velt/collections (internal): `Line`, the 32 `u16` words of a B-tree node, internal.

modules.doc:
velt/collections (internal): the nodes of `BTreeMap` (velt/collections/btree_map), internal.

A B+tree whose nodes live in flat pools, a struct of arrays, nodes linked by `u32` index:
node `n`'s keys are slots `n * F .. n * F + F`. Leaves hold up to `CAP` entries and link to
both neighbors; inner nodes hold up to `CAP` separators and `CAP + 1` children, every key of
child `i` at least separator `i - 1` and below separator `i`. The leaf pools are in chunks of
256 leaves, so they grow without copying (and hold at most a chunk unused). A freed node goes on
a free list. Leaf entries: velt/collections/btree/leaf; inserts: velt/collections/btree/insert;
deletes: velt/collections/btree/remove; the smallest and largest key:
velt/collections/btree/edges.

A node's 32 `u16` words (`leafLines` / `innerLines`, 64 bytes, each in one cache line) are
what a search reads first: slot `HEAD` holds the node's count and prefix, and the slots below
it, for keys with an order-preserving encoding (velt/collections/btree/inline_key: numbers,
`bool`, strings), two bytes of each key's encoding past the prefix all of the node's keys
share (`prefixFor`); strings keep the next two in a second line next to it, a four-byte
word in all. Vector compares count the words below the target's, which is its rank unless
words tie with it; only those keys are compared in full. So a level of a lookup reads one line
and one child index. Keys without an encoding are compared one by one.

Unused key slots hold `fill[0]`, so that the pools stay arrays of plain `K`; value slots
likewise (`vals`, with `valFill[0]`); unused word slots are `EMPTY`. A filler is the type's
blank value (velt/mem `Blank`: `""`, a number), which owns no memory, or for a type without
one a share of a live key or value. A deleted key or value is released: when a live
filler's entry is deleted or its value replaced, a live entry from the middle of the tree
gives new fillers (`refill`), a separator that is a deleted key that owns memory follows to
the next key, and the last delete drops the pools (velt/collections/btree/remove).
modules.summary: velt/collections (internal): the nodes of `BTreeMap` (velt/collections/btree_map), internal.

members.doc:

`valFill[0]`, the first value stored (as unused key slots hold one of `fill[0]`): a removed
value is dropped when its slot gets the filler. Values that own nothing take their own size
per slot, objects a pointer.

elsewhere.

modules.doc:
velt/collections (internal): deletes from a `Pool` (velt/collections/btree/pool), internal.

A leaf below `MIN_LEAF` entries takes entries from a sibling that has more, or merges with it,
by rank (velt/collections/btree/leaf `moveRanks`, no leaf is sorted), and the parent loses a
separator, which may leave it short in turn (an inner node below `MIN_INNER` separators
borrows one or merges), up to the root; a root left with one child gives way to it. A leaf
whose range widens keeps its prefix when that still holds (`keepPrefix`, `mergeInto`), else
gets its words again; one whose range narrows keeps its prefix, true if shorter than it could
be. Inner nodes whose separators change get their prefix and words again (`refreshInner`); a
node that moves to another parent keeps its separators, so its words stay.
modules.summary: velt/collections (internal): deletes from a `Pool` (velt/collections/btree/pool), internal.

modules.doc:
velt/collections (internal): `BTreeMap<K, V>`, a map that keeps its keys in ascending order
(`K extends Comparable<K>`: numbers, strings, bool, user types that implement `Comparable`).

A B+tree of 32-slot nodes in flat pools (velt/collections/btree/pool): lookups, inserts and
deletes are O(log n) and touch a few cache lines per level; ordered walks follow the linked
leaves. Keys with an order-preserving encoding (`InlineKey`: numbers, `bool`, strings, and user
types that implement it) are searched by two bytes of it per key, eight keys per compare. Values are shared as `Map` shares them (objects are not copied); keys are shared too.
modules.summary: velt/collections (internal): `BTreeMap<K, V>`, a map that keeps its keys in ascending order (`K extends Comparable<K>`: numbers, strings, bool, user types that implement `Comparable`).

modules.doc:
velt/collections (internal): `ConcurrentMap.getManyInto`: many lookups at once, their descents
interleaved.
modules.summary: velt/collections (internal): `ConcurrentMap.getManyInto`: many lookups at once, their descents interleaved.

exports.name: getManyInto
exports.signature: function getManyInto<K, V extends Frozen>(cm: ConcurrentMap<K, V>, keys: K[], values: V[]): u64
exports.doc:
Looks up `keys` (at most 64) together into `values`: where bit `i` of the result is set,
`values[i]` is the value of `keys[i]` (`values` grows to `keys.length` if shorter; its other
elements are unspecified). Unlike `BTreeMap.getMany`, which returns a new array, it fills the
caller's, so a loop of batches allocates nothing. Faster than one `get` per key when the map
is larger than the caches: the keys descend the tree in lockstep, and each prefetches its next
node while the others search theirs, so their cache misses overlap. For `u64` keys and values
only for now (other maps panic with a RangeError). Panics with a RangeError for more than 64
keys.
exports.summary: Looks up `keys` (at most 64) together into `values`: where bit `i` of the result is set, `values[i]` is the value of `keys[i]` (`values` grows to `keys.length` if shorter; its other elements are unspecified).

modules.doc:
velt/collections (internal): `ConcurrentMap`, a map from `u64` or `string` keys to values
that many threads read and write at once, through a `shared` value: a B+ tree with optimistic
lock coupling (Leis et al., "The ART of Practical Synchronization"; bbtree's concurrent map
uses the same protocol). Built only on public std APIs: `Atomic<u64>`, velt/simd
(`loadOptimistic`), `Atomic.fence`, array `prefetch`.

Every node is 128 words of one `Atomic<u64>[]` arena (allocated whole by `create`), addressed
by index and never moved, so a reader that holds a stale index still reads a node and finds
its version changed. Readers write nothing. A delete that empties a leaf unlinks it, with any
inner nodes above it left with no other child, from the lowest ancestor that keeps a child,
and puts them on a free list (`spare`) that `alloc` takes from first. A node's version only
grows, through being freed and reused too, so a reader that read it before sees it changed.

Node layout (words):
  0: latch (bit 0 exclusive, then shared holders, the version from bit 21: velt/sync's
     `VersionLatch` word)
  1: meta: the number of keys | `LEAF_BIT` for a leaf | an inner node's level from bit 40
  leaf:  16-bit tags (hashes) of the keys, 4 to a word, at 2..16, tag 0 for an empty slot; key
         i at 16 + 2i, its value at 17 + 2i. Unsorted (a lookup only needs equality, a split
         sorts): a key sits in its home slot (other bits of its hash) when that was free, else
         in any free slot, so most lookups read the home pair without waiting for the tags.
  inner: an index at 2..8 (key 8g + 7 for group g), then from word 16 groups of 16 words, one
         cache line each: 8 keys, then the 8 children left of them (child 8g + j between keys
         8g + j - 1 and 8g + j); unused key slots hold `MAX_KEY`. A level reads the index line
         and one group line. Key i separates child i (keys below it) from child i + 1.
A reader reads a node's words with relaxed loads (several at a time with `loadOptimistic`),
then checks its version (`isUnchanged`), and starts over from the root when a writer changed
it. A writer takes the node's latch at the version it read, so a node that changed since
fails the take; a full node is split on the way down while its parent is held as well, so a
parent always has room for the separator.

String keys: the tree's key words are the strings' first 8 bytes in order (`inlineKey(0)`, so
a < b gives word(a) <= word(b)), and the strings themselves sit beside the nodes, in `skeys`:
a leaf's key in slot j at `node * SKEYS + j`, and the string of the separator left of a node
in its parent at `node * SKEYS + FENCE` (the node's fence: separator i of an inner node is the
fence of its child i + 1, so separators move between slots without their strings). Words that
tie are told apart by the strings: an inner node's separators with the key's word that are
greater than the key send it left of them (`backTies`, a binary search over the tied run), and
a leaf slot whose tag and word match is the key's only if its string is (`sameKey`). Tags and
home slots hash the whole string, so keys that share a prefix do not share tags. A reader reads
the strings as it reads the words, optimistically: borrowed, inside the epoch section the
compiler opens around the function that loads them, so one that a writer replaces meanwhile
stays readable until the section ends, and the node's version check after says whether what it
compared was the node's (a fence is read through the parent's child word, and changes only
while the parent is held: set before its node is linked, cleared when the node is unlinked or
becomes its parent's first child, whose fence is never read). A writer changes strings only
while it holds their node (or before the node is linked), and moves as few as it can: each one
replaced is retired to the epoch.
modules.summary: velt/collections (internal): `ConcurrentMap`, a map from `u64` or `string` keys to values that many threads read and write at once, through a `shared` value: a B+ tree with optimistic lock coupling (Leis et al., "The ART of Practical Synchronization"; bbtree's concurrent map uses the same protocol).

exports.name: ConcurrentMap
exports.signature: class ConcurrentMap<K = u64, V extends Frozen = u64>
exports.doc:
A map from `K` keys (`u64` or `string`; `u64` when not written) to `V` values (`u64` when not
written) for many threads at once: share it (`shared(ConcurrentMap.create(n))`) and call its
methods from any task. A value other than a `u64` is boxed once, and read in place by `read`;
a string key is kept once, beside its leaf. Lookups write no shared memory, so readers on many
cores never slow each other; writers take a latch per node. A lookup waits (spins) while a
writer holds its node, so it is not lock-free. Its keys are kept in key ranges, but a leaf's
are unsorted and leaves are not linked: there is no ordered walk, iteration or size yet
(#1688). Its room is fixed when it is created, and given back as leaves empty.
exports.summary: A map from `K` keys (`u64` or `string`; `u64` when not written) to `V` values (`u64` when not written) for many threads at once: share it (`shared(ConcurrentMap.create(n))`) and call its methods from any task.

members.name: create
members.doc:
An empty map with room for at least `capacity` entries (its memory, about 40 bytes an
entry, and 17 more for string keys, is taken now; a string key's own copy when it is set).
A `set` that needs more room panics with a RangeError. A deleted
entry frees a slot in its leaf, and a leaf whose last entry is deleted is reused, so keys
that keep moving to new ranges (ids or timestamps that only grow, old ones deleted) fit for
as long as the entries present at once do. Leaves are not merged, though: entries spread
thinly over many leaves (most of a large map's keys deleted at random) can hold a node each
and need more room than their number. A `set` of a key the map holds can also need room,
when its leaf is full and splits first. Panics with a RangeError above 10^11 entries, and
for keys other than `u64` and `string`.
members.summary: An empty map with room for at least `capacity` entries (its memory, about 40 bytes an entry, and 17 more for string keys, is taken now; a string key's own copy when it is set).

Looks up `keys` (at most 64) together into `values`: where bit `i` of the result is set,
`values[i]` is the value of `keys[i]` (`values` grows to `keys.length` if shorter; its other
elements are unspecified). Unlike `BTreeMap.getMany`, which returns a new array, it fills the

node while the others search theirs, so their cache misses overlap. For `u64` keys and values
only for now (other maps panic with a RangeError). Panics with a RangeError for more than 64

modules.doc:
velt/collections (internal): `Deque<T>`, a double-ended queue on a growable ring buffer: O(1)
amortized push and pop at both ends, O(1) indexing.

Slots are `(T | undefined)[]` (empty slots are `undefined`) with a power-of-two capacity plus
one spare slot at the end that is always empty. An element can't be moved out of an array
index, so taking one swaps it into the spare slot and `pop()`s it, then pushes a fresh
`undefined` back (no reallocation: the array's buffer keeps its capacity). Growing appends
empty slots and swaps the wrapped-around prefix up behind the old end, so elements are never
cloned or copied. A `T` holding `null` (`Deque<i64 | null>`) keeps its `null` apart from an
empty slot; a `T` holding `undefined` is a compile error (it could not be told from one).
modules.summary: velt/collections (internal): `Deque<T>`, a double-ended queue on a growable ring buffer: O(1) amortized push and pop at both ends, O(1) indexing.

members.name: getManyInto
members.doc:
Looks up `keys` (at most 64) together into `values`: where bit `i` of the result is set,
`values[i]` is the value of `keys[i]` (`values` grows to `keys.length` if shorter; its other
elements are unspecified). Unlike `BTreeMap.getMany`, which returns a new array, it fills the
caller's, so a loop of batches allocates nothing. Faster than one `get` per key when the map
is larger than the caches: the keys descend the tree in lockstep, and each prefetches its next
node while the others search theirs, so their cache misses overlap. For `u64` keys and values
only for now (other maps panic with a RangeError). Panics with a RangeError for more than 64
keys.

velt/collections (internal): `PriorityQueue<T>`, a binary heap ordered by a comparator.

`cmp(a, b) < 0` means `a` comes out first, so `(a, b) => a - b` is a min-heap and
`(a, b) => b - a` a max-heap (the `sort(cmp)` convention). Elements are only swapped inside the
heap array, never cloned; `pop` moves the top element out by swapping it to the end.
Elements that compare equal come out in unspecified order (a heap is not stable). The queue
keeps `cmp`, and a comparator may capture variables.
modules.summary: velt/collections (internal): `PriorityQueue<T>`, a binary heap ordered by a comparator.

velt/collections (internal): `Set<T>`, an insertion-ordered hash set with JS `Set` semantics,
plus the ES2025 set algebra (`union`, `intersection`, `difference`, `symmetricDifference`,
`isSubsetOf`, `isSupersetOf`, `isDisjointFrom`).

Built on the prelude `Map<T, bool>` (Robin Hood index over dense insertion-ordered entries),
so elements compare as map keys do: numbers, bool and strings by value, objects (class
instances, object types, arrays, interface and function values) by identity, as in JS, and
tuples part by part. `add` takes ownership of the element; `values()` and the algebra results
hold the stored elements (objects shared, as in JS); `forEach` borrows.

velt/collections (internal): `SortedMap<K, V>`, a map that keeps its keys in ascending order
(`K extends Comparable<K>`: numbers, strings, bool, user types that implement `Comparable`).

Two parallel sorted arrays searched by binary search: O(log n) lookups, O(n) inserts and
deletes (element swaps, cache friendly), which beats a tree for small and read-mostly maps.
Ordered queries (`first`, `last`, `floorKey`, `ceilingKey`, `range`) are O(log n) plus the
output. Keys are ordered by `compareTo`: as `<`, with a float NaN after every other value and
equal to itself. `set` takes ownership; `get` / `keys` / `values` / `entries` return clones
(unlike `Map`, which shares stored objects).
modules.summary: velt/collections (internal): `SortedMap<K, V>`, a map that keeps its keys in ascending order (`K extends Comparable<K>`: numbers, strings, bool, user types that implement `Comparable`).

modules.doc:
velt/compress (internal): the input of a Brotli stream and the bit reader over it.

The input is kept in one buffer of its own, followed by at least `PAD` zero bytes, so the
reader loads eight bytes at a time (one 16-byte vector load) without a check per byte; bits
past the input read as zeros. Whether a step read past the input is found afterwards, from the
bit position (`overran`): the decoder then waits for more input or reports a truncated stream.
The hot loop of commands.velt copies `bits`, `count` and `pos` into locals and refills the same
way; the methods here are for the headers.
modules.summary: velt/compress (internal): the input of a Brotli stream and the bit reader over it.

exports.name: PAD
exports.doc:
Zero bytes kept after the input. A step of the command loop starts at most 8 bytes past the
input (at a byte position that a committed step reached) and reads at most 21 bytes more, so
its 16-byte loads end within 53 bytes of the input: twice that leaves a margin.
exports.summary: Zero bytes kept after the input.

exports.doc: The input buffer and the bit reader's position in it.
exports.summary: The input buffer and the bit reader's position in it.

modules.doc:
velt/compress (internal): Brotli decompression (RFC 7932), the `br` content coding of HTTP.

`brotliDecompress` decodes a whole stream at once into one array that grows as the
meta-blocks' headers announce their lengths. `BrotliDecoder` takes the input in pieces and
hands out the output in chunks of at most the size asked for, keeping only the window that
back-references can reach and what has not been read, so a small input that expands
enormously never needs more memory than that. The decoder itself is in compress/brotli/.

velt/compress (internal): the insert-and-copy alphabet of RFC 7932 section 5, one entry per
symbol so that a command's lengths take one table lookup.

`COMMANDS[symbol]` is the insert length's extra bits (bits 0-7) and the copy length's (8-15),
then their base lengths (16-31 and 32-47). Symbols below 128 also reuse the last distance.
Generated by scripts/gen-brotli-commands.py from the RFC's tables of insert and copy length
codes and its cells of 64 symbols.
modules.summary: velt/compress (internal): the insert-and-copy alphabet of RFC 7932 section 5, one entry per symbol so that a command's lengths take one table lookup.

modules.doc:
velt/compress (internal): the commands of a compressed meta-block (RFC 7932 section 9.3):
literals inserted, then a back-reference copied or a word of the static dictionary written.

This is where decoding spends its time, so the bit reader, the output position and the whole
command and block state live in locals for the length of the loop (one function, so that
they stay in registers), and prefix codes are decoded inline: one table lookup, two for codes
longer than 8 bits. Block switches, distances and dictionary words go through calls, with the
locals they touch written back around them.

The loop works in steps: a command's lengths, one literal (the last one of a command
together with the distance), a distance, a copy. After each it stops when the next byte to
load is past `safeEnd` or the output reached `limit`. The driver
(decoder.velt) passes a `safeEnd` 16 bytes before the end of the input, so no step (at most 117
bits) reads past the input; near the end it passes -1, runs one step at a time and checks
afterwards whether the step needed more input than there is. A step's refill loads 8 bytes
at `pos`, which the zeros after the input (bits.velt) keep inside the buffer.
modules.summary: velt/compress (internal): the commands of a compressed meta-block (RFC 7932 section 9.3): literals inserted, then a back-reference copied or a word of the static dictionary written.

modules.doc:
velt/compress (internal): the literal context lookup of RFC 7932 section 7.1, for the four
context modes in one table of 256 numbers.

Byte `m` (mode m: 0 LSB6, 1 MSB6, 2 UTF8, 3 signed) of `CONTEXT[b]` is what the previous byte
`b` adds to the context, byte `4 + m` what the byte before it adds. The two are disjoint bit
fields, so a literal's context is
`((CONTEXT[p1] | CONTEXT[p2] >> 32) >> 8 * mode) & 63`: two loads, one table for every mode.
modules.summary: velt/compress (internal): the literal context lookup of RFC 7932 section 7.1, for the four context modes in one table of 256 numbers.

modules.doc:
velt/compress (internal): the decoder's driver: it runs the stream's parts in order (headers,
uncompressed and metadata blocks, commands) as far as the input and the room for output allow,
and keeps the output buffer.

Input may stop anywhere. A step that can run out of it (a header, or a command step within 16
bytes of the input's end) starts from a saved state: when it turns out to have needed more
input than there is, the state is put back and the step is run again once more input came
(or, after the last input, the stream is truncated). Away from the end the command loop runs
without saving anything.

The output buffer keeps what back-references can still reach (the window) and what has not
been read; `brotliDecompress` keeps all of it, which is then the result.
modules.summary: velt/compress (internal): the decoder's driver: it runs the stream's parts in order (headers, uncompressed and metadata blocks, commands) as far as the input and the room for output allow, and keeps the output buffer.

modules.doc:
velt/compress (internal): the static dictionary of RFC 7932 (appendix A) and its 121 word
transforms (appendix B).

The dictionary is 122,784 bytes that are not all UTF-8, so it cannot be one string literal,
and an array literal of that many numbers is a source file of as many lines once formatted.
It is kept as two string constants instead, which the compiler joins into read-only data
(no module state, nothing built at run time): `LOW` holds each byte's low seven bits (ASCII,
escaped where needed) and `HIGH` its top bit, as `@` (bit 6 set) or a space. A word is put
back together sixteen bytes at a time: `low | (high & 0x40) << 1`. Both end with sixteen
bytes of padding, so a 16-byte load at any word's start stays inside them.

The strings were generated from the dictionary of the `brotli-decompressor` crate; the
transforms are packed as described at `TRANSFORMS`.
modules.summary: velt/compress (internal): the static dictionary of RFC 7932 (appendix A) and its 121 word transforms (appendix B).

exports.name: writeWord
exports.signature: function writeWord(out: u8[], at: usize, len: usize, wordId: usize): i64
exports.doc:
Writes the dictionary reference `wordId` (a distance past the window, less the window and one)
of copy length `len` at `out[at]`: the word with its transform applied. Returns the number of
bytes it stands for, or -1 when `len` has no words or the transform does not exist. Writes up
to 48 bytes past `at` (16-byte stores), which `out` must have room for.
exports.summary: Writes the dictionary reference `wordId` (a distance past the window, less the window and one) of copy length `len` at `out[at]`: the word with its transform applied.

velt/compress (internal): the stream header and meta-block headers of RFC 7932 (sections 9.1 and
9.2), and block switches (section 6).

A compressed meta-block's header sets up everything its commands are decoded with: the block
types of the three categories, the context modes and maps, and the prefix code tables, all
of them back to back in `State.tables`. It is read in one go, as one step of the decoder
(decoder.velt starts it over when the input runs out before its end).

modules.doc:
velt/compress (internal): prefix codes (RFC 7932 section 3) read from the stream and turned into
lookup tables.

A table is `u32` entries `symbol << 16 | length`, indexed by the next 8 input bits (the
root). A code longer than 8 bits has its root entry point at a second-level table instead:
`offset << 16 | (8 + bits)`, the offset relative to the root, indexed by the next `bits`
input bits. This is the reference decoder's layout; one table lookup decodes most symbols.
Bits arrive first-bit-lowest, so a code's table index is its bits reversed.
modules.summary: velt/compress (internal): prefix codes (RFC 7932 section 3) read from the stream and turned into lookup tables.

and a zlib stream (Adler-32, RFC 1950 §9) end with, computed as the output is made.

CRC-32 folds 64 bytes per step with carry-less multiplication where the CPU has it (Intel's
"Fast CRC Computation for Generic Polynomials Using PCLMULQDQ", the constants of
`crc32fast`), and otherwise takes eight bytes per step through the slicing-by-8 tables (one
16-byte load gives two steps); Adler-32 sums 5552 bytes between reductions, the most that
cannot overflow 32 bits.

modules.doc:
velt/compress (internal): the inner loop of a DEFLATE block, the literals
and matches of its Huffman codes (RFC 1951 §3.2.5).

`fast` runs while 16 input bytes and a longest match (plus 16 bytes of slack) of output room
are left: it refills the bit buffer with one 8-byte load per symbol, without a branch (the
buffer then holds at least 56 bits, and a literal or length code with its extra bits and a
distance code with its extra bits take at most 48), and copies a match 16 bytes at a time when
its distance allows. `slow` decodes one symbol near the end of the input or the output, with
every bit counted: when the input runs out in the middle of a symbol it puts everything back
as it was before the symbol, to be decoded again once more input arrives.

modules.doc:
velt/compress (internal): the decoding tables of a DEFLATE block's Huffman
codes (RFC 1951 §3.2.2), built as zlib's `inflate_table` builds them.

A table is indexed by the next bits of the input, least significant first, which are a code
read backwards: a root table of `root` bits holds every code that short (repeated for each
value of the bits after it), and a longer code's root entry points to a subtable indexed by
the bits after the root. An entry is one `u32`, so a symbol costs one load (two for a long
code):

- bits 0-3: the bits the entry's code takes at its level (the root's bits for a pointer);
- bits 4-7: the extra bits after a length or distance code, or a subtable's index bits;
- bits 8-12: what the entry is (`LITERAL`, `BASE`, `END`, `SUBTABLE`; 0 is no code);
- bits 16-31: the literal, the length or distance before its extra bits, or where the
  subtable starts.

A set of code lengths that does not make a prefix code is refused as zlib refuses it:
over-subscribed always, incomplete unless it is a single code of one bit (or no code at all,
for a block that uses no distances), whose missing entries stay 0 and fail if they are read.
modules.summary: velt/compress (internal): the decoding tables of a DEFLATE block's Huffman codes (RFC 1951 §3.2.2), built as zlib's `inflate_table` builds them.

zlib (RFC 1950) and gzip (RFC 1952, several members in a row as one stream), in Velt.

`gunzip`, `inflate` and `inflateRaw` decode a whole stream into one buffer, sized from the
gzip trailer's length when there is one. `InflateDecoder` decodes a stream that arrives in
pieces into chunks of a bounded size, so a small input that expands enormously is still
handed out a chunk at a time. Both check the stream's CRC-32 or Adler-32.

modules.doc:
velt/crypto: SHA-256 and SHA-1 (FIPS 180-4), HMAC (RFC 2104), secure random bytes/integers
and constant-time comparison.

The hashes are Velt: where the CPU has SHA instructions (`velt/simd`, #1330: ARMv8 SHA2, x86
SHA-NI with SSSE3 and SSE4.1) whole blocks go through functions gated on them, which run the
bare instructions; elsewhere (other CPUs, WebAssembly, debug builds, `VELT_SIMD_DISABLE=sha`)
through portable rounds over `u32` words (integer arithmetic wraps, `>>>` is a logical shift).
Randomness comes from the OS generator through the runtime. SHA-1 is broken for collision
resistance: use it only for legacy protocols (WebSocket handshakes, HMAC-SHA1 in TOTP, git
object ids).
docs/std/crypto.md.

modules.doc:
velt/db: what database drivers share (docs/std/db.md): rows of any source into typed values, and the parameters of a statement out of them. A driver written in Velt (a database's wire protocol parsed in place, a file format) implements `RowSource`, and `readRows` fills a `T` per row: each column the field of its name, as `JSON.parse` fills fields from keys, with the same conversions and the same messages for a row that does not fit. A native driver (a package with a Rust library) hands over a row cursor instead, which `decodeRows` reads the same way, and takes a statement's parameters as typed values through `bindParams

`.
modules.summary: velt/db: what database drivers share (docs/std/db.md): rows of any source into typed values, and the parameters of a statement out of them.

exports.name: decodeRows
exports.doc:
Every row of a native driver's row cursor (its handle) as a `T`: each column fills the field
of its name, as `readRows` fills them from a `RowSource` (the same conversions and messages).
The cursor stays the driver's: give the handle back to the driver afterwards, which then
reports a failure met while stepping. Throws `RowError` for a row that does not fit `T`, and
for a handle that names no open row cursor.
exports.summary: Every row of a native driver's row cursor (its handle) as a `T`: each column fills the field of its name, as `readRows` fills them from a `RowSource` (the same conversions and messages).

exports.name: bindParams
exports.signature:
function bindParams

(sink: u64, params: P): bool
exports.doc:
Hands `params` to a native driver's parameter sink (its handle) value by value: an array, a tuple or a lone
value by position, an object's fields by name, each value bound as its JSON text would read
back (an integral number an integer, NaN null, a `u8[]` field a blob). True once they went to
the sink; false, having done nothing, for a type it cannot take that way (a nested object, a
union): the driver then takes `JSON.stringify(params)` instead, which binds the same values.
False too for a handle that names no open parameter sink (nothing reaches memory; the driver
finds the handle dead when it is handed on).
exports.summary: Hands `params` to a native driver's parameter sink (its handle) value by value: an array, a tuple or a lone value by position, an object's fields by name, each value bound as its JSON text would read back (an integral number an integer, NaN null, a `u8[]` field a blob).

modules.doc:
velt/db (internal): what a native driver (a package with a Rust library on the native SDK,
docs/book/native-packages.md) hands std to decode its rows and to bind a statement's
parameters: a row cursor and a parameter sink (docs/internals/contracts/native_abi.md "Row
cursors" and "Parameter sinks"). Both are handles, `u64` keys the runtime gave the driver when
it registered the cursor or sink (`velt_text::rows_cursor::open_cursor` / `open_sink`), never
addresses: std looks each one up, so a number that names no open cursor or sink (made up,
closed already, the other kind) never reaches memory: `decodeRows` throws `RowError`,
`bindParams` binds nothing. The driver keeps
owning what it registered and takes it back by the same handle.

The decoder and the binder are generated per type by source generators (velt/db/generate,
velt/encoding/json/generate): a row is read cell by cell from the driver's memory into the
`T` being built, and parameters go to the driver value by value, without JSON text in between.
modules.summary: velt/db (internal): what a native driver (a package with a Rust library on the native SDK, docs/book/native-packages.md) hands std to decode its rows and to bind a statement's parameters: a row cursor and a parameter sink (docs/internals/contracts/native_abi.md "Row cursors" and "Parameter sinks").

modules.doc:
velt/dev (internal): the graceful stop of a server under `velt dev`. Before the supervisor
starts the next version of the program, it asks this one to stop: a server that joined then
stops accepting (the supervisor keeps the listening socket, so new connections wait for the
next version), answers its in-flight requests, and says it `drained`; the runtime exits once
every server that joined did (or after a bounded wait). Outside `velt dev` nothing joins.
modules.summary: velt/dev (internal): the graceful stop of a server under `velt dev`.

modules.doc:
velt/encoding (internal): `btoa` and `atob` (globals, as in Node): Base64 of a "binary
string", whose code units are bytes (0..255).

Both read the string's UTF-8 bytes once: a code unit up to 0x7F is one byte, one from 0x80
to 0xFF the two bytes `C2`/`C3 xx`, and any larger one starts with a higher byte. `btoa`
collects the bytes in one buffer and encodes it with std/encoding's `base64Encode`; `atob`
decodes into one buffer of UTF-8 and turns it into a string with one runtime copy. Bad input
throws Node's `DOMException` (`InvalidCharacterError`, with Node's messages).
modules.summary: velt/encoding (internal): `btoa` and `atob` (globals, as in Node): Base64 of a "binary string", whose code units are bytes (0..255).

modules.doc:
velt/encoding/csv: RFC 4180 CSV parsing and writing.

The parser scans the text once with `charCodeAt` (the delimiter, quotes and line breaks are
ASCII, so an ASCII text is read inline); unquoted fields are slices of the input, quoted fields
are slices with `""` unescaped. Records end at LF, CRLF or a lone CR; a final line break does
not start another record, and a leading byte order mark (U+FEFF) is skipped. Quoted fields may
contain delimiters and line breaks. Fields are strings; no type inference.
docs/std/encoding/csv.md.
modules.summary: velt/encoding/csv: RFC 4180 CSV parsing and writing.

velt/encoding: byte <-> text encodings — Base64 (RFC 4648 §4 and the URL-safe §5 alphabet),
lowercase hex, and UTF-8 (strict and lossy decoding, validation).

Strings are stored as UTF-8, so `utf8Encode` is a copy of a string's bytes (a lone surrogate
written as U+FFFD) and decoding validates them. Encoders build the output as ASCII bytes and turn them into a string with one
runtime copy. Decoders throw `EncodingError` on malformed input.

modules.doc:
velt/encoding/json (internal): `JSON.stringify` of a dynamic value (`any`, `unknown`, and an
interface value, written as the `any` it converts to), in Velt over velt/reflect: what the
value holds at run time, and its entries. Typed values are written by the code velt/encoding/
json/generate/write generates per type, which calls these for the dynamic parts.

As in Node, `undefined`, a function and a symbol are left out as an object member and written
as `null` as an array element; `JSON.stringify` of one itself is a `TypeError` (Velt's
returns a string). An object, an array, a tuple or a `shared` cell seen again while it is
being written is Node's `TypeError: Converting circular structure to JSON`.

modules.doc:
velt/encoding/json (internal): the generator of `parseJsonTop<T>` and `readJson<T>`
(generated.velt), run at compile time (docs/internals/design/source-generators.md): one
function per type that decodes a value of that type with the pull reader (reader.velt), as
`JSON.parse<T>` does, with the messages and paths of its errors (`expected string at
$.items[3].name`). It uses nothing a package could not: the model of `velt/generate` and, in
the code it writes, the public `Reader`, `JsonFail`, `JsonError` and `__construct<T>`.

A decoder reads its value or throws a `JsonFail` saying what it expected; each level the
failure passes through puts its path segment (`.name`, `[3]`) in front, so paths cost
nothing on success. `parseJsonTop` turns the failure into the `JsonError` the reader's
`message` words.

What it decodes: numbers (integers range-checked, as their type is named in the message),
booleans, strings, literal types, enums, options, arrays, tuples, unions (read_union.velt),
`Map<string, V>`, `Record<K, V>`, `JsonValue`, and objects, structs and classes of those
(public fields, built without running a constructor). A type it cannot decode is reported at
each call that parses it (parse_check.velt).
modules.summary: velt/encoding/json (internal): the generator of `parseJsonTop<T>` and `readJson<T>` (generated.velt), run at compile time (docs/internals/design/source-generators.md): one function per type that decodes a value of that type with the pull reader (reader.velt), as `JSON.parse<T>` does, with the messages and paths of its errors (`expected string at $.items[3].name`).

modules.doc:
velt/encoding/json (internal): the generator of `writeJson<T>` and `writeJsonKeyed<T>`
(generated.velt), run at compile time (docs/internals/design/source-generators.md): one
function per type that appends what `JSON.stringify` writes for a value of that type, with
each object's constant text (`{"id":`, `,"name":`) appended as one literal. It uses nothing a
package could not: the model of `velt/generate`, `__arm` for a union's members, and in the
code it writes `StringBuilder`, the `appendJson*` functions, velt/reflect and the writer of
dynamic values (any.velt).

What it writes, as Node does: numbers, booleans, strings, literal types, enums (numeric and
string), arrays, tuples, options, objects, structs and classes (JavaScript's key order, array
indexes first; optional and `T | undefined` fields left out when empty, a present `null` of
`a?: T | null` written; ES private fields and functions left out, `private` fields written),
a class value as its dynamic class (an `instanceof` chain, most derived first) and through
its `toJSON(key)`, `Map<string, V>` and `Record<K, V>` as objects, `JsonValue` as its text,
a `shared<T>` as the `T` it holds, a union as its active member, a function as `null` (an
array element; a member holding one is left out), and dynamic values (`any`, interface
values, typed proxies) through any.velt. A recursive object type that meets itself is an
error, as in Node.
modules.summary: velt/encoding/json (internal): the generator of `writeJson<T>` and `writeJsonKeyed<T>` (generated.velt), run at compile time (docs/internals/design/source-generators.md): one function per type that appends what `JSON.stringify` writes for a value of that type, with each object's constant text (`{"id":`, `,"name":`) appended as one literal.

modules.doc:
velt/encoding/json (internal): the pull reader under the decoders `JSON.parse<T>` compiles for
each type.

The reader lexes its source on demand. The first failure is sticky: every later call fails
too, and `message` turns it into the `JsonError` message. Commas and colons are handled by
`nextKey` / `arrayNext`: the reader only needs to know whether the last token it consumed
was an opening bracket.

A driver's rows (std/db) are read by the runtime's row reader: such a reader starts out
failed (`ROWS`), so every method takes its failure branch, which forwards to the row reader;
reading text pays nothing for it.

Port of crates/velt_rt/src/json/reader.rs and error.rs (#1668), with the same results and
messages.
modules.summary: velt/encoding/json (internal): the pull reader under the decoders `JSON.parse<T>` compiles for each type.

modules.doc:
velt/encoding/json (internal): a parsed JSON document as one flat tape (#1660, part of #1655):
what a `JsonValue` from `JSON.parseValue` reads. No allocation per value: two words per value in
one array, numbers decoded once, strings left in the source until a reader asks for one (only
strings with escapes are decoded while parsing), and each array's elements and each object's keys
listed together in one array of positions, so `at(i)` is O(1).

A tape's values never change after it is built (only `find` adds the hash index of a large
object it searches); values share it. Editing a value (`set`, `push`, …) turns that value into
the runtime's tree (prelude `JsonValue`), so it never shows through the tape.
modules.summary: velt/encoding/json (internal): a parsed JSON document as one flat tape (#1660, part of #1655): what a `JsonValue` from `JSON.parseValue` reads.

exports.name: Tape
exports.doc:
A parsed document. Value `v`'s words are `words[2v]` (kind, and a container's member count
from bit 32) and `words[2v + 1]` (a number's bits, a string's range or decoded index, a
container's first position in `kids`). An array's `kids` are its elements; an object's are its
key strings, each followed on the tape by its value (`key + 1`). Value 0 is the root.

Every lookup is O(1) but `find` in a small object (at most `INDEX_THRESHOLD` keys, compared in
place), so walking any value is linear in its size.

exports.name: writeTape
exports.signature: function writeTape(t: Tape, out: string, v: u32): void
exports.doc:
Appends value `v` as compact JSON text (`JSON.stringify`) to the builder `out`. Every call
that takes `out` gets no argument that is itself a call (it would make a copy of `out`
first, and the text would go to the copy): such arguments are made into locals before.
Iterative, with the open containers on a stack of its own, so a value nested as deeply as
the parser allowed writes without running out of native stack. The text is gathered in a
byte array handed to the builder in chunks: punctuation, strings and numbers cost stores,
not a call each.

modules.doc:
velt/encoding/json (internal): what `JSON.stringify<T>` writes for numbers and strings, in Velt
(#1668).

The writers append to the string builder of the glue the compiler generates (`out`, a
`VeltStrBuf` the functions only pass on to the builder's primitives, never read: every call
passes it first, with no argument after it that is a call) and write
exactly what `JSON.stringify` writes: numbers as JavaScript prints them (`null` for NaN and
the infinities), strings quoted, with `"`, `\`, control characters and lone surrogates
escaped (well-formed `JSON.stringify`).

Port of velt_text's json_escape.rs and the JSON number path of fmt.rs.
modules.summary: velt/encoding/json (internal): what `JSON.stringify<T>` writes for numbers and strings, in Velt (#1668).

exports.name: writeString
exports.signature: function writeString(out: string, s: string): void
exports.doc: Appends `s` as a quoted, escaped JSON string literal, as `JSON.stringify(s)` writes it.
exports.summary: Appends `s` as a quoted, escaped JSON string literal, as `JSON.stringify(s)` writes it.

exports.name: nextEscape
exports.signature: function nextEscape(s: string, from: usize, n: usize): usize
exports.doc:
The first byte of `s` from `from` to `n` (its length, or the end of a range of whole
characters within it) that needs escaping, or `n`. Sixteen bytes at a time: a block stops the
scan at its first byte below 0x20, `"` or `\`, or 0xED (the lead byte of U+D000–U+DFFF) with
0xA0 or above next (the bytes after the block's as a second vector), so Hangul and the rest of
U+D000–U+D7FF stay in the vector loop and only a lone surrogate stops it. The bytes after the
last whole block are read as the range's last sixteen (those already checked are clean); in
that block, 0xED is checked byte by byte. Shorter ranges are checked byte by byte. (The 0xED
check and the last block come from #1066.)
exports.summary: The first byte of `s` from `from` to `n` (its length, or the end of a range of whole characters within it) that needs escaping, or `n`.

Whole blocks while sixteen bytes of `s` are left (the last may run up to 15 bytes past `end`
in `buf`: room the caller keeps, and overwrites later), then byte by byte.
exports.summary: Copies bytes `start` to `end` of `s` (`n` bytes) to `buf` at `o`; the position after them.

exports.name: shortNumber
exports.doc:
`x` (finite) as the digits `JSON.stringify` writes for it without an exponent, when it has at
most 15 significant digits, between 10^-6 and 10^15; else `ok` false (the general printer).
At most 15 significant digits name a single double (decimals that close are farther apart
than doubles), so if `a = |x|` is such a decimal, it is the integer `m` nearest `a * 10^top`,
at the largest scale `top` that keeps that product below 10^15, over 10^top: the product is
within 0.18 of `m` (`a`'s own rounding, below 2^-53 of it, is at most 0.111 there, the
product's half an ulp at most 0.0625), and dividing back is correctly rounded, so it gives `a`
exactly when `m`'s digits name `a`. Those digits without trailing zeros are JavaScript's
shortest; at 10^-6 and above JavaScript writes them without an exponent. One multiply and one
divide, whatever the digits.
exports.summary: `x` (finite) as the digits `JSON.stringify` writes for it without an exponent, when it has at most 15 significant digits, between 10^-6 and 10^15; else `ok` false (the general printer).

(blocks the calling thread). Failures throw `IoError` (from "velt/io") with a Node-style `code`.
`openRead` and `openWrite` read and write files in chunks; Node's file-descriptor API
(`openSync`, `readSync`, `writeSync`, ...) calls the C library directly, on macOS and Linux.
docs/std/fs.md.
modules.summary: velt/fs: file system access over the runtime (docs/internals/contracts/rt_abi_async.md §5).

exports.name: readSync
exports.signature: function readSync(fd: number, buffer: u8[] | ArrayBufferView, offset: number | null = 0, length?: number | null, position?: number | null): number
exports.doc:
Reads up to `length` bytes into `buffer` from byte `offset` on (Node's `fs.readSync`): at
`position` in the file, or at the file's own position (which then advances) when `position`
is left out, `null` or -1. Returns the number of bytes read, 0 at the end of the file.
`offset` defaults to 0 and `length` to the rest of the buffer; a number is coerced as Node
does (`length` truncated to a 32-bit integer, `position` validated strictly). `buffer` is a
`u8[]` (Node's `Buffer`), a typed array or a `DataView`; `offset` and `length` count bytes of
it. Velt's typed API takes positional arguments, not Node's `(fd, buffer, options)` object.
exports.summary: Reads up to `length` bytes into `buffer` from byte `offset` on (Node's `fs.readSync`): at `position` in the file, or at the file's own position (which then advances) when `position` is left out, `null` or -1.

exports.name: writeSync
exports.signature: function writeSync(fd: number, buffer: u8[] | ArrayBufferView | string, offset: number | null = null, length?: number | null, position?: number | null): number
exports.doc:
Writes `length` bytes of `buffer` from byte `offset` on (Node's `fs.writeSync`): at
`position` in the file, or at the file's own position when `position` is left out, `null` or
not a valid byte offset (at its end for a file opened to append). Returns the number of bytes
written. `offset` defaults to 0 and `length` to the rest of the buffer. `buffer` is a `u8[]`
(Node's `Buffer`), a typed array or a `DataView`; a string is written as UTF-8, and its third
argument is then the position.
exports.summary: Writes `length` bytes of `buffer` from byte `offset` on (Node's `fs.writeSync`): at `position` in the file, or at the file's own position when `position` is left out, `null` or not a valid byte offset (at its end for a file opened to append).

struct params are passed as `const T*`; a struct result becomes a trailing out-pointer and the
runtime function returns nothing. Paths and data are borrowed by the runtime and copied at the
call, so the wrappers never copy.

modules.doc:
velt/fs (internal): reading and writing files in chunks (rt_abi_async.md §14.7), for files too
large to hold in memory or produced incrementally (logs, exports, line-by-line processing).

`openRead` gives a `FileReader` (bytes, text chunks or lines); `openWrite` a buffered
`FileWriter`. Operations run on the runtime's blocking pool like the rest of std/fs and
throw `IoError`. Like std/net's `TcpStream`, both are Copy handles (so `await r.readLine()`
can be called repeatedly; async methods take `this` by copy) released by `close()`: an
unclosed handle leaks until exit; after `close()` through any copy, the others throw
`IoError` `EBADF` and closing again does nothing. A writer's `close()` also flushes and
reports write errors.
modules.summary: velt/fs (internal): reading and writing files in chunks (rt_abi_async.md §14.7), for files too large to hold in memory or produced incrementally (logs, exports, line-by-line processing).

modules.doc:
velt/generate: source generators (docs/internals/design/source-generators.md). A library
declares `declare generated("./gen") function f<T>(…): R;`, and the module `./gen` exports a
function `f(req: InstanceRequest, out: Output): void` that writes the body of `f` for each concrete
instance the program uses. The compiler runs it at compile time, in a separate process, and
checks the code it writes with the program. A generator reads the types of its instance from
`req.model`, a read-only description of every type the instance reaches (`Type`, `Field`),
and writes Velt source to `out`.

modules.doc:
velt/hash: a stable, non-cryptographic hash (docs/std/hash.md) for sharding, bucketing and
consistent hashing. 64-bit FNV-1a: the same input gives the same hash on every platform, run
and version. It is not seeded, so it does not resist hash flooding (an attacker can choose
keys that collide); use `velt/crypto` where an adversary picks the input.

modules.doc:
velt/io (internal): WHATWG streams (https://streams.spec.whatwg.org) as in Node 22:
`ReadableStream` with its default controller and reader. They are globals (docs/std/io/streams.md).

A stream's state lives in its controller (`ReadableStreamDefaultController`): the queue of
chunks, the pending reads, and the flags of the spec's algorithms (`started`, `pulling`,
`pullAgain`, `closeRequested`). Nothing points back from the controller to the stream or a
reader, so a stream is freed with its last reference (Velt counts references; a cycle would
never be freed). The source's callbacks run in the spec's order: `start` in the constructor,
`pull` once `start` has settled (a microtask later) and again while the queue is below its
high-water mark or a read is waiting, never two at once; a read takes a queued chunk at once.
modules.summary: velt/io (internal): WHATWG streams (https://streams.spec.whatwg.org) as in Node 22: `ReadableStream` with its default controller and reader.

generic, so the component's own error type cannot travel through the tree: its value is
formatted like `${e}` into `message`, and `component` names the component
(`"<module path>#<Name>"`). Also thrown by `renderToStringSync` for a tree that still has a
pending async component (`component` is then "").

modules.doc:
velt/jsx (internal): HTML escaping of text and attributes (docs/internals/contracts/jsx.md
"Escaping").

Text and attribute values escape `&`, `<`, `>`, `"` and `'` as react-dom does: like std/html
`escapeHtml`, but `'` is `'` (`velt_rt_jsx_escape`, one pass in the runtime). The compiler
escapes static text and attributes of precompiled templates the same way, and leaves those with a
`'` to `jsxEscape`/`jsxAttr`, so both lowerings render the same bytes.

`<Card …/>`: std/jsx has no context to set up, so it calls the component at once. What the
component throws does not propagate from here: the node then fails when it is rendered, with
a `RenderError` naming the component, like an async component's rejection. `name`
(`"<module path>#<Name>"`) is for providers that emit hydration markers; std/jsx renders none.

exports.name: RenderError
exports.doc:
Thrown while rendering when a component threw or an async component rejected. Element is not
generic, so the component's own error type cannot travel through the tree: its value is
formatted like `${e}` into `message`, and `component` names the component
(`"<module path>#<Name>"`). Also thrown by `renderToStringSync` for a tree that still has a
pending async component (`component` is then "").
exports.summary: Thrown while rendering when a component threw or an async component rejected.

exports.signature: type Child = Element | Element[] | string | i64 | f64 | bool | null
exports.doc:
What may appear as a child: text is escaped, numbers render like `${n}`, `true`, `false` and
`null` render nothing, and an array renders its elements in order.
exports.summary: What may appear as a child: text is escaped, numbers render like `${n}`, `true`, `false` and `null` render nothing, and an array renders its elements in order.

exports.name: jsx
exports.signature: function jsx(tag: string, names: string[], values: AttrValue[], children: Child[], key: string | null): Element
exports.doc:
An intrinsic element `children`. `names` are compile-time attribute names; children of a void element (`
`) are dropped. `key` is not rendered.

exports.name: Fragment
exports.signature: function Fragment(children: Child[], key: string | null): Element
exports.doc: `<>children</>`: the children's markup, nothing around it.
exports.summary: `<>children</>`: the children's markup, nothing around it.

exports.name: jsxComponent
exports.signature: function jsxComponent<P, E>(component: (props: P) => Element throws E, props: P, key: string | null, name: string): Element
exports.doc:
`<Card …/>`: std/jsx has no context to set up, so it calls the component at once. What the
component throws does not propagate from here: the node then fails when it is rendered, with
a `RenderError` naming the component, like an async component's rejection. `name`
(`"<module path>#<Name>"`) is for providers that emit hydration markers; std/jsx renders none.
exports.summary: `<Card …/>`: std/jsx has no context to set up, so it calls the component at once.

exports.name: jsxAsyncComponent
exports.signature: function jsxAsyncComponent<P, E>(component: (props: P) => Promise<Element, E>, props: P, key: string | null, name: string): Element
exports.doc:
`<Posts …/>` for an async component: calls it now, so siblings load concurrently, and keeps
its promise in the node; rendering awaits it in document order, and a rejection surfaces then
as a `RenderError` naming the component.
exports.summary: `<Posts …/>` for an async component: calls it now, so siblings load concurrently, and keeps its promise in the node; rendering awaits it in document order, and a rejection surfaces then as a `RenderError` naming the component.

exports.signature: const jsxVoidElements = "area base br col embed hr img input link meta source track wbr"
exports.doc:
The provider export `jsxVoidElements` (docs/internals/contracts/jsx.md "Void elements"): the
compiler rejects children of these tags and writes them without an end tag in templates.
exports.summary: The provider export `jsxVoidElements` (docs/internals/contracts/jsx.md "Void elements"): the compiler rejects children of these tags and writes them without an end tag in templates.

modules.doc:
velt/jsx: server-side rendering of JSX to HTML (the default JSX provider,
docs/internals/contracts/jsx.md).

JSX in a module compiles to calls into std/jsx/jsx-runtime; this module is what programs import
to render the result: `renderToString`, `renderToStringSync`, `renderToStream` (a streamed
`Response` body), `raw` (unescaped markup), `Fragment`, and the `JSX` types. Internals:
node.velt (the Element), factory.velt (what compiled JSX calls), escape.velt, void_elements.velt,
render.velt, intrinsic*.velt (the HTML tags and attributes).
modules.summary: velt/jsx: server-side rendering of JSX to HTML (the default JSX provider, docs/internals/contracts/jsx.md).

exports.name: Element
exports.doc:
A rendered or partly rendered JSX node (see the module comment). Its fields are std/jsx's
internals (render.velt and factory.velt use them): read the markup with `renderToString`, as a
template node keeps it in `tree` and its `html` is "".
exports.summary: A rendered or partly rendered JSX node (see the module comment).

members.name: html
members.doc: Markup rendered so far: everything when `rest` is null. Unused ("") in a template node.
members.summary: Markup rendered so far: everything when `rest` is null.

members.name: tree
members.doc: A template node's strings and child nodes (null for a node of one string, almost all).
members.summary: A template node's strings and child nodes (null for a node of one string, almost all).

members.name: rest
members.doc: What follows `html` when the node contains an async component or a component that threw.
members.summary: What follows `html` when the node contains an async component or a component that threw.

members.name: isComplete
members.doc:
True when the node is rendered completely (no async or failed component inside): its
markup is `html`, or `tree` in a template node.
members.summary: True when the node is rendered completely (no async or failed component inside): its markup is `html`, or `tree` in a template node.

exports.name: raw
exports.doc:
`html` inserted as it is, without escaping: the only way to emit markup from a string. Never
pass it text from users.
exports.summary: `html` inserted as it is, without escaping: the only way to emit markup from a string.

exports.name: renderToString
exports.signature: async function renderToString(el: Element): Promise<string> throws RenderError
exports.doc:
The HTML of `el`, after awaiting its async components. Throws the `RenderError` of the
first (in document order) component that threw or rejected.
exports.summary: The HTML of `el`, after awaiting its async components.

exports.name: renderToStringSync
exports.signature: function renderToStringSync(el: Element): string throws RenderError
exports.doc:
The HTML of `el` when it has no async component (no await needed). Throws the `RenderError`
of the first component that threw, or one saying the tree has an async component.
exports.summary: The HTML of `el` when it has no async component (no await needed).

exports.name: renderToStream
exports.doc:
The HTML of `el` as a streamed `Response` body (like React's `renderToReadableStream`):
`new Response(renderToStream(el), ...)`. The markup above each pending async component is sent
before the component is awaited, so it reaches the client while the component loads. Once
the client has gone away, rendering stops. A component that throws cuts the response off (its
`RenderError` is printed to stderr).
exports.summary: The HTML of `el` as a streamed `Response` body (like React's `renderToReadableStream`): `new Response(renderToStream(el), ...)`.

modules.doc:
velt/jsx (internal): the JSX types of std/jsx (docs/internals/contracts/jsx.md): which lower-case
tags exist and which attributes each accepts (attribute types: std/jsx/attrs/*.velt). A tag or
attribute that is not listed is a compile error, so typos are caught; custom elements
(`<my-widget>`, `<annotation-xml>`) and hyphenated attributes (`data-*`, `aria-*`,
`stroke-width`) are not checked. There are no event handler attributes: std/jsx renders HTML
on the server.
modules.summary: velt/jsx (internal): the JSX types of std/jsx (docs/internals/contracts/jsx.md): which lower-case tags exist and which attributes each accepts (attribute types: std/jsx/attrs/*.velt).

modules.doc:
velt/jsx (internal): the value every JSX expression evaluates to (internal; std/jsx and
std/jsx/jsx-runtime export it).

std/jsx renders eagerly: building an element renders it, so a tree without async components
is its markup by the time it is complete. Text and attributes are escaped as they arrive. A
complete node is either one string (`html`), or the strings and child nodes of a template
(`tree`: `strings[0] slots[0] strings[1] … strings[n]`): a template, fragment or element keeps the
arrays its children came in, as JSX moves them there, instead of copying their markup. The
markup is copied once, when the tree is rendered into one string or written into a response
(`markupOf`, `writeMarkup`).

Only an async component cannot be rendered up front: its node holds the component's started
promise, and every node above it keeps its finished markup in `html` plus the rest, in order,
in `rest.parts` (a component that threw is kept the same way, as a node that fails when
rendered). The renderer (render.velt) writes `html`, then awaits `rest.pending`, then renders
`rest.parts`, so markup before a pending component can be sent while it still loads.
modules.summary: velt/jsx (internal): the value every JSX expression evaluates to (internal; std/jsx and std/jsx/jsx-runtime export it).

modules.doc:
velt/jsx (internal): turns an Element into HTML, as one string or as a streamed response body.

A complete element already is its HTML, as a string or a tree of template strings (node.velt)
joined or written once. Otherwise the renderer walks the node's
pieces in document order with an explicit stack (no async recursion): `html`, then the
awaited async component, then the other parts. Every async component started when its node was
created, so awaiting them one after the other still lets them load concurrently.
modules.summary: velt/jsx (internal): turns an Element into HTML, as one string or as a streamed response body.

exports.name: renderToString
exports.signature: async function renderToString(el: Element): Promise<string> throws RenderError
exports.doc:
The HTML of `el`, after awaiting its async components. Throws the `RenderError` of the
first (in document order) component that threw or rejected.
exports.summary: The HTML of `el`, after awaiting its async components.

exports.name: renderToStringSync
exports.signature: function renderToStringSync(el: Element): string throws RenderError
exports.doc:
The HTML of `el` when it has no async component (no await needed). Throws the `RenderError`
of the first component that threw, or one saying the tree has an async component.
exports.summary: The HTML of `el` when it has no async component (no await needed).

exports.name: renderToStream
exports.doc:
The HTML of `el` as a streamed `Response` body (like React's `renderToReadableStream`):
`new Response(renderToStream(el), ...)`. The markup above each pending async component is sent
before the component is awaited, so it reaches the client while the component loads. Once
the client has gone away, rendering stops. A component that throws cuts the response off (its
`RenderError` is printed to stderr).
exports.summary: The HTML of `el` as a streamed `Response` body (like React's `renderToReadableStream`): `new Response(renderToStream(el), ...)`.

velt/jsx (internal): the `style` attribute's object form (`style={{ color: c, fontSize: 12 }}`),
rendered with React's rules, so the value is react-dom 19's: `color:red;font-size:12px`.
Names are camelCase CSS properties written in kebab-case (`msTransition` is
`-ms-transition`; custom properties such as `--accent` stay as written), numbers get `px`
unless the property takes plain numbers (`lineHeight`, `opacity`, `zIndex`, …) or the number
is 0, strings are trimmed, and empty strings are left out.

velt/lang/bytes (internal): searching and XOR-masking byte arrays sixteen bytes at a time with
SIMD vectors (std/prelude/bytes.velt): here in Velt so that they are compiled into their
caller; long searches by memchr in the runtime.
modules.summary: velt/lang/bytes (internal): searching and XOR-masking byte arrays sixteen bytes at a time with SIMD vectors (std/prelude/bytes.velt): here in Velt so that they are compiled into their caller; long searches by memchr in the runtime.

exports.name: xorMaskRange
exports.signature: function xorMaskRange(d: u8[], mask: u32, start: usize, stop: usize)
exports.doc:
XORs `d[start..stop]` with the four bytes of `mask` (most significant first), repeating from
`start`. 128 bytes per step, then 64, then sixteen; the last bytes are done by a vector ending
at `stop`, which overlaps bytes already masked: it masks only its lanes past them, with the
mask's bytes rotated to where that vector starts.
exports.summary: XORs `d[start..stop]` with the four bytes of `mask` (most significant first), repeating from `start`.

exports.name: indexOfByte
exports.signature: function indexOfByte(d: u8[], byte: u8, start: usize): i64
exports.doc:
First position at or after `start` holding `byte`, or -1. Up to `SHORT_SEARCH` bytes here:
one vector first (most searches end within a few bytes), then four per step with one test
for all of them, and the last bytes in a vector ending at the array's end, which may overlap
bytes already seen (none of them matched, so its first match is past them). Longer searches
in the runtime.
exports.summary: First position at or after `start` holding `byte`, or -1.

modules.doc:
velt/lang/equal/generate: the generator of `equalByContent<T>` and `equalByFields<T>`
(velt/lang/equal/generated), run at compile time (docs/internals/design/source-generators.md):
one function per type that tells whether two values are deeply equal, as `deepEqual` (Node's
`util.isDeepStrictEqual`) and `toEqual` (Vitest's) compare them. It uses nothing a package
could not: the model of `velt/generate`, `__arm` for a union's members, and in the code it
writes `===`, `Object.is`, velt/reflect and the helpers of generated.velt.

What it compares: numbers (SameValueZero; `toEqual`: `Object.is`), booleans, strings, enums
and literal types by value; arrays, tuples, options, object values and structs by content;
a union by its active member (two number members by their numbers, exactly); `Map` and
`Record` by their entries in any order (`Map`'s private `deepEquals`, with the access of the
collection's type); a `JsonValue` by its JSON content (an object's members in any order);
class instances, `Set`, `Date`, `shared` cells, interface, function and promise values by
identity. An optional field left out differs from one set to `undefined`. `toEqual` compares class instances by the fields of their own
class (an `instanceof` chain, most derived first: objects of two classes differ), a `Set` by
its members, a `Date` by its time, and an interface value or a std type whose state is
private by what its dynamic type lists (`equalDynamic`). A type whose values can hold
themselves is compared under the cycle guard (`beginPair`): the same pair met again is equal,
an object met again with another partner is not.
modules.summary: velt/lang/equal/generate: the generator of `equalByContent<T>` and `equalByFields<T>` (velt/lang/equal/generated), run at compile time (docs/internals/design/source-generators.md): one function per type that tells whether two values are deeply equal, as `deepEqual` (Node's `util.isDeepStrictEqual`) and `toEqual` (Vitest's) compare them.

exports.summary: The generator of `equalByContent<T>(a: T, b: T): bool` (`deepEqual`, `assertEq`).

modules.doc:
velt/lang/equal (internal): structural equality, generated per type at compile time by
velt/lang/equal/generate (docs/internals/design/source-generators.md). `equalByContent<T>` is
what `deepEqual` and `assertEq` compare (Node's `util.isDeepStrictEqual`), `equalByFields<T>`
what `velt test`'s `toEqual` compares (Vitest's). The code generated for them calls the
functions declared here. The helpers read identities and dynamic values with the intrinsics
velt/reflect is written on (the prelude loads this module, and velt/reflect only on use).

The operators of the language stay the compiler's: `===`, `Object.is`, and the `Map` key
comparison (`keyEq`, SameValueZero), which the helpers below use on values whose structure no
generator sees (`any`).
modules.summary: velt/lang/equal (internal): structural equality, generated per type at compile time by velt/lang/equal/generate (docs/internals/design/source-generators.md).

exports.name: equalByContent
exports.signature: function equalByContent<T>(a: T, b: T): bool
exports.doc:
Deep equality as `deepEqual` and `assertEq` compare: arrays, tuples, structs and object values
by content, `Map` and `Record` by their entries in any order, class instances, interface and
function values by identity, numbers with SameValueZero (`NaN` equals itself, `0` equals
`-0`). Values that hold themselves stop at a cycle, as in Node (one function per type,
generated).
exports.summary: Deep equality as `deepEqual` and `assertEq` compare: arrays, tuples, structs and object values by content, `Map` and `Record` by their entries in any order, class instances, interface and function values by identity, numbers with SameValueZero (`NaN` equals itself, `0` equals `-0`).

exports.name: equalByFields
exports.signature: function equalByFields<T>(a: T, b: T): bool
exports.doc:
Vitest's `toEqual`: as `equalByContent`, but class instances (a `Date`, a `Set`, a value held
as an interface or a base class) by the fields of their own class, and numbers with
`Object.is` (`0` doesn't equal `-0`).
exports.summary: Vitest's `toEqual`: as `equalByContent`, but class instances (a `Date`, a `Set`, a value held as an interface or a base class) by the fields of their own class, and numbers with `Object.is` (`0` doesn't equal `-0`).

modules.doc:
velt/lang/hooks (internal): the containers of interface adapters (issue #1153;
docs/reference/types.md "Generic interfaces with `unknown` arguments"; velt_sema
`body/expr/iface_adapt.rs`).

A `Handler<Map<unknown, unknown>, E>` converted to `Handler<unknown, unknown>` receives an
`unknown` that may hold a map of any type (`Map<string, number>`), whose elements are stored
unboxed. The adapter passes the method a copy holding the elements boxed (`…In`), and when the
method returns writes the copy back into the map it was made from (`…Out`), so the caller's
map sees every change. Each element written back converts to the map's own element types,
checked as a conversion out of `any` is. The hooks for `Set<unknown>` are in any_set.velt,
which a program naming `Set` loads.

Its bodies use dynamic operations without making the program pay for them: sema counts a
program as using `any` members only when it converts such a value.
modules.summary: velt/lang/hooks (internal): the containers of interface adapters (issue #1153; docs/reference/types.md "Generic interfaces with `unknown` arguments"; velt_sema `body/expr/iface_adapt.rs`).

`anyNum_<name>(n, args)` and for a boolean `anyBool_<name>(b, args)` (velt_vir

JavaScript converts them (`ToString`, `ToIntegerOrInfinity`); the result goes back as an

any_array_methods.velt.
