exports.name: anyPrimitive
exports.signature: function anyPrimitive(v: any, hint: string, at: string): any
exports.doc:
JavaScript's `ToPrimitive(v, hint)` of an `any` holding an object or a function (`hint` is
`"string"`, `"default"` or `"number"`; a primitive is its own, which the callers keep, so
this only borrows `v`): an object's `[Symbol.toPrimitive](hint)`, else its
`valueOf()` and `toString()` (`toString()` first for `"string"`), the first primitive one
returns kept as it is (a number stays a number). A `Date` takes `"default"` as `"string"`. Sema
writes the dispatch over the program's classes into this body (any_prim.rs); other values go
to `anyPrimitivePlain`.
exports.summary: JavaScript's `ToPrimitive(v, hint)` of an `any` holding an object or a function (`hint` is `"string"`, `"default"` or `"number"`; a primitive is its own, which the callers keep, so this only borrows `v`): an object's `[Symbol.toPrimitive](hint)`, else its `valueOf()` and `toString()` (`toString()` first for `"string"`), the first primitive one returns kept as it is (a number stays a number).

exports.name: anyPrimitivePlain
exports.signature: function anyPrimitivePlain(v: any, hint: string, at: string): any
exports.doc:
`ToPrimitive(v, hint)` of an object that is no class instance with a `[Symbol.toPrimitive]`,
`valueOf()` or `toString()`: an array as its `join`, an object literal by its own `valueOf` /
`toString` in the hint's order, another object as `Object.prototype.toString` writes it. A
function's `ToPrimitive` is its source text, which a compiled function doesn't keep: `NaN`
stands for it where only its number counts (`"number"`, and `==`, which `"default"` is for
here, because the text is never a number or a boolean).

modules.doc:
velt/lang/hooks (internal): array views (#1485; velt_vir lower/array_view.rs). An `any`
holding an array of another element type, converted to `T[]` (`kids as JSXChild[]`, or a cast
`xs as T[]` of an existing array, which sema writes through `any`), is a view of that one
array, as in Node: the `T[]` value's header points at an `ArrayView<T>`, which holds the
original array as an `any` and a mirror of its elements converted to `T`. Lowering brings the
mirror up to date before each access to the view's contents (`arrayViewSync`) and writes it
back after each change through the view (`arrayViewFlush`), so reads see the original's
current elements and writes reach the original. Most accesses need only part of the mirror:
`length` is the original's, a read of element `i` (an index, a `for...of` step, a callback
method's step) brings only that element up to date (`arrayViewSyncAt`), and a write of
element `i` writes back only that element (`arrayViewFlushAt`). The mirror converts the
original's elements in order, up to the last one a read reaches, so the elements after it are
never converted. Nothing here is called in a program without views.
modules.summary: velt/lang/hooks (internal): array views (#1485; velt_vir lower/array_view.rs).

exports.name: ArrayView
exports.doc: The state of one view: the original array and the mirror of its elements as `T`.
exports.summary: The state of one view: the original array and the mirror of its elements as `T`.

exports.name: arrayViewNew
exports.doc: A view of the array `target` holds (moved in) as a `T[]`.
exports.summary: A view of the array `target` holds (moved in) as a `T[]`.

exports.name: arrayViewSync
exports.doc:
The mirror brought up to date with the original: an element that is still the original's
(`===` through `any`) is kept, so a borrow of it stays valid; any other is the original's
element converted again (a `TypeError` when it is not a `T`). The mirror has the original's
length afterwards.
exports.summary: The mirror brought up to date with the original: an element that is still the original's (`===` through `any`) is kept, so a borrow of it stays valid; any other is the original's element converted again (a `TypeError` when it is not a `T`).

exports.name: arrayViewFlush
exports.doc:
The mirror written back to the original after a change through the view: each element that
is not the original's (`===` through `any`) is stored into it, converted to the original's
element type (a `TypeError` when it cannot hold it), and a shorter mirror shortens it.

original's current one.

exports.name: arrayViewSort
exports.signature: function arrayViewSort<T, C>(v: ArrayView<T>, cmp: (x: T, y: T) => C, neg: (c: C) => bool)
exports.doc:
`sort(cmp)` of a view (`less(a, b)`: `cmp(a, b) < 0`): a copy of the mirror, brought up to
date, sorted by the stable sort, becomes the mirror and is written back. The comparator may
read the view meanwhile: it sees the unsorted elements, as the stable sort's own buffer
gives no other view of them either.
exports.summary: `sort(cmp)` of a view (`less(a, b)`: `cmp(a, b) < 0`): a copy of the mirror, brought up to date, sorted by the stable sort, becomes the mirror and is written back.

modules.doc:
velt/lang/hooks (internal): the compiler's hooks for numbers (std-layout.md §10b): a number's
`toString(radix)` and the conversions a float index or an int32 product compiles to. Nothing
imports these; the compiler calls them (velt_common `std_hooks.rs`).
modules.summary: velt/lang/hooks (internal): the compiler's hooks for numbers (std-layout.md §10b): a number's `toString(radix)` and the conversions a float index or an int32 product compiles to.

exports.name: f64ToString
exports.signature: function f64ToString(x: f64, radix: f64): string
exports.doc:
`x.toString(radix)` on a float: the compiler compiles a `toString` call with an argument to
it. Digits as in JS (V8): `(255).toString(16)` is "ff", `(0.5).toString(2)` is "0.1",
fractions are written until they tell `x` apart from its neighbours. `NaN` and ±Infinity are
`String(x)`; a radix outside 2 to 36 is a RangeError.
exports.summary: `x.toString(radix)` on a float: the compiler compiles a `toString` call with an argument to it.

exports.name: i64ToString
exports.signature: function i64ToString(x: i64, radix: f64): string
exports.doc: `x.toString(radix)` on a signed integer, exact over the whole `i64` range.
exports.summary: `x.toString(radix)` on a signed integer, exact over the whole `i64` range.

exports.name: u64ToString
exports.signature: function u64ToString(x: u64, radix: f64): string
exports.doc: `x.toString(radix)` on an unsigned integer.
exports.summary: `x.toString(radix)` on an unsigned integer.

exports.name: mulToInt32
exports.signature: function mulToInt32(a: f64, b: f64): i32
exports.doc:
ToInt32 of the product `a * b` of two JS numbers (`(y * k) | 0`; sema `int32.rs` inserts the
call). JS multiplies doubles, so a product past 2^53 is rounded before its low 32 bits are
taken. For int32 operands that is `velt_rt_math_mul_int32` (one multiply when `numrep` proves
the product within 2^53); other values multiply as doubles.
exports.summary: ToInt32 of the product `a * b` of two JS numbers (`(y * k) | 0`; sema `int32.rs` inserts the call).

exports.name: floatIndex
exports.doc:
`xs[i]` with a float `i` (a JS number; the compiler inserts the call, `sema` `numbers.rs`): a
whole number indexes as usual. Anything else would read `undefined` in JS; here it panics like
an index out of bounds.
exports.summary: `xs[i]` with a float `i` (a JS number; the compiler inserts the call, `sema` `numbers.rs`): a whole number indexes as usual.

exports.name: floatPosition
exports.doc:
A `number` given as a position or lane index of a SIMD method (the compiler inserts the call,
`sema` `numbers.rs`): a whole number from 0 up as itself. Anything else is the largest `usize`,
which is out of range everywhere, so `fits` gives `false` and the others a `RangeError`.
exports.summary: A `number` given as a position or lane index of a SIMD method (the compiler inserts the call, `sema` `numbers.rs`): a whole number from 0 up as itself.

exports.name: topLevelAwaitAt

Compiler-internal: marks the top-level `await`s after it as at `site` (`path:line:col`, a

modules.doc:
velt/lang/hooks (internal): the operations on `any` that a proxy answers with its traps, which
sema calls in a program that has loaded `Proxy` (std/prelude/global/proxy.velt) instead of the
hooks of any_object.velt: a spread, `Object.hasOwn`, `Object.values` / `entries` and
`delete` of an `any`; the operations whose key is a symbol constant (`p[KEY]`, `KEY in p`,
`delete p[KEY]`, `Object.hasOwn(p, KEY)`); and `new Proxy(target, handler)` with a handler typed
`any` (issue #823; docs/reference/types.md "Proxy and Reflect").

A symbol constant names a member of a typed value by its key name (U+FFFF and `Symbol(d)`,
velt_sema's `symbols.rs`); sema passes both that name and the symbol itself, so a plain value
is read by the name, as before, and a proxy's trap sees the symbol, as in JavaScript.
modules.summary: velt/lang/hooks (internal): the operations on `any` that a proxy answers with its traps, which sema calls in a program that has loaded `Proxy` (std/prelude/global/proxy.velt) instead of the hooks of any_object.velt: a spread, `Object.hasOwn`, `Object.values` / `entries` and `delete` of an `any`; the operations whose key is a symbol constant (`p[KEY]`, `KEY in p`, `delete p[KEY]`, `Object.hasOwn(p, KEY)`); and `new Proxy(target, handler)` with a handler typed `any` (issue #823; docs/reference/types.md "Proxy and Reflect").

modules.doc:
velt/lang/intrinsics (internal): arrays below their public methods: capacity, raw moves and
bounds-checked rearranging that never clones or drops an element. The public surface is
`Array`'s methods (std/prelude/array.velt): `reserve`, `truncate`, `swap`, `rotateLeft` …

exports.name: arrayWithCapacity
exports.signature: declare intrinsic function arrayWithCapacity<T>(capacity: usize): T[]
exports.doc: A new empty array with room for `capacity` elements (one allocation).
exports.summary: A new empty array with room for `capacity` elements (one allocation).

exports.name: arrayTruncate
exports.signature: declare intrinsic function arrayTruncate<T>(xs: Mut<T[]>, length: usize): void
exports.doc: Drops the elements from `length` on (nothing when the array is not longer).
exports.summary: Drops the elements from `length` on (nothing when the array is not longer).

exports.name: arraySetLen
exports.signature: declare intrinsic function arraySetLen<T>(xs: Mut<T[]>, length: usize): void
exports.doc:
Sets the length to `length` (growing the capacity when it is smaller) without dropping or
initializing any element: slots past the old length must be written (`arrayMove`) before they
are read, and slots that are not owned any more must be cut off with it before the array is
dropped.
exports.summary: Sets the length to `length` (growing the capacity when it is smaller) without dropping or initializing any element: slots past the old length must be written (`arrayMove`) before they are read, and slots that are not owned any more must be cut off with it before the array is dropped.

exports.name: arrayReserve
exports.signature: declare intrinsic function arrayReserve<T>(xs: Mut<T[]>, extra: usize): void
exports.doc:
Makes room for `extra` more elements: when the capacity is under `length + extra`, the buffer
is reallocated to exactly that (no doubling); the length and the elements stay.
exports.summary: Makes room for `extra` more elements: when the capacity is under `length + extra`, the buffer is reallocated to exactly that (no doubling); the length and the elements stay.

exports.name: arraySwap
exports.signature: declare intrinsic function arraySwap<T>(xs: Mut<T[]>, i: usize, j: usize): void
exports.doc: Exchanges elements `i` and `j` (both bounds-checked): their bits, nothing cloned.
exports.summary: Exchanges elements `i` and `j` (both bounds-checked): their bits, nothing cloned.

exports.name: arraySwapNested
exports.signature: declare intrinsic function arraySwapNested<T>(xs: Mut<T[][]>, a: usize, i: usize, b: usize, j: usize): void
exports.doc:
Exchanges `xs[a][i]` and `xs[b][j]` (all four bounds-checked): the bits of two elements, also
between two inner arrays, which one call may not otherwise change both of.
exports.summary: Exchanges `xs[a][i]` and `xs[b][j]` (all four bounds-checked): the bits of two elements, also between two inner arrays, which one call may not otherwise change both of.

exports.name: arrayRemove
exports.signature: declare intrinsic function arrayRemove<T>(xs: Mut<T[]>, i: usize): T
exports.doc: Removes element `i` (bounds-checked) and returns it; the elements after it move down.
exports.summary: Removes element `i` (bounds-checked) and returns it; the elements after it move down.

exports.name: arrayRotateRight
exports.signature: declare intrinsic function arrayRotateRight<T>(xs: Mut<T[]>, lo: usize, hi: usize): void
exports.doc:

exports.name: arrayRotateLeft

exports.doc: As `arrayRotateRight`, one slot down: the element at `lo` moves to `hi`.
exports.summary: As `arrayRotateRight`, one slot down: the element at `lo` moves to `hi`.

exports.name: arrayPrefetch
exports.signature: declare intrinsic function arrayPrefetch<T>(xs: T[], i: usize): void
exports.doc:

bounds-checked: a prefetch never faults, and an index past the end only wastes the load.
exports.summary: A hint that element `i` is read soon, so the CPU starts loading its cache line.

exports.name: arrayMove
exports.signature: declare intrinsic function arrayMove<T>(dst: Mut<T[]>, d: usize, src: T[], s: usize, n: usize): void

themselves (the stable sort's scratch buffer, std/lang/sort/stable.velt).

ordering the call of the `Atomic` method names, after checking that the operation may have it.

box); nothing else reads or writes one.

exports.name: hash
exports.signature: declare intrinsic function hash<T>(value: T): u64
exports.doc:
A hash agreeing with `keyEq` (`Map` and `Set` keys): numbers, bool and strings by value,
objects by identity, unions, options and tuples part by part.

exports.doc:
JavaScript's SameValueZero, the `Map` and `Set` key comparison: `===` with floats compared so
that `NaN` equals itself and `0` equals `-0`. Objects compare by identity, as `hash` hashes
them.

modules.summary: velt/lang/intrinsics (internal): stepping generators, below the methods of the prelude's `Generator` and `AsyncGenerator` (std/prelude/iter.velt; docs/internals/contracts/hir_encodings.md "Generators" and "Async generators").

exports.name: generatorResume
exports.signature: declare intrinsic function generatorResume<T, E, N>(g: Mut<Generator<T, E, N>>): bool
exports.doc:
Runs the generator to its next `yield` (true: a value is in its slot) or to its end (false;
also every later call). An error the body throws (an `E`) is thrown here.
exports.summary: Runs the generator to its next `yield` (true: a value is in its slot) or to its end (false; also every later call).

exports.name: generatorResumeWith
exports.signature: declare intrinsic function generatorResumeWith<T, E, N>(g: Mut<Generator<T, E, N>>, value: N): bool
exports.doc:
`next(value)`: like `generatorResume`, and the paused `yield` evaluates to (a copy of)
`value`; a generator that has not started ignores it.
exports.summary: `next(value)`: like `generatorResume`, and the paused `yield` evaluates to (a copy of) `value`; a generator that has not started ignores it.

exports.name: generatorThrow
exports.signature: declare intrinsic function generatorThrow<T, E, N>(g: Mut<Generator<T, E, N>>, error: any): u32
exports.doc:
`throw(error)`: resumes the body with `error` thrown at the paused `yield`. 1: the body caught
it and yielded again (the value is in the slot); 0: it caught it and finished; 3: nothing caught
it (the generator is closed, as by `return()`, or it had not started or was finished), and the
caller throws it. An error the body throws (after catching) is thrown here.
exports.summary: `throw(error)`: resumes the body with `error` thrown at the paused `yield`.

exports.name: generatorValue
exports.signature: declare intrinsic function generatorValue<T, E, N>(g: Mut<Generator<T, E, N>>): T
exports.doc:
Moves the value of the last `yield` out of the slot (once, after `generatorResume` returned
true).
exports.summary: Moves the value of the last `yield` out of the slot (once, after `generatorResume` returned true).

exports.name: generatorReturn
exports.signature: declare intrinsic function generatorReturn<T, E, N>(g: Mut<Generator<T, E, N>>): void
exports.doc:
Closes the generator: a suspended body runs its `finally` blocks and disposes its `using`
values as if the `yield` were a `return`; then it is done.
exports.summary: Closes the generator: a suspended body runs its `finally` blocks and disposes its `using` values as if the `yield` were a `return`; then it is done.

exports.name: asyncGeneratorResume
exports.signature: declare intrinsic function asyncGeneratorResume<T, E>(g: Mut<AsyncGenerator<T, E>>): Promise<bool, E>
exports.doc:
Runs the async generator to its next `yield` (true) or its end (false; also every later call),
suspending the awaiting function while the generator awaits; only as the operand of `await`.
An error the body throws rejects it.
exports.summary: Runs the async generator to its next `yield` (true) or its end (false; also every later call), suspending the awaiting function while the generator awaits; only as the operand of `await`.

exports.name: asyncGeneratorValue
exports.signature: declare intrinsic function asyncGeneratorValue<T, E>(g: Mut<AsyncGenerator<T, E>>): T
exports.doc: Like `generatorValue`.
exports.summary: Like `generatorValue`.

exports.name: asyncGeneratorReturn
exports.signature: declare intrinsic function asyncGeneratorReturn<T, E>(g: Mut<AsyncGenerator<T, E>>): Promise<void, never>
exports.summary: Closes the async generator, only as the operand of `await`: a body suspended at a `yield` runs its `finally` blocks and disposals (which may `await`) as if the `yield` were a `return`; one suspended at an `await` is cancelled.

exports.name: asyncGeneratorDispose
exports.signature: declare intrinsic function asyncGeneratorDispose<T, E>(g: Mut<AsyncGenerator<T, E>>): void
exports.doc:
Closes the async generator without awaiting (its drop): like `asyncGeneratorReturn`, except
that a body whose cleanup at that `yield` would `await` is cancelled instead.
exports.summary: Closes the async generator without awaiting (its drop): like `asyncGeneratorReturn`, except that a body whose cleanup at that `yield` would `await` is cancelled instead.

modules.doc:
velt/lang/intrinsics: the compiler's intrinsics, declared (docs/internals/design/std-layout.md
§10): operations the compiler emits inline, such as a bounds-checked swap, a byte of a string
or a per-type equality, which no Velt code can express. Each file of this folder declares an
area's with `export declare intrinsic function`; the declaration is the signature calls are
checked against (modes.velt says how arguments are passed), and the compiler's table
(`crates/velt_sema/src/body/expr/intrinsics.rs`) maps each name to the operation, a test
checking that the two name the same set. std code imports them like any function; programs
and packages cannot (`velt/lang` is internal), so they use the public APIs instead.

modules.doc:
velt/lang/intrinsics (internal): how an intrinsic takes each argument. Velt infers a
function's parameter modes from its body; an intrinsic has none, so its declaration says it:
a parameter of a number, `bool` or `symbol` type is copied, any other is borrowed (read where
it is, for the call only), and one of these wrappers says otherwise. Each is its type
argument itself, so TypeScript and every tool read the declaration as the plain type; the
compiler reads the wrapper only on a `declare intrinsic function`'s parameter.

modules.doc:
velt/lang/map (internal): the layout of the prelude's `Map` (std/prelude/map.velt): its
constants (table sizes, the hash multiplier, the position mask and the null-prototype mark), and
how the map is laid out:

Layout (like CPython's dict / indexmap):
- Entries live in two dense parallel arrays (`entryKeys`, `entryValues`) in insertion order,
  so iteration is a linear scan and order matches JS. A deleted entry's value is dropped at
  once (set to null); its key stays as a tombstone until the next compaction. (One array of
  `{ key, value }` entries measured ~20% slower on k-nucleotide: probing reads only keys, and
  they pack densest on their own. Values stay `V | null` so a delete drops the value at once.)
- A null value marks a deleted entry only where `V` excludes null. When `V` includes null
  (`Map<string, number | null>`, a `Record<string, T | null>`), `V | null` is `V` and a live
  entry may hold null too: such an entry is live when the map has no tombstones (`dead == 0`,
  the common case) or a slot of the index points at it (a delete removes the entry's slot at
  once, its key stays). `holdsNull` is a constant per instantiation, so maps
  whose `V` excludes null keep this layout and code unchanged (no extra field, no per-entry
  flag). Maps whose `V` includes null pay only while they have tombstones: `keys()`,
  `values()`, `entries()`, `compact` and the other bulk readers then mark the live positions
  from the slot words in one pass (`liveBits`), and `forEach`, `for...of` and the formatting
  and JSON glue probe the index for each null-valued entry, deleted ones included (`liveNull`).
- `slots` is an open-addressing index (power-of-two capacity) of packed `u64` words:
  the top 32 bits of the entry's scrambled hash `p = hash * 2^64/phi` (Fibonacci hashing,
  which spreads even weak hashes such as sequential integers), and in the low 32 bits the
  entry position + 1 (0 = empty slot). The home slot of `p` is its top bits, so the stored
  tag also gives every slot's home: probing rejects most non-matching slots without loading
  the key, and growing or deleting never rehashes keys.
- Collisions use Robin Hood linear probing: every probe cluster is kept sorted by home slot,
  so a lookup stops at the first slot whose resident is closer to its own home than the key
  would be (misses are short even at high load), inserts shift the rest of the cluster one
  slot right, and deletes shift it back (no tombstones in the index). The index grows at 3/4
  load (as fast as plain linear probing grown at 5/8 in bench/hashmap.velt, with half the
  index memory at some sizes; bench/RESULTS.md).

Ownership: `set` takes ownership of the key and value. `get` returns the stored value like JS
(an object is shared — another reference to it — and numbers or strings are copied); `upsert`
/ `update` change a value in place. `keys()`, `values()` and `entries()` return the stored
keys and values the same way; `forEach` borrows. A map holds at most 2^31 entries.

Live iteration (JS order: entries added while a loop runs are visited, deleted ones are not):
`forEach` and `for...of` over a map (or its `keys()`, `values()`, `entries()`, through a
`MapCursor`) walk the entry positions. A compaction, the pop of the newest entry and clearing
renumber positions; they alone bump `renumbers`, and a loop that sees it changed finds its
place again by *sequence number*: every entry has one, increasing in insertion order and never
reused. The sequence number of the entry at position `p` is `p + off`, with `off` from the
last breakpoint at or before `p` in (`seqPos`, `seqOff`); a map that never renumbered has no
breakpoints (`off` is 0). Renumbering rebuilds the breakpoints (at most one per run of
removed entries), so set, get and append never touch them.

exports.signature: type Settlement<T, E> = { status: "pending" } | { status: "abandoned" } | { status: "fulfilled"; value: T } | { status: "rejected"; reason: E }

exports.doc:
The state `resolve`, `reject` and the waiting promise share: the outcome (at most one element:
an array, so the promise can move it out with `pop()`), and the runtime latch that wakes the
promise once it is settled.
exports.summary: The state `resolve`, `reject` and the waiting promise share: the outcome (at most one element: an array, so the promise can move it out with `pop()`), and the runtime latch that wakes the promise once it is settled.

members.doc:
The first settlement wins; later calls of `resolve` or `reject` are ignored, like JS.
Returns the latch to open once the lock is released (0: already settled).
members.summary: The first settlement wins; later calls of `resolve` or `reject` are ignored, like JS.

members.doc: The settlement, moved out (`pending` if there is none).

exports.name: Settlers
exports.signature: type Settlers<T, E> = { resolve: (value: T) => void; reject: (reason: E) => void }
exports.doc:
A promise's `resolve` and `reject`: heap closures over its slot, so they may be stored,
returned and moved to other tasks; both hold the guard. A value settled on the promise's own
task is shared with the awaiter, like JS. One settled from another task crosses threads, so it
is transferred like a `spawn` argument (moved if nothing else references it, copied if it is
still shared): after the settling statement has finished with it (`fulfillLater`), so a value
made just for the call moves (#263). A value that cannot reach a counted object (a number, a
string) has nothing to transfer and settles at once, so the reply costs no extra step.
exports.summary: A promise's `resolve` and `reject`: heap closures over its slot, so they may be stored, returned and moved to other tasks; both hold the guard.

exports.signature: function settlers<T, E>(slot: shared<Mutex<PromiseSlot<T, E>>>): Settlers<T, E>

exports.name: runExecutor
exports.signature: function runExecutor<T, E>(executor: (resolve: (value: T) => void, reject: (reason: E) => void) => void throws E, slot: shared<Mutex<PromiseSlot<T, E>>>)
exports.doc:
Run the executor with its `resolve` and `reject`. A function of its own, so that once it
returns only what the executor kept still references the guard.
exports.summary: Run the executor with its `resolve` and `reject`.

exports.name: takeSettlement
exports.signature: function takeSettlement<T, E>(slot: shared<Mutex<PromiseSlot<T, E>>>): Settlement<T, E>
exports.doc:
The slot's settlement, moved out. A plain value comes out as `with`'s result. One that
reaches an object is taken out through `taken` instead: `with`'s result is transferred as it
leaves the lock (a copy where it is still shared), but a value settled on this promise's own
task is the awaiter's same object (JS identity), and one settled from another task was
transferred when it was settled.
exports.summary: The slot's settlement, moved out.

exports.signature: async function settlement<T, E>(slot: shared<Mutex<PromiseSlot<T, E>>>): Promise<T> throws E
exports.doc: Waits for the slot to be settled (holding only the slot, not the executor).
exports.summary: Waits for the slot to be settled (holding only the slot, not the executor).

velt/lang/proxy (internal): the array methods called on a proxy of an array (`push`, `pop`,
`shift`, `unshift`, `splice`, `map`, `filter`, `forEach`, `some`, `every`, `find`, `includes`,
`indexOf`, `join`, `slice`, `reverse`, `sort`; issue #823, docs/reference/types.md "Proxy and
Reflect").

`p.push(x)` on a proxy reads `push` through the `get` trap. When the trap forwards to an array
(`Reflect.get(target, key, receiver)`), the method it reads is an `ArrayMethod`, and the call
runs the method's generic algorithm from the ECMAScript specification with the proxy as `this`
(`Proxy[PROXY_ARRAY_CALL]`, which velt_vir's proxy call slot calls): every read of `length` or of an
element, every write, `in` test and delete goes through the traps, in Node's order.
modules.summary: velt/lang/proxy (internal): the array methods called on a proxy of an array (`push`, `pop`, `shift`, `unshift`, `splice`, `map`, `filter`, `forEach`, `some`, `every`, `find`, `includes`, `indexOf`, `join`, `slice`, `reverse`, `sort`; issue #823, docs/reference/types.md "Proxy and Reflect").

show it as the function it stands for (velt_vir's `is_array_method`); called any other way,
it is not supported yet. Each read makes a new one (the standard library keeps no module
state), so two reads of a method are not `===`.

modules.doc:
velt/lang/proxy: JavaScript's `Proxy` and `Reflect` (issue #823; docs/reference/types.md "Proxy
and Reflect"), globals loaded when a module names one of them (std/prelude/global/proxy.velt).

A proxy is a dynamic value: `new Proxy(target, handler)` has the type `any` and holds a
`Proxy` object. Its descriptor slots (velt_vir `lower/any_proxy.rs`) call the keyed methods
below, so `p.k` runs the handler's `get` trap, `p.k = v` its `set` trap and `"k" in p` its
`has` trap, each with the target, the key and the proxy itself as the receiver. A trap the
handler leaves out forwards to the target, as in JavaScript. `Reflect.get` / `set` / `has`
do what the operations do on a plain value, and pass the receiver on to a proxy target.

Its bodies use dynamic operations without making the program pay for them: sema counts a
program as using `any` members only when its own code constructs a `Proxy` or calls `Reflect`.
A program that never names them doesn't load this module, and its operations on `any` don't
test for a proxy (velt/lang/hooks/proxy).
modules.summary: velt/lang/proxy: JavaScript's `Proxy` and `Reflect` (issue #823; docs/reference/types.md "Proxy and Reflect"), globals loaded when a module names one of them (std/prelude/global/proxy.velt).

exports.name: Proxy
exports.doc:
A proxy for another object: the operations on it run the handler's traps. Create one with
`new Proxy(target, handler)`; the result is an `any`.
exports.summary: A proxy for another object: the operations on it run the handler's traps.

members.name: constructor
members.doc: A proxy of `target` whose operations run the traps of `handler`.
members.summary: A proxy of `target` whose operations run the traps of `handler`.

members.name: [PROXY_GET_GETTER]
members.doc:
`p.twice` of a class getter on a class instance brand that is this proxy (velt_sema
`proxy_getters.rs`): the `get` trap's answer, with the proxy as its receiver. While the trap
runs, the read is marked on the proxy, so a trap that forwards it with
`Reflect.get(target, key, receiver)` stops with a `TypeError` there (#1732): Node would run
the getter with `this` the proxy, Velt runs it on the target. Without a `get` trap nothing
forwards a receiver, and the read is the target's, as in Node.
members.summary: `p.twice` of a class getter on a class instance brand that is this proxy (velt_sema `proxy_getters.rs`): the `get` trap's answer, with the proxy as its receiver.

members.name: [PROXY_READS_GETTER]
members.doc: Whether this proxy's `get` trap is answering a brand's class getter read of `key`.
members.summary: Whether this proxy's `get` trap is answering a brand's class getter read of `key`.

members.name: [PROXY_VIEW]
members.doc:
A view of `target` as an object type (velt_vir `lower/any_view.rs`): an `any` holding an
object of another type converted to an object type. It has no traps, so every read and
write reaches the target, and converting the view back to `any` gives the target itself:
to the program the view is the target, as in Node. The conversion calls this only for an
object without a live view: it asks the runtime's table of views first (`any_view.rs`).
members.summary: A view of `target` as an object type (velt_vir `lower/any_view.rs`): an `any` holding an object of another type converted to an object type.

members.name: [PROXY_IS_VIEW]

members.name: [RECORD_DEFINE_ACCESSOR]
members.signature: [ [RECORD_DEFINE_ACCESSOR]<E, F>(key: K | symbol, get: () => V throws E, set: (value: V) => void throws F, configurable: bool)
members.doc:
`Object.defineProperty(r, key, { get, set, configurable })`: the accessor replaces an entry
with the key. Defining again a property that is not configurable is Node's `TypeError`.

`x` goes before `y` when `neg(cmp(x, y))`. Elements move between an array and a scratch

at any time each element is owned by exactly one of the two arrays and the slot it left

modules.doc:
velt/lang/sort (internal): the stable sort behind `sort(cmp)` and `toSorted(cmp)`
(std/prelude/sort.velt): the shape of Rust's driftsort. One scan finds the long natural runs
(ascending, or strictly descending and then reversed, which keeps the sort stable); the stretches
between them are sorted by a stable quicksort; then neighbouring runs are merged pairwise
(std/lang/sort/merge.velt). O(n log n) comparisons and moves, O(n) for sorted, reversed or
sorted-then-appended input.

The quicksort partitions into a scratch buffer as long as the array: elements less than
the pivot fill it from the front in order, the others from the back, and come back in order
(Rust's stable quicksort). Each element is written to both ends and only one cursor moves,
so the loop has no data-dependent branch, and its comparisons do not wait for each other
(a merge's next comparison depends on the previous one, which a comparator that loads from
memory pays for in full). A pivot equal to the one of the enclosing partition separates
the elements equal to it, which are then done: inputs with many duplicates take O(n log k).
Too many unbalanced partitions switch to merge sort (`mergeSortRange`).

Elements move with `arrayMove` (raw bits, no clone, no drop): each one is
owned by exactly one array at any time, the slots it left keep stale copies, and the
buffers' lengths go back to 0 before they are dropped. Every partition and merge moves each
element exactly once whatever the comparator answers, and the depth is bounded, so an
inconsistent comparator (NaN results, random answers) gives some permutation: never a
crash, a lost or duplicated element, or a loop.

A comparator can still reach the array through an alias (`const ys = xs`, or a shared object
holding it), so the sort works on buffers of its own:
- Elements that need no drop (numbers, booleans, plain structs) are copied into them and the
  sorted result is written back over the array at the end, as JavaScript does: the
  comparator sees the array unchanged, and what it stores into it is overwritten. A
  comparator that captures nothing reaches no array (there is no mutable module-level
  state, and such elements hold no references), so then a short array is sorted in place,
  without a buffer (for long ones the copy costs nothing measurable).
- Other elements (strings, arrays, objects) are moved, and the array stays empty until the
  sort is done: a store, `pop` or `truncate` through the alias must not drop or take an
  element whose bits the buffers hold. Reading it is out of bounds; what the comparator
  pushes ends up after the sorted elements. This holds for short arrays too, and whatever
  the comparator captures: its arguments are borrows into the array being sorted, and an
  element can itself hold the array (`[string, Holder]` with the holder owning it), so a
  push through it would reallocate the buffer under them.
modules.summary: velt/lang/sort (internal): the stable sort behind `sort(cmp)` and `toSorted(cmp)` (std/prelude/sort.velt): the shape of Rust's driftsort.

exports.signature: function stableSort<T, C>(xs: T[], cmp: (x: T, y: T) => C, neg: (c: C) => bool)
exports.doc:

that both stay known closures that the optimizer specializes and inlines.)
exports.summary: Stable sort of `xs`: `x` goes before `y` when `neg(cmp(x, y))`; equivalent elements keep their order.

velt/lang/typed_array (internal): the conversions and the byte loads and stores of the typed
arrays of, and the conversions their elements go through (ES2024 §25.1, §10.4.5; the numbers are
JS's: `ToUint8`, `ToUint8Clamp`, `ToInt32`, …). Programs use the global.

An `ArrayBuffer` owns a `u8[]` of fixed length. Views (`Uint8Array`, `Float64Array`,
`DataView`, …) keep a reference to the buffer and a byte range of it, so two views of one
buffer see each other's writes, as in JS. Multi-byte elements are little-endian, as on every
platform Velt targets (JS uses the platform's order; `DataView` takes the order as an argument).

modules.doc:
velt/lang/typed_array (internal): `subarray` of a `u8[]` (Node's `buf.subarray` of a `Buffer`): a
`Uint8Array` over the array's bytes, sharing them, as Node's `Buffer` (a `Uint8Array`) does.
Loaded for a program that mentions `subarray` (std/prelude/global/bytes_view.velt).

The view's `buffer` is the array itself (`ArrayBuffer.over`): writes through either are seen by
both, and every access through the view is checked against the array's current length, so a
view stays safe when the array shrinks or grows (an index past the array's end panics, as
any index does). Only a program that keeps such a view (a field, a return, a closure) makes
its `u8[]` values counted; a view used where it is made borrows the array.
modules.summary: velt/lang/typed_array (internal): `subarray` of a `u8[]` (Node's `buf.subarray` of a `Buffer`): a `Uint8Array` over the array's bytes, sharing them, as Node's `Buffer` (a `Uint8Array`) does.

velt/lang/typed_array (internal): `ArrayBuffer` (`BufferView`, what typed arrays and
`DataView` are, is in buffer_view.velt). The small part of the typed arrays that `fetch` bodies
need: a program that uses `Response` loads this module, and the typed array classes only when it
names one or reads `bytes()` (std/prelude/global/fetch_bytes.velt). Programs use the globals.

An `ArrayBuffer` owns a `u8[]` of fixed length. Views (`Uint8Array`, `Float64Array`,
`DataView`, …) keep a reference to the buffer and a byte range of it, so two views of one
buffer see each other's writes, as in JS.

velt/lang/typed_array (internal): `Float32Array` (ES2024 §23.2), a view of a byte range of an
`ArrayBuffer` (std/lang/typed_array/buffer.velt) as 32-bit floats (`f32`). Programs use the
global.

Elements read as numbers and are converted when written, as in JS (`ToUint8`: 300 is 44,
`-1` is 255; `Uint8ClampedArray` clamps; `Float32Array` rounds to `f32`). `xs[i]` reads
element `i` (std's `[INDEX]`, which sema calls for `xs[i]`: crates/velt_sema/src/body/expr/
indexers.rs) and panics out of range like an array index (JS reads `undefined`); `xs[i] = v`
writes it and does nothing out of range, as in JS. `subarray` shares the buffer, `slice`
copies.

Generated by scripts/gen-typed-arrays.py: change the script, not this file.

modules.doc:
velt/lang/typed_array (internal): `Float64Array` (ES2024 §23.2), a view of a byte range of an
`ArrayBuffer` (std/lang/typed_array/buffer.velt) as 64-bit floats (numbers). Programs use the
global.

Elements read as numbers and are converted when written, as in JS (`ToUint8`: 300 is 44,
`-1` is 255; `Uint8ClampedArray` clamps; `Float32Array` rounds to `f32`). `xs[i]` reads
element `i` (std's `[INDEX]`, which sema calls for `xs[i]`: crates/velt_sema/src/body/expr/
indexers.rs) and panics out of range like an array index (JS reads `undefined`); `xs[i] = v`
writes it and does nothing out of range, as in JS. `subarray` shares the buffer, `slice`
copies.

Generated by scripts/gen-typed-arrays.py: change the script, not this file.
modules.summary: velt/lang/typed_array (internal): `Float64Array` (ES2024 §23.2), a view of a byte range of an `ArrayBuffer` (std/lang/typed_array/buffer.velt) as 64-bit floats (numbers).

`ArrayBuffer`, `DataView`, `Uint8Array`, `Int8Array`, `Uint8ClampedArray`, `Int16Array`,
`Uint16Array`, `Int32Array`, `Uint32Array`, `Float32Array` and `Float64Array`. Each is also a
global of its own (std/prelude/global/), so a program loads only the classes it names.

`DataView`): `getUint16(offset, littleEndian)`, `setFloat64(offset, value, littleEndian)`, ….

the view throws a `RangeError`.

exports.name: Int8Array
exports.signature: class Int8Array extends TypedArray implements Iterable<number>
exports.doc:
An array of 8-bit signed integers in an `ArrayBuffer` (JS `Int8Array`): `new Int8Array(n)` (`n` zeros),
`new Int8Array([1, 2])` (a copy, converted), `new Int8Array(buffer, byteOffset, length)` (a view of
`buffer`, sharing it), or a copy of another typed array.

modules.doc:
velt/lang/typed_array (internal): `Int16Array` (ES2024 §23.2), a view of a byte range of an
`ArrayBuffer` (std/lang/typed_array/buffer.velt) as 16-bit signed integers. Programs use the
global.

Elements read as numbers and are converted when written, as in JS (`ToUint8`: 300 is 44,
`-1` is 255; `Uint8ClampedArray` clamps; `Float32Array` rounds to `f32`). `xs[i]` reads
element `i` (std's `[INDEX]`, which sema calls for `xs[i]`: crates/velt_sema/src/body/expr/
indexers.rs) and panics out of range like an array index (JS reads `undefined`); `xs[i] = v`
writes it and does nothing out of range, as in JS. `subarray` shares the buffer, `slice`
copies.

Generated by scripts/gen-typed-arrays.py: change the script, not this file.

velt/lang/typed_array (internal): `Uint16Array` (ES2024 §23.2), a view of a byte range of an
`ArrayBuffer` (std/lang/typed_array/buffer.velt) as 16-bit unsigned integers. Programs use the
global.

Elements read as numbers and are converted when written, as in JS (`ToUint8`: 300 is 44,
`-1` is 255; `Uint8ClampedArray` clamps; `Float32Array` rounds to `f32`). `xs[i]` reads
element `i` (std's `[INDEX]`, which sema calls for `xs[i]`: crates/velt_sema/src/body/expr/
indexers.rs) and panics out of range like an array index (JS reads `undefined`); `xs[i] = v`
writes it and does nothing out of range, as in JS. `subarray` shares the buffer, `slice`
copies.

velt/lang/typed_array (internal): `Uint8Array` (ES2024 §23.2), a view of a byte range of an
`ArrayBuffer` (std/lang/typed_array/buffer.velt) as 8-bit unsigned integers (bytes). Programs use
the global.

Elements read as numbers and are converted when written, as in JS (`ToUint8`: 300 is 44,
`-1` is 255; `Uint8ClampedArray` clamps; `Float32Array` rounds to `f32`). `xs[i]` reads
element `i` (std's `[INDEX]`, which sema calls for `xs[i]`: crates/velt_sema/src/body/expr/
indexers.rs) and panics out of range like an array index (JS reads `undefined`); `xs[i] = v`
writes it and does nothing out of range, as in JS. `subarray` shares the buffer, `slice`
copies.

modules.doc:
velt/math (internal): arbitrary-precision integers (JS `BigInt`), backed by the runtime
(dashu-int).

Velt has no operator overloading, so arithmetic is methods: `a.add(b)` returns a new BigInt
like JS `a + b`; `a.addAssign(b)` changes `a` in place like `a += b`, reusing its buffer (hot
loops such as a pidigits spigot should use the in-place forms). The arithmetic operations
have machine-integer twins (`mulInt(10)`, `mulIntAssign(k)`) that skip building a BigInt for
the small operand. Division truncates and `rem` takes the dividend's sign, like JS; dividing
by zero panics with a RangeError, as JS throws one. A negative shift count panics with a
RangeError too, where JS shifts the other way (`1n << -1n` is `0n`).

A BigInt owns a runtime handle: `clone()` copies the number, `[Symbol.dispose]()` frees it.
modules.summary: velt/math (internal): arbitrary-precision integers (JS `BigInt`), backed by the runtime (dashu-int).

modules.doc:
velt/mem (internal): a typed memory pool (region). Values are appended to one growing array and
named by their `u32` index, and the whole pool is released at once with `reset()`, which keeps
the memory for the next round: a per-iteration tree costs no allocation after the first one.

Best with Copy structs that link to each other by index
(`struct Node { left: u32; right: u32 }`), the arena shape of Rust's bumpalo / typed-arena
programs. `u32` indices are half the size of pointers, so twice as many nodes fit in each cache
line. Indices stay valid until `reset()`.
modules.summary: velt/mem (internal): a typed memory pool (region).

exports.name: Blank
exports.doc:
A value that owns no memory, for a container to keep in the slots it does not use (an array
of plain `T` has no holes), so that a value it removes is released at once: `""` for a
string. Every type has it: one whose values own no memory (`needsDrop` is false) is its own
blank, and one without a blank value gives the value itself (`hasBlank()` is false), which a
container then replaces when that value goes. A type implements `Blank` to give one.
exports.summary: A value that owns no memory, for a container to keep in the slots it does not use (an array of plain `T` has no holes), so that a value it removes is released at once: `""` for a string.

objects and class instances (and structs or unions holding any) do; numbers, `bool` and
SIMD vectors do not. The same for every value of a type, and a constant where the type is

modules.doc:
velt/native (internal): `IoResult<T>`, the result runtime and native-package functions return,
and `unwrapIo`, which turns a failed one into `IoError`.

Runtime I/O functions (docs/internals/contracts/rt_abi_async.md §3) report failures as an `IoResult<T>`
with the C layout `{ i32 code; u32 pad; VeltStr message; T value /* @32 */ }`, which is exactly
the natural layout of the Velt struct below. `code == 0` means success: `message` is an empty
static string and `value` is initialized. Otherwise `value` is all-zero bytes, which every type's
drop glue treats as "owns nothing", so dropping a failed result is safe. Operations without a
value return `IoStatus` (velt/native/status).
modules.summary: velt/native (internal): `IoResult<T>`, the result runtime and native-package functions return, and `unwrapIo`, which turns a failed one into `IoError`.

modules.doc:
velt/net/http (internal): a response body as it arrives on its connection, its
framing undone (RFC 9112 §6): a `content-length`, chunks (`transfer-encoding: chunked`), or
everything until the server closes the connection.

`all` receives the rest of a body into one array: one sized from `content-length` (up to
4 MiB at first, doubled as the body arrives, so a length the server only claims costs
nothing), read into straight from the socket. A read straight into a piece of its own takes
at most 256 KiB, however much the body or a chunk claims to have left.
`next` hands the body over piece by piece, at most `max` bytes at a time. Once the body is
complete the connection goes back to the pool, unless the response said to close it.
modules.summary: velt/net/http (internal): a response body as it arrives on its connection, its framing undone (RFC 9112 §6): a `content-length`, chunks (`transfer-encoding: chunked`), or everything until the server closes the connection.

modules.doc:
velt/net/http (internal): one HTTP/1.1 connection of the client while a request
uses it: the stream, a read buffer, and the request's signal, which every wait races so an
abort stops the request at once (the stream is then closed, never pooled). Between requests a
keep-alive connection is parked in the runtime's pool under its origin (`TcpStream.park`,
crates/velt_rt/src/net/park.rs), which every task takes connections from.

Reads go straight into the buffer (`tryRead`, nothing copied on the way for plain TCP). I/O
errors become `fetch failed: …` with the code of the error, as Node words them.
modules.summary: velt/net/http (internal): one HTTP/1.1 connection of the client while a request uses it: the stream, a read buffer, and the request's signal, which every wait races so an abort stops the request at once (the stream is then closed, never pooled).

modules.doc:
velt/net/http (internal): undoing the codings a server compressed a body with
(`content-encoding`), as Node's `fetch` does: `gzip` / `x-gzip` (several members), `deflate`
(zlib-wrapped or raw, decided by the first byte) and `br`, in any combination of up to five,
the last one undone first. A list naming another coding leaves the body as it is; an empty
body is empty in any coding; a body cut off before its compressed stream ends is an error.

A body read whole is decoded whole (velt/compress's one-shot functions, the output sized from
gzip's trailer); a body read piece by piece goes through a chain of streaming decoders, each
handing out at most `CHUNK` bytes at a time, so a small body that expands enormously still
arrives in bounded pieces.
modules.summary: velt/net/http (internal): undoing the codings a server compressed a body with (`content-encoding`), as Node's `fetch` does: `gzip` / `x-gzip` (several members), `deflate` (zlib-wrapped or raw, decided by the first byte) and `br`, in any combination of up to five, the last one undone first.

of velt/net/http/fetch/response holds it: the status, the head kept as it was read (headers are made
into strings only when a program asks for them), the URL, and the body still to receive.

A body that arrived whole with its head (most small responses) is kept as a range of the read
buffer and its connection goes back to the pool at once, so it is reused even if nobody reads
the body. Any other body is received when it is read, decoded as its `content-encoding` says.

velt/net/http (internal): `H2Body`, a response body arriving over an HTTP/2 client session, as
the request's task reads it: DATA pieces from the request's channel, each read giving its
window back to the session (so a body nobody reads holds at most the stream's window), an

(RFC 9113), served by a task of its own: requests from any task arrive on its channel
(`H2Call`) and become streams on the one connection, as many at once as the server allows
(more wait in order); responses go back on each request's channel (`H2Event`). The session
reads frames into its own buffer and parses them in place (h2/frames.velt), and the frames it

after `IDLE_MS` without streams, after a GOAWAY once its streams are done, or on an error.

modules.doc:
velt/net/http (internal): a request's URL as the client uses it: its WHATWG
serialization (what `res.url` reports), where to connect, the `host` header and the
request-target.

WHATWG URL parsing costs more than the rest of making a request. Most URLs a program fetches
are already in the form the parser serializes them to (`http://host:port/path?query`, a
lowercase ASCII host), so `target` first checks for that form, in one pass over the text, and
takes such a URL as it is; anything else goes through `velt/net/url`. The check accepts only what
it can tell the parser leaves unchanged: a lowercase scheme, a host of lowercase letters,
digits, `-` and `.` (no IDNA label, and a dotted-decimal IPv4 address if its last label is a
number), a port only when it is not the default one and has no leading zero, and a path and
query of bytes the parser neither percent-encodes nor rewrites, without dot segments.

modules.doc:
velt/net/http (internal): HTTP/1.1 on the wire (RFC 9112): the request head the client
writes (the response head it reads is in head.velt).

A request head goes into one byte array with its body when the body is small, so most
requests leave in one write. The headers `fetch` adds (`host`, `accept`, `user-agent`,
`accept-encoding`) are written unless the caller set them; the caller's names and values are
checked as hyper checks them (a token; no control characters but tab). The framing is always
the client's own, as undici's: `content-length` is written from the body (a caller's must
agree with it), and a caller's `transfer-encoding` is refused, so a header cannot make the
server read a different body than the one sent (request smuggling).

modules.doc:
velt/net/http (internal): the WHATWG `Headers` class of `fetch` (docs/std/net/http.md), also the
type of a received request's `headers` (source.velt).

One flat list, `[name, value, name, value, …]`, in insertion order: names are lowercased when
they are added (header names are case-insensitive), values have surrounding whitespace removed.
The `fetch` client parses a response's headers into that format, so they arrive as one array
without being copied again. Lookups scan the list: a message has a handful of headers, for which
a scan beats hashing. A received request's headers stay with its server (its `RequestSource`)
until something needs all of them: `get` and `has` look one name up there. The headers of a
response made here start with the `content-type` its body implies held as a number (`implied`),
which the server writes as it is; it becomes the list's first entry when something reads or
changes `content-type` or needs the whole list. The first header added to an empty `Headers` is
kept as it was given, outside the list (a new response usually gets one or two:
`res.headers.set("server", "velt")` makes no list and lowercases nothing); anything else moves it
into the list first.

As in the standard, `get` joins repeated headers with ", " and iteration yields the names in
sorted order with repeats joined, except `set-cookie`, whose values are yielded one by one
(`getSetCookie()` returns them as an array). Unlike JavaScript, an invalid name or value is
not rejected here: `fetch` rejects it with `IoError` "EINVAL" when it sends the request (a
server answers 500). A fetched response's and a received request's headers are immutable, as
in JS: changing them stops the program (`TypeError: immutable`), a programming error like an
index out of bounds.

modules.doc:
velt/net/http (internal): the WHATWG `Request` (docs/std/net/http.md; `RequestInit` is in
request_init.velt): a request
`fetch` can send, made from a URL and the same options `fetch` takes, or one a server received
(`serverRequest`, source.velt).

A received request reads its server's `RequestSource` lazily, as a fetched
`Response` does: its URL, method and headers are made the first time they are read, and its
body is received while it is read (`text()`, `json()`, `bytes()`, or chunk by chunk through
`req.body`). So a handler pays only for what it looks at, and the state only a request made
here has (body, redirect mode, signal, CA) is one null field. It is valid until its handler
settles; what was read stays readable.

modules.doc:
velt/net/http (internal): the WHATWG `Response` (docs/std/net/http.md): what `fetch` resolves to,
what a server handler returns (`serve`), or a response built with `new Response(body, init)`
/ `Response.json(data)`.

A fetched response holds the client's response (`Fetched`, std/net/http/fetch/client/fetched.velt) whose
head has arrived; its body is received by the first `text()`, `json()`, `bytes()` or
`arrayBuffer()`, or chunk by chunk through `res.body` (a second read throws, as in JS). A
compressed body (`content-encoding: gzip`, `deflate`, `br`) arrives decoded. Dropping the
response closes the connection of a body nobody read. The status text and headers are made
into strings the first time they are read (most programs read neither), and stay readable
after the body was read. A built response
makes no `Headers` until they are read: the `content-type` its body implies waits in
`headImplied`, and a server sends it from there.
modules.summary: velt/net/http (internal): the WHATWG `Response` (docs/std/net/http.md): what `fetch` resolves to, what a server handler returns (`serve`), or a response built with `new Response(body, init)` / `Response.json(data)`.

modules.doc:
velt/net/http/h2 (internal): `HpackDecoder`, HPACK header block decoding (RFC 7541 §6) into
a `FieldList`.

One decoder per connection: every header block of the connection goes through it, in order,
since each may change the dynamic table the next ones refer to. Strings are written straight
into the list's buffer (Huffman-decoded there when coded); an entry added to the dynamic table
is copied out of it. A block whose fields exceed the list's limit is still decoded to its end,
so the table stays as the peer's encoder has it, but the fields beyond the limit are not kept
(`overflow`): a small block that refers to a large entry many times (an "HPACK bomb") costs
the time to read it and nothing more.
modules.summary: velt/net/http/h2 (internal): `HpackDecoder`, HPACK header block decoding (RFC 7541 §6) into a `FieldList`.

members.doc:
Decodes the block `src[start..end)` into `out` (appended): false when it is not valid HPACK

`out.overflow` and are not kept.

modules.doc:
velt/net/http/h2 (internal): `HpackEncoder`, HPACK encoding (RFC 7541 §6) of
header blocks into a connection's `FrameWriter`.

What a server sends repeats from response to response (`server`, `content-type`, the `date`
of this second), so a field is added to the dynamic table the first time and sent as one index
byte after that. `content-length` changes with every response and is sent without indexing,
by its static name; `set-cookie` and `authorization` are never indexed (RFC 7541 §7.1.3), so
an intermediary does not compress them either. A literal string is Huffman-coded when that is
shorter.
modules.summary: velt/net/http/h2 (internal): `HpackEncoder`, HPACK encoding (RFC 7541 §6) of header blocks into a connection's `FrameWriter`.

modules.doc:
velt/net/http/h2 (internal): the HPACK Huffman code (RFC 7541 §5.2, Appendix B): decoding
through the tables of h2/huffman_table.velt, and encoding.

Decoding keeps up to 64 bits of input in a register: the next 8 bits find a code of 8 bits or
fewer (most characters of a header) in one lookup, a longer code is found by its length, as
the code is canonical. Nothing is allocated: the output goes into the caller's buffer.
Padding is checked as §5.2 asks: fewer than 8 bits, all ones, and EOS never appears.
modules.summary: velt/net/http/h2 (internal): the HPACK Huffman code (RFC 7541 §5.2, Appendix B): decoding through the tables of h2/huffman_table.velt, and encoding.

exports.name: huffmanDecode
exports.signature: function huffmanDecode(src: u8[], start: i64, end: i64, out: u8[], at: i64): i64
exports.doc:
Decodes the Huffman-coded bytes `src[start..end)` into `out` from `at`: the end of what was
written, or -1 for input that is not a valid code (EOS, or padding that is not up to 7 one
bits). `out` must have room for `(end - start) * 8 / 5` bytes (the shortest code is 5 bits).
exports.summary: Decodes the Huffman-coded bytes `src[start..end)` into `out` from `at`: the end of what was written, or -1 for input that is not a valid code (EOS, or padding that is not up to 7 one bits).

Writes the Huffman code of `src[start..end)` into `out` from `at` (room for `huffmanLength`

exports.name: huffmanDecode
exports.signature: function huffmanDecode(src: u8[], start: i64, end: i64, out: u8[], at: i64): i64
exports.doc:
Decodes the Huffman-coded bytes `src[start..end)` into `out` from `at`: the end of what was
written, or -1 for input that is not a valid code (EOS, or padding that is not up to 7 one
bits). `out` must have room for `(end - start) * 8 / 5` bytes (the shortest code is 5 bits).
exports.summary: Decodes the Huffman-coded bytes `src[start..end)` into `out` from `at`: the end of what was written, or -1 for input that is not a valid code (EOS, or padding that is not up to 7 one bits).

exports.doc:
Writes the Huffman code of `src[start..end)` into `out` from `at` (room for `huffmanLength`
bytes), padded with one bits: the end of what was written.
exports.summary: Writes the Huffman code of `src[start..end)` into `out` from `at` (room for `huffmanLength` bytes), padded with one bits: the end of what was written.

modules.doc:
velt/net/http: the HTTP client and the web types both sides of HTTP share, as the web globals
of Node, Deno and Bun: `fetch` (HTTP/1.1, and HTTP/2 where the origin offers it), `Request`,
`Response`, `Headers` and their bodies; and what a server written in Velt needs of them
(`RequestSource`, `responseParts`, `statusText`; packages/http-server is one). HTTP/2's wire
format is velt/net/http/h2. docs/std/net/http.md.
modules.summary: velt/net/http: the HTTP client and the web types both sides of HTTP share, as the web globals of Node, Deno and Bun: `fetch` (HTTP/1.1, and HTTP/2 where the origin offers it), `Request`, `Response`, `Headers` and their bodies; and what a server written in Velt needs of them (`RequestSource`, `responseParts`, `statusText`; packages/http-server is one).

generator's: `new Response(BodyStream.from(rows()))` sends each chunk as it is made. The

exports.name: fetch
exports.signature: async function fetch(input: string | URL | Request, init: RequestInit = {}): Promise<Response, IoError | AbortError>
exports.doc:
Sends a request. Rejects with `IoError` when there is no response (`ECONNREFUSED`,
`ETIMEDOUT`, a TLS failure, an invalid URL or header: `EINVAL`), and with the signal's
`AbortError` (`TimeoutError` for `AbortSignal.timeout`) when it is aborted. An HTTP error
status is a response, not an error: check `res.ok`.
exports.summary: Sends a request.

modules.doc:
velt/net: TCP, and TLS over TCP, over the runtime (docs/internals/contracts/rt_abi_async.md
§6). A TLS connection (`connectTls`, a `listenTls` listener) is a `TcpStream` like any other.

Handles: the runtime's `VeltListener` / `VeltStream` are opaque `u64` handles (rt_abi_async.md
§3.2), declared and defined as `u64` on every target.
`TcpListener` and `TcpStream` are Copy structs around that handle, like file descriptors:
- async methods take `this` by copy, so `await conn.readString()` never moves `conn` and a
  listener can be moved into a spawned task while its `port` is still read outside;
- the handle is released only by `close()`: an unclosed handle leaks until process exit. The
  handle is a key into a runtime table, not an address: after `close()` through any copy,
  every copy is dead: its operations throw `IoError` `EBADF` ("handle is closed") and closing
  again does nothing. They cannot use a `[Symbol.dispose]()` drop hook: a type with one is
  never Copy, and an async method owns (moves) its `this`, so `await conn.readString(); await
  conn.write(...)` would not compile. The runtime keeps a socket alive while an operation is
  in flight, so `close()` may be called at any time.
modules.summary: velt/net: TCP, and TLS over TCP, over the runtime (docs/internals/contracts/rt_abi_async.md §6).

members.name: readInto
members.doc:
Reads what has arrived into `buf`, at most `buf.length` bytes, straight from the socket
(nothing is allocated or copied on the way for a plain TCP stream): the number of bytes
read, or `null` at the end of the stream (as Deno's `conn.read`). Waits only when nothing
has arrived yet. An empty `buf` reads nothing and returns 0. Reusing one buffer per
connection, and `subarray` views of what was read, keeps a server from copying its input.
members.summary: Reads what has arrived into `buf`, at most `buf.length` bytes, straight from the socket (nothing is allocated or copied on the way for a plain TCP stream): the number of bytes read, or `null` at the end of the stream (as Deno's `conn.read`).

members.name: tryRead
members.signature: tryRead(buf: u8[] | Uint8Array, start: number = 0, end?: number): number | null
members.doc:
Reads what has arrived into `buf[start..end]` without waiting: the number of bytes read,
`0` when nothing has arrived yet (`await readable()`, then try again), or `null` at the end
of the stream. A plain TCP stream reads straight into `buf`, so a parser can read into its
own buffer with nothing allocated or copied (`readInto` does the waiting for a
`Uint8Array`). `RangeError` for an empty or out-of-range range.
members.summary: Reads what has arrived into `buf[start..end]` without waiting: the number of bytes read, `0` when nothing has arrived yet (`await readable()`, then try again), or `null` at the end of the stream.

members.name: readable
members.doc:
Resolves once a `tryRead` may find data, the end of the stream or an error (it may also
find nothing yet: wait again). Holds no buffer while it waits.
members.summary: Resolves once a `tryRead` may find data, the end of the stream or an error (it may also find nothing yet: wait again).

members.name: readableWithin
members.signature: async readableWithin(ms: number, signal: AbortSignal | null = null): Promise<bool>
members.doc:
`readable()` with a limit: true once a `tryRead` may find something, false when `ms`
milliseconds passed first or `signal` was aborted. One wait in the runtime, so nothing of it
is left behind (unlike `Promise.race` with a timer): a server waiting for the next request on
each idle connection.
members.summary: `readable()` with a limit: true once a `tryRead` may find something, false when `ms` milliseconds passed first or `signal` was aborted.

members.summary: The protocol TLS's ALPN chose (`"h2"`), or null (none, not TLS); waits for the handshake.

members.signature: async writeBytes(data: u8[] | Uint8Array, start: number = 0, end?: number): Promise<void>
members.doc:
Resolves once every byte is written. What the socket takes at the call is written from

members.summary: Resolves once every byte is written.

members.name: tryWrite
members.signature: tryWrite(data: u8[] | Uint8Array, start: number = 0, end?: number): i64
members.doc:
Writes what the socket takes of `data` right now, without waiting, and returns the number
of bytes written (0 when it takes nothing now, while an earlier `write` is still going on,
for a TLS stream, and after an error, which the next `write` reports). For protocols that
send small messages: when everything was written there is nothing to await.
members.summary: Writes what the socket takes of `data` right now, without waiting, and returns the number of bytes written (0 when it takes nothing now, while an earlier `write` is still going on, for a TLS stream, and after an error, which the next `write` reports).

members.name: writeLater
members.doc:
Queues `data` to be sent when the current task next waits (or finishes), together with
everything else it queued until then: one system call where a write each would make
several, and nothing held back past a wait. Returns the number of bytes still to be sent on
this stream; `await drained(max)` keeps that bounded. A `write` goes after what was queued
before it. Throws `IoError` once sending failed (the error a `write` would have reported),
the stream was aborted or the handle closed.
members.summary: Queues `data` to be sent when the current task next waits (or finishes), together with everything else it queued until then: one system call where a write each would make several, and nothing held back past a wait.

members.name: writeBytesLater
members.signature: writeBytesLater(data: u8[] | Uint8Array, start: number = 0, end?: number): i64
members.doc: `writeLater` of bytes `start..end` of `data` (copied at the call).
members.summary: `writeLater` of bytes `start..end` of `data` (copied at the call).

members.name: drained
members.doc:
Resolves once at most `max` bytes queued by `writeLater` (or a `write` after them) are still
to be sent: right away when there are no more, otherwise once the peer has read enough.
Throws `IoError` when sending failed.
members.summary: Resolves once at most `max` bytes queued by `writeLater` (or a `write` after them) are still to be sent: right away when there are no more, otherwise once the peer has read enough.

members.name: shutdown
members.doc:
Half-close: the peer reads end of stream, after every byte written or queued (`writeLater`)
before; this side can still read.
members.summary: Half-close: the peer reads end of stream, after every byte written or queued (`writeLater`) before; this side can still read.

members.summary: The peer's "ip:port" ("" once the handle is closed).

members.name: abort
members.doc:
Fails the operations in flight on this stream (a `write` to a peer that stopped reading
would otherwise never finish) and every later one; nothing more is sent or received. The
handle stays open until `close()`.
members.summary: Fails the operations in flight on this stream (a `write` to a peer that stopped reading would otherwise never finish) and every later one; nothing more is sent or received.

members.name: close

Releases the handle: later operations through any copy throw `IoError` `EBADF`, and closing

modules.doc:
velt/net/url (internal): percent-encoding and UTF-8 helpers shared by std/url.

Works on the UTF-8 bytes of a string: an encoder copies them into a `u8[]` once, escapes what
its set asks for, and turns the bytes back into a string once. The copy writes a lone
surrogate as U+FFFD (what `URL` and `URLSearchParams` encode, `%EF%BF%BD`, as WHATWG says);
`encodeURI`/`encodeURIComponent` refuse one instead, and decoding never makes one (surrogate
bytes such as `%ED%A0%BD` are invalid UTF-8). Decoders and `encodeUri` return null where the
public API throws (std/url owns the error class), so this module has no dependency on it.
modules.summary: velt/net/url (internal): percent-encoding and UTF-8 helpers shared by std/url.

exports.summary: WHATWG percent-encode sets (url.spec.whatwg.org §1.3).

modules.doc:
velt/net/url (internal): the WHATWG host parser (url.spec.whatwg.org §3.5) for std/url.

Supported: ASCII domains (percent-decoded, lowercased, checked for forbidden code points), IPv4
in every WHATWG spelling (`127.1`, `0x7f.0.0.1`, `2130706433`) normalized to dotted decimal,
bracketed IPv6 literals (validated and lowercased but not compressed), and the opaque hosts of
non-special schemes. Not supported: IDNA / punycode — a host that is not ASCII after decoding
is rejected. Every parser returns null where the URL is invalid.
modules.summary: velt/net/url (internal): the WHATWG host parser (url.spec.whatwg.org §3.5) for std/url.

modules.doc:
velt/net/url: WHATWG-style `URL` and `URLSearchParams`, plus JS's `encodeURIComponent` family.

Parsing follows the WHATWG URL Standard for the inputs people write (std/net/url/parse.velt):
special schemes (http https ws wss ftp file) get lowercased hosts, dropped default ports,
`\` as a path separator and dot-segment removal; other schemes keep opaque hosts and paths.
Components are percent-encoded with the spec's encode sets. Known gaps: no IDNA/punycode
(a non-ASCII host is invalid), IPv6 literals are validated loosely and not compressed
(`[0:0::1]` stays as written). `file:` URLs follow the spec's Windows drive-letter rules:
`/x` keeps the base's drive letter, `..` never removes it, a first segment `C|` is `C:`, and a
relative path or a host that starts with a drive letter switches to it.

Mutation: `searchParams` returns a copy; to change the query, edit the copy and assign it
back (`const p = u.searchParams; p.set("a", "1"); u.searchParams = p;`). Setters follow JS:
invalid values are ignored, except `href`, which throws like JS. Like the WHATWG setters, the
ones that run the URL parser drop tabs and newlines from the value first.
modules.summary: velt/net/url: WHATWG-style `URL` and `URLSearchParams`, plus JS's `encodeURIComponent` family.

modules.doc:
velt/net/url (internal): the URL parser, for velt/net/url's `URL`.

A simplified WHATWG basic URL parser (url.spec.whatwg.org §4.4): the input is split into
scheme, authority, path, query and fragment by scanning for delimiters instead of running the
spec's character state machine, which gives the same results for the inputs the spec accepts
(minus the gaps listed in std/net/url/index.velt). Relative references resolve against a base
record like RFC 3986 §5.2 with WHATWG's special-scheme rules (`\` is a separator, empty hosts
are invalid, default ports are dropped). Parsers return null where the URL is invalid.
modules.summary: velt/net/url (internal): the URL parser, for velt/net/url's `URL`.

modules.doc:
velt/net/websocket: WebSocket connections (RFC 6455) written in Velt on velt/net streams:
opened as a client (`connectWebSocket("ws://…")`, `wss://` over TLS), or over a connection a
server upgraded (`webSocketOver`; packages/http-server's `upgradeWebSocket` makes one).
docs/std/net/websocket.md.

`WebSocket` is a handle like velt/net's `TcpStream` (its copies share one connection, so one
task can wait in `receive` while another `send`s), released by `close()`: a `receive` already
waiting then sees the peer's close (null), and later operations through any copy throw
`IoError` `EBADF` ("handle is closed"). Messages are pulled with `receive` (null once the peer
has closed); pings are answered automatically.
modules.summary: velt/net/websocket: WebSocket connections (RFC 6455) written in Velt on velt/net streams: opened as a client (`connectWebSocket("ws://…")`, `wss://` over TLS), or over a connection a server upgraded (`webSocketOver`; packages/http-server's `upgradeWebSocket` makes one).

members.name: close
members.signature: async close(code: i64 = 1000, reason: string = ""): Promise<void>
members.doc:
Sends a close frame (`code` 1000 = normal closure; 1000-1003, 1007-1014 or 3000-4999, else
`IoError` "EINVAL", nothing is sent and the connection stays open) after everything queued,
waits until it is written, and releases the handle. Closing a connection the peer already closed, or closing
twice, is fine; other operations on the handle (through any copy) throw `IoError` `EBADF`
afterwards.

server upgraded (`server` true: this side reads masked frames and sends unmasked ones), or one
a client opened. `head` holds what was already read from `stream` past the handshake (the
peer's first frames, if it did not wait). The connection is the socket's from then on.
exports.summary: A WebSocket over `stream`, a connection whose opening handshake is done: an HTTP connection a server upgraded (`server` true: this side reads masked frames and sends unmasked ones), or one a client opened.

modules.doc:
velt/net/websocket (internal): the sending side of a connection. Not part of the public
API.

A send encodes its frame into the connection's `SendQueue` at the call, under the queue's
lock, so frames go out in call order from any task, also before a server-side upgrade has
completed. Whoever queues into an idle connection starts its flusher (std/websocket/writer),
which writes everything queued in one write; an idle connection has no task and no buffer.

exports.name: DIRECT
exports.doc:
The connection was idle and its reading task has a message in hand with no more input
waiting, so this is most likely its reply in a request/reply exchange: the caller writes the
queue to the socket itself (`writeDirect`), since there is nothing a flusher could batch it
with. (A frame another task sends in that moment is written at once too; only batching is
lost.)

modules.doc:
velt/net/websocket (internal): the receiving side of a connection. Not part of the
public API.

The connection's `Reader` holds the bytes read and not yet parsed, and a fragmented message
so far. It lives in the connection's `SendQueue` (std/net/websocket/queue.velt), under the same lock,
and is only touched in short steps under it: `next` takes a whole message out of
the buffer, or says that more bytes are needed; the task that asked reads them from the
stream with the lock released and hands them over with `feed`. So nothing of the state lives
in a task, one task at a time reads the socket, and the buffer is dropped once every byte in
it is used: an idle connection holds none.
modules.summary: velt/net/websocket (internal): the receiving side of a connection.

exports.doc:

connection, so one task can wait in `receive` while another `send`s. Released by `close()`.
exports.summary: An open WebSocket connection.

members.name: close
members.signature: async close(code: i64 = 1000, reason: string = ""): Promise<void>
members.doc:
Sends a close frame (`code` 1000 = normal closure; 1000-1003, 1007-1014 or 3000-4999, else
`IoError` "EINVAL", nothing is sent and the connection stays open) after everything queued,
waits until it is written, and releases the handle. Closing a connection the peer already closed, or closing
twice, is fine; other operations on the handle (through any copy) throw `IoError` `EBADF`
afterwards.
members.summary: Sends a close frame (`code` 1000 = normal closure; 1000-1003, 1007-1014 or 3000-4999, else `IoError` "EINVAL", nothing is sent and the connection stays open) after everything queued, waits until it is written, and releases the handle.

exports.name: webSocketOver
exports.signature: function webSocketOver(stream: TcpStream, server: bool, head: u8[] = []): WebSocket
exports.doc:
A WebSocket over `stream`, a connection whose opening handshake is done: an HTTP connection a
server upgraded (`server` true: this side reads masked frames and sends unmasked ones), or one
a client opened. `head` holds what was already read from `stream` past the handshake (the
peer's first frames, if it did not wait). The connection is the socket's from then on.
exports.summary: A WebSocket over `stream`, a connection whose opening handshake is done: an HTTP connection a server upgraded (`server` true: this side reads masked frames and sends unmasked ones), or one a client opened.

modules.doc:
velt/net/websocket (internal): publish/subscribe. Not part of the public API.

A publish encodes the frame once and appends the same bytes to every subscriber's queue, so a
message to many sockets costs one encode and one queue append per socket. An idle
subscriber's queue is then written from the publishing task (`writeDirect`): a socket nearly
always takes a frame at once, and a task per subscriber would cost more than the write (on
several threads each one wakes another worker). Only a socket that does not take it all gets
a flusher. A subscriber with more than `PUBLISH_LIMIT` bytes
already queued is skipped for that message, so one slow reader cannot grow the server's
memory without bound (a direct `send` waits instead). Topics are process-wide (one registry,
a runtime slot, rt_abi_async.md §2.2); a connection leaves all of them when it is closed.

Locks, always in this order: the registry, a topic, a connection's queue.
modules.summary: velt/net/websocket (internal): publish/subscribe.

exports.name: subscribe
exports.signature: function subscribe(stream: TcpStream, tx: Tx, topic: string): bool
exports.doc: Subscribes the connection (`stream`, queue `tx`) to `topic`; false if its handle was released.
exports.summary: Subscribes the connection (`stream`, queue `tx`) to `topic`; false if its handle was released.

exports.name: leave
exports.doc: Removes the connection with queue `tx` from `topic`; an emptied topic goes away.
exports.summary: Removes the connection with queue `tx` from `topic`; an emptied topic goes away.

exports.name: unsubscribe
exports.doc: `leave`, also taking `topic` off the connection's own list.
exports.summary: `leave`, also taking `topic` off the connection's own list.

exports.name: publish
exports.signature: function publish(topic: string, frame: u8[], payloadAt: i64, except: Tx | null): i64
exports.doc:
Queues `frame` (a whole unmasked frame whose payload starts at `payloadAt`) for every
subscriber of `topic` except the connection with queue `except` (null: none); the number of
connections.
exports.summary: Queues `frame` (a whole unmasked frame whose payload starts at `payloadAt`) for every subscriber of `topic` except the connection with queue `except` (null: none); the number of connections.
