velt/net/websocket (internal): the flusher that writes a connection's `SendQueue`, and
what a send or a close waits for. Not part of the public API.
modules.summary: velt/net/websocket (internal): the flusher that writes a connection's `SendQueue`, and what a send or a close waits for.

exports.name: CLOSE_FLUSH_MS
exports.doc:
How long a closing connection's flusher gets to write what is queued (a peer that stopped
reading must not keep the socket and its queue alive): 30 s, as the `ws` package.
exports.summary: How long a closing connection's flusher gets to write what is queued (a peer that stopped reading must not keep the socket and its queue alive): 30 s, as the `ws` package.

exports.name: flush
exports.signature: async function flush(stream: TcpStream, tx: Tx): Promise<void>
exports.doc:
Writes what is queued, one write per batch, until nothing is: frames queued together (the
replies to messages that arrived together, a broadcast) cost one write. Started by whoever
queued into an idle connection (`START`). On a server-side connection the first write waits
for the upgrade. After the close frame, or a failed write, the socket is shut down and the
queue is stopped.
exports.summary: Writes what is queued, one write per batch, until nothing is: frames queued together (the replies to messages that arrived together, a broadcast) cost one write.

exports.name: flushRest
exports.signature: async function flushRest(stream: TcpStream, tx: Tx, rest: u8[]): Promise<void>
exports.doc: `flush` after `rest`, what `writeDirect` could not write at once.
exports.summary: `flush` after `rest`, what `writeDirect` could not write at once.

exports.name: writeDirect
exports.doc:
Writes the queue to the socket from the calling task (`DIRECT`: a reply by the connection's
own reading task, with nothing to batch it with). No task is started unless the socket does
not take everything at once, or more was queued meanwhile.
exports.summary: Writes the queue to the socket from the calling task (`DIRECT`: a reply by the connection's own reading task, with nothing to batch it with).

exports.name: start
exports.signature: function start(stream: TcpStream, tx: Tx, r: i64)
exports.doc: Starts what a queued frame's status `r` asks for: a flusher (`START`) or a direct write.
exports.summary: Starts what a queued frame's status `r` asks for: a flusher (`START`) or a direct write.

exports.name: pongRoom
exports.doc:
Waits until at most `HIGH_WATER` bytes of pongs are queued (never throws): a peer that sends
pings and reads nothing is not read from either until it takes the answers. The application's
own frames do not count, so a ping never stops reading from a peer that is just slow.
exports.summary: Waits until at most `HIGH_WATER` bytes of pongs are queued (never throws): a peer that sends pings and reads nothing is not read from either until it takes the answers.

exports.name: settle
exports.signature: async function settle(stream: TcpStream, tx: Tx, r: i64): Promise<void>
exports.doc:
Finishes a send whose frame got `r` from the queue: starts the flusher if the connection was
idle, waits for room past the high-water mark, throws if the frame was not queued.
exports.summary: Finishes a send whose frame got `r` from the queue: starts the flusher if the connection was idle, waits for room past the high-water mark, throws if the frame was not queued.

exports.name: settleQuietly
exports.signature: function settleQuietly(stream: TcpStream, tx: Tx, r: i64)
exports.doc: `settle` for frames the connection sends by itself (pongs, close replies): never throws.
exports.summary: `settle` for frames the connection sends by itself (pongs, close replies): never throws.

exports.name: finish
exports.signature: async function finish(stream: TcpStream, tx: Tx, flushMs: i64): Promise<void>
exports.doc:
Waits until the flusher has written the close frame (queued by the caller, or earlier) and
stopped; a peer that does not take it within `flushMs` is cut off.
exports.summary: Waits until the flusher has written the close frame (queued by the caller, or earlier) and stopped; a peer that does not take it within `flushMs` is cut off.

exports.name: closeDown
exports.signature: async function closeDown(stream: TcpStream, tx: Tx, payload: u8[]): Promise<string[] | null>
exports.doc:
The rest of `close()` once the close frame `payload` is known: queues it, waits (bounded) for
the flusher to write it and stop, and releases the queue. Returns the topics the connection
was subscribed to (to leave), or null if the handle was released already.
exports.summary: The rest of `close()` once the close frame `payload` is known: queues it, waits (bounded) for the flusher to write it and stop, and releases the queue.

modules.doc:
Prelude: JS-style methods on every array `T[]` (implicitly imported into every module).

Conventions (see std/README.md):
- Callbacks are non-escaping function params; elements are passed to them as borrows, so
  iterating never copies non-Copy elements. Like JS, they also get the element's index (a
  callback may take fewer parameters: `xs.map((x) => …)`). A callback may throw: the method throws what its
  callback throws (`E`, inferred per call; `never` when the callback cannot throw).
- A callback may change the array through another reference (an alias, or an object holding
  it). Lowering passes a share of the element instead of a borrow when the array is one
  other references may reach (velt_vir stabilize.rs), so the argument stays valid when a
  push moves the buffer or a `pop` drops the element. The methods visit the indices below
  the length they started with, and stop at the length the callback leaves when it is
  shorter: `forEach`, `filter`, `reduce`, `some` and `every` skip the missing indices as JS
  does; JS's `find` family visits them with `undefined`, which a `T` cannot be; `map`, whose
  JS result would have holes, panics. `mayAlias(this)` is a constant, false when
  no other reference to an array of this type can exist: the length cannot change then, and
  the plain loop on `this.length` is all that is compiled. Otherwise the loop compares the
  index with one bound `n`, lowered after a callback shortened the array.
- Methods that return elements *out of* the array (`find`, `filter`, `slice`, `concat`) return
  the elements themselves, like JS: objects are shared (another reference to the same object,
  a count increment), numbers, bool and strings are copied.
- Indices are `usize` internally; positions reported to users (`indexOf`, `findIndex`) are
  `i64` with -1 for "absent", like JS.
- Sorting (`sort()`, `sort(cmp)`) lives in sort.velt, the methods that edit an array in place or
  copy it edited in array_edit.velt, `join` of typed arrays in array_join.velt. `clone()` (a deep
  copy) is compiler-provided.
modules.summary: Prelude: JS-style methods on every array `T[]` (implicitly imported into every module).

members.name: forEach
members.signature: forEach<E>(f: (x: T, i: i64) => void throws E) throws E
members.doc: Performs the specified action for each element in an array.
members.summary: Performs the specified action for each element in an array.

params.name: f
params.doc:
A function that accepts up to two arguments, the element and its index. forEach
calls `f` one time for each element in the array, in order. Elements pushed meanwhile are
not visited, and elements removed meanwhile are skipped, as in JS.

members.name: map
members.signature: map<U, E>(f: (x: T, i: i64) => U throws E): U[] throws E
members.doc:
Calls a defined callback function on each element of an array, and returns an array that
contains the results.
members.summary: Calls a defined callback function on each element of an array, and returns an array that contains the results.

params.name: f
params.doc:
A function that accepts up to two arguments, the element and its index. The map
method calls `f` one time for each element in the array. If `f` shortens the array (through
another reference to it), `map` panics, where JS would return an array with holes.

members.name: filter
members.signature: filter<E>(keep: (x: T, i: i64) => bool throws E): T[] throws E
members.doc:
Returns the elements of an array that meet the condition specified in a callback function.
The elements themselves are returned, like JS: objects are shared, not copied.
members.summary: Returns the elements of an array that meet the condition specified in a callback function.

params.name: keep
params.doc:
A function that accepts up to two arguments, the element and its index. The
filter method calls `keep` one time for each element in the array.

members.name: reduce
members.signature: reduce<A, E>(f: (acc: A, x: T, i: i64) => A throws E, init: A): A throws E
members.doc:
Calls the specified callback function for all the elements in an array. The return value of
the callback function is the accumulated result, and is provided as an argument in the next
call to the callback function.
members.summary: Calls the specified callback function for all the elements in an array.

params.name: f
params.doc:
A function that accepts up to three arguments: the accumulated value, the element
and its index. The reduce method calls `f` one time for each element in the array.

params.name: init
params.doc:
The initial value of the accumulation, passed to the first call of `f`.
Unlike JS, it is required.

tags.returns: the accumulated value: `init` for an empty array.

members.name: find
members.signature: find<E>(pred: (x: T, i: i64) => bool throws E): T | undefined throws E
members.doc: First element matching `pred` (see header), or `undefined`.
members.summary: First element matching `pred` (see header), or `undefined`.

members.doc: Index of the first element matching `pred`, or -1.
members.summary: Index of the first element matching `pred`, or -1.

members.doc: Last element matching `pred` (see header), or `undefined`.
members.summary: Last element matching `pred` (see header), or `undefined`.

members.summary: Index of the last element matching `pred`, or -1.

members.name: at
members.doc:
The element at `index` (negative counts from the end; see header), or `undefined` when
out of range.
members.summary: The element at `index` (negative counts from the end; see header), or `undefined` when out of range.

members.name: fill
members.doc:
Sets the elements in [start, end) to `value` (positions as in `slice`). JS also returns
the array; here the result is `void`, like `reverse` and `sort`: returning the array would
share it, which makes every array of its type reference counted in the whole program.
`new Array<T>(n).fill(v)` still works (the compiler builds the array in one step).
members.summary: Sets the elements in [start, end) to `value` (positions as in `slice`).

members.name: some
members.signature: some<E>(pred: (x: T, i: i64) => bool throws E): bool throws E
members.doc: Determines whether the specified callback function returns true for any element of an array.
members.summary: Determines whether the specified callback function returns true for any element of an array.

params.name: pred
params.doc:
A function that accepts up to two arguments, the element and its index. The
some method calls `pred` for each element in the array until it returns true, or until the
end of the array.

members.name: every
members.signature: every<E>(pred: (x: T, i: i64) => bool throws E): bool throws E
members.doc: Determines whether all the members of an array satisfy the specified test.
members.summary: Determines whether all the members of an array satisfy the specified test.

params.name: pred
params.doc:
A function that accepts up to two arguments, the element and its index. The
every method calls `pred` for each element in the array until it returns false, or until the
end of the array.

members.name: indexOf
members.doc:
Position of the first element `===` `x`, or -1: objects by identity, numbers by value, so
`NaN` is never found and `null` does not find `undefined` (JS `indexOf` semantics).
members.summary: Position of the first element `===` `x`, or -1: objects by identity, numbers by value, so `NaN` is never found and `null` does not find `undefined` (JS `indexOf` semantics).

members.name: lastIndexOf
members.doc:
Returns the index of the last occurrence of a specified value in an array, or -1 if it is not
present. Compares like `indexOf`.
members.summary: Returns the index of the last occurrence of a specified value in an array, or -1 if it is not present.

params.doc: The value to locate in the array.

Determines whether an array includes a certain element, returning true or false as
appropriate. Compares like `indexOf` (objects by identity, tuples part by part), except

members.summary: Determines whether an array includes a certain element, returning true or false as appropriate.

params.name: x
params.doc: The element to search for.

members.doc:
The elements in [start, end), themselves (objects are shared, as in JS). JS semantics:

defaults to the length.
members.summary: The elements in [start, end), themselves (objects are shared, as in JS).

members.summary: New array with this array's elements followed by `other`'s.

`this[index]` read where the program expects `T | undefined` (the compiler calls it, sema

of range, negative or not a whole number), as in JS.

modules.doc:
Prelude: the array methods that change an array in place or copy it changed (`splice`, `shift`,
`unshift`, `reverse`, `with`, `toSpliced`, …), and `length`, `entries` and `join` (array.velt
has the others).
modules.summary: Prelude: the array methods that change an array in place or copy it changed (`splice`, `shift`, `unshift`, `reverse`, `with`, `toSpliced`, …), and `length`, `entries` and `join` (array.velt has the others).

members.name: swap
members.doc:
Exchanges elements `i` and `j` (each must be below the length): their bits change places,
nothing is copied or dropped.
members.summary: Exchanges elements `i` and `j` (each must be below the length): their bits change places, nothing is copied or dropped.

members.name: rotateLeft
members.doc:
Rotates the elements in `[start, end)` one place down: the one at `start` moves to `end - 1`
and the others one place towards `start`, by one memory move (what `splice` would do with
a removal and an insert). `end` must be at most the length, `start` at most `end`.
members.summary: Rotates the elements in `[start, end)` one place down: the one at `start` moves to `end - 1` and the others one place towards `start`, by one memory move (what `splice` would do with a removal and an insert).

members.name: rotateRight
members.doc: As `rotateLeft`, one place up: the element at `end - 1` moves to `start`.
members.summary: As `rotateLeft`, one place up: the element at `end - 1` moves to `start`.

members.name: prefetch
members.doc:
A hint that element `i` is read soon: the CPU starts loading it, so that the read does not
wait for memory (a hint only, it changes nothing; an index past the end does nothing).
members.summary: A hint that element `i` is read soon: the CPU starts loading it, so that the read does not wait for memory (a hint only, it changes nothing; an index past the end does nothing).

members.name: reserve
members.doc: Makes room for `extra` more elements without growing again (the length stays).
members.summary: Makes room for `extra` more elements without growing again (the length stays).

members.name: reverse
members.doc: Reverses in place (JS also returns the array; here the result is `void`, see `fill`).
members.summary: Reverses in place (JS also returns the array; here the result is `void`, see `fill`).

members.name: splice
members.signature: splice(start: i64, deleteCount: i64 = 9223372036854775807, ... items: T[] = ): T[]
members.doc:
Removes `deleteCount` elements from `start` (positions as in `slice`; omitted: the rest),
inserts `items` there, and returns the removed elements, like JS. O(length).
members.summary: Removes `deleteCount` elements from `start` (positions as in `slice`; omitted: the rest), inserts `items` there, and returns the removed elements, like JS.

members.name: shift
members.doc:
Removes and returns the first element, or `undefined` when the array is empty.
O(length): the other elements move down by one, as V8 does for large arrays. A queue that
takes from the front belongs in a `Deque` (velt/collections/deque), which does it in O(1).
members.summary: Removes and returns the first element, or `undefined` when the array is empty.

members.name: unshift
members.doc:
Inserts `items` at the front, in order, and returns the new length, like JS. O(length +
items): the items are pushed, then rotated to the front by three reversals.
members.summary: Inserts `items` at the front, in order, and returns the new length, like JS.

members.name: truncate
members.doc:
Shortens the array to `length` elements, dropping the rest (JS `xs.length = n`); a longer
`length` leaves it unchanged. Panics on a negative `length`, like JS's RangeError.
members.summary: Shortens the array to `length` elements, dropping the rest (JS `xs.length = n`); a longer `length` leaves it unchanged.

members.name: length
members.doc:
The number of elements, for `xs.length -= k` and `xs.length--` (which set it through the
setter below); a plain read of `xs.length` compiles to the length itself.
members.summary: The number of elements, for `xs.length -= k` and `xs.length--` (which set it through the setter below); a plain read of `xs.length` compiles to the length itself.

members.name: length
members.doc:
`xs.length = n`, as in JS: drops the elements from `n` on (`xs.length = 0` empties the
array). A length that is not a whole number from 0 to 2^52 - 1, the most elements a Velt
array holds (JS stops at 2^32 - 1), panics with `RangeError: Invalid array length`
(`arrayLength`). A larger `n` than the array's length panics too: JS would add empty
slots, which Velt has no value for (push the elements, or build the array with
`new Array<T>(n).fill(v)`).
members.summary: `xs.length = n`, as in JS: drops the elements from `n` on (`xs.length = 0` empties the array).

members.name: toReversed
members.doc: The elements in reverse order.
members.summary: The elements in reverse order.

members.name: toSpliced
members.signature: toSpliced(start: i64, deleteCount: i64 = 9223372036854775807, ... items: T[] = ): T[]
members.doc:
`splice(start, deleteCount, ...items)` on a copy: the array with the elements removed and
`items` inserted.
members.summary: `splice(start, deleteCount, ...items)` on a copy: the array with the elements removed and `items` inserted.

members.name: with
members.doc:
A copy with `value` at `index` (negative counts from the end). Panics like JS's RangeError
when `index` is out of range.
members.summary: A copy with `value` at `index` (negative counts from the end).

members.name: isEmpty
members.doc: Whether the array has no elements (`xs.length == 0`).
members.summary: Whether the array has no elements (`xs.length == 0`).

members.name: entries
members.doc:
`[index, element]` pairs (see header). JS returns an iterator; an array
serves the same `for (const [i, x] of xs.entries())` loops.
members.summary: `[index, element]` pairs (see header).

members.name: join
members.doc:
`join` for element types without their own (string enums, literal unions, objects): each
element as JS's `String(x)` writes an array element (a class instance through its
`toString()`, `[object Object]` for another object, `[object Map]` for a map). A struct
with its own `toString()`, an `Error` or a `RegExp` element is a compile error: write
`xs.map((x) => x.toString()).join(sep)`. Strings, numbers and bools have exact ones
below; arrays of arrays and of nullable elements have JS's in array_nested.velt.
members.summary: `join` for element types without their own (string enums, literal unions, objects): each element as JS's `String(x)` writes an array element (a class instance through its `toString()`, `[object Object]` for another object, `[object Map]` for a map).

Exchanges `this[a][i]` and `this[b][j]` (every index must be in range), also between two
inner arrays, where `[x, y] = [y, x]` would count and drop the elements it copies: their
bits change places, nothing is copied or dropped. For data kept in chunks (`T[][]`).

exports.doc:
Deep equality (`deepEqual`: contents, not identity). On failure throws an `AssertionError`
whose message shows both values, as Node's `util.inspect` writes them (`'a'`, `[ 1, 2 ]`).

exports.signature: function deepEqual<T>(a: T, b: T): bool

Deep (structural) equality, like Node's `util.isDeepStrictEqual`: arrays, structs and object
literals compare their contents, recursively; `Map` and `Record` their keys and values in any
key order; other class instances by identity. `==` compares every object by identity, like JS.

Calls `f` and returns the error it throws, so a test can check it

modules.doc: Prelude: `AsyncGenerator<T, E, N>`, what an `async function*` returns (docs/internals/design/iteration.md).
modules.summary: Prelude: `AsyncGenerator<T, E, N>`, what an `async function*` returns (docs/internals/design/iteration.md).

exports.name: AsyncGenerator
exports.signature: class AsyncGenerator<T, E = never> implements AsyncIterator<T, E>, AsyncIterable<T, E>, AsyncIterableIterator<T, E>
exports.doc:
An async generator (`async function*`, docs/reference/functions.md "Async generators"): what
calling one creates. Each `next()` runs the body up to its next `yield`, awaiting what the body
awaits on the way; its promise rejects with what the body throws (`E`). `return()` closes a
generator suspended at a `yield`: its `finally` blocks run (and may `await`) and its `using`
/ `await using` values are disposed, as if the `yield` were a `return`. Dropping it closes it
too, without awaiting: cleanup that would `await` is then cancelled (drops only), like a
cancelled async function. After it finished, threw, or was closed, `next()` reports `done`.

Like JS, `next()` and `return()` calls are queued: a call made while another one is still
running waits for its turn, so each promise settles with its own step, in call order. A call
whose promise nobody awaits still takes its turn (its value is dropped).

The compiler creates these objects: the generator's state follows the class's fields, and the
queue fields start at zero.
exports.summary: An async generator (`async function*`, docs/reference/functions.md "Async generators"): what calling one creates.

members.name: next
members.doc:
Runs the body up to its next `yield` (awaiting what it awaits) and resolves to that value,
or a `done` result; rejects with what the body throws. Calls are queued, in call order.
members.summary: Runs the body up to its next `yield` (awaiting what it awaits) and resolves to that value, or a `done` result; rejects with what the body throws.

members.name: return
members.doc:
Closes the generator: a body suspended at a `yield` runs its `finally` blocks (which may
`await`) and disposes its `using` values. Resolves to a finished result.
members.summary: Closes the generator: a body suspended at a `yield` runs its `finally` blocks (which may `await`) and disposes its `using` values.

members.doc: An async generator is its own iterator.
members.summary: An async generator is its own iterator.

members.summary: `await using` support: closes the generator, like `return()`.

members.name: [Symbol.dispose]

modules.doc:
Prelude: `Atomic<T>` (docs/std/sync.md, docs/internals/design/atomics.md), and the interfaces
that bound what one holds (`AtomicValue`) and what may be shared without a lock (`Frozen`). The
compiler turns every call of an `Atomic` method into the instruction with the ordering its call
site names; the bodies here, `seqcst` whatever the ordering (only ever stronger), run only
through a function value of a method.

Lowering calls `pin` and `unpin` around a function that loads an `Atomic` of a `shared` value,
and `retire` for each reference such an `Atomic` gives up (velt_vir `epoch_sections.rs`,
`atomic_ref.rs`).
modules.summary: Prelude: `Atomic<T>` (docs/std/sync.md, docs/internals/design/atomics.md), and the interfaces that bound what one holds (`AtomicValue`) and what may be shared without a lock (`Frozen`).

exports.name: Atomic
exports.doc:
A number, `bool` or `shared` value that threads read and change at once, without a lock:
`new Atomic<u64>(0)`
(docs/std/sync.md). It is stored in place, as a plain `T`, in the object or array that holds
it, and it is the one part of a `shared<T>` that changes: `s.hits.add(1)` changes the word in
the `shared` value every thread reads. Each method is one instruction (or a short loop where
the CPU has none). `T` is an integer type, `f64`, `f32` or `bool`; a float's `add`, `sub`,
`max` and `min` are compare-and-swap loops. `T` may also be `shared<U>` or `shared<U> | null`:
`load`, `store` and `exchange` then move references, and `compareExchange` compares identity
and returns whether it swapped (docs/std/sync.md). An `Atomic<string>` is the same, except that
`compareExchange` compares contents.

Every method takes a memory ordering, `"seqcst"` when left out, as JavaScript's `Atomics`:
`"relaxed"` (only this word is atomic), `"acquire"` (later reads see what the thread that
released saw), `"release"`, `"acqrel"` (both) or `"seqcst"` (also one order of all `seqcst`
operations). It must be a string literal. An `Atomic` cannot be copied or shared, only used
where it is: `a.load()` reads it.
exports.summary: A number, `bool` or `shared` value that threads read and change at once, without a lock: `new Atomic<u64>(0)` (docs/std/sync.md).

members.name: load
members.doc: The value.
members.summary: The value.

members.name: store
members.doc: Makes `v` the value.
members.summary: Makes `v` the value.

members.name: exchange
members.doc: Makes `v` the value; returns the previous one.
members.summary: Makes `v` the value; returns the previous one.

members.name: compareExchange
members.signature: compareExchange(expected: T, v: T, order: "relaxed" | "acquire" | "release" | "acqrel" | "seqcst" = "seqcst", failure: "relaxed" | "acquire" | "seqcst" = "seqcst"): T
members.doc:
Makes `v` the value if it is `expected`; returns the previous value, which is `expected`
when it did. `failure` is the ordering of the read when it did not (by default `order`
without its release part). On an `Atomic` of a `shared` value it compares identity (the same
reference), on an `Atomic<string>` contents, and returns whether it made `v` the value; when
it did not, `v` is dropped.
members.summary: Makes `v` the value if it is `expected`; returns the previous value, which is `expected` when it did.

members.name: compareExchangeWeak
members.signature: compareExchangeWeak(expected: T, v: T, order: "relaxed" | "acquire" | "release" | "acqrel" | "seqcst" = "seqcst", failure: "relaxed" | "acquire" | "seqcst" = "seqcst"): bool
members.doc:
`compareExchange` that may fail even when the value is `expected` (call it in a loop), and
that is cheaper on CPUs without a compare-and-swap instruction; returns whether it made `v`
the value.
members.summary: `compareExchange` that may fail even when the value is `expected` (call it in a loop), and that is cheaper on CPUs without a compare-and-swap instruction; returns whether it made `v` the value.

members.doc:

power and gives a sibling hardware thread its turn (`pause`, `isb`). It changes no memory.
members.summary: A hint for a loop that waits for another thread to change a value: the CPU spends less power and gives a sibling hardware thread its turn (`pause`, `isb`).

exports.name: AtomicValue
exports.doc:
The types an `Atomic` can hold: the integer types, `f32`, `f64`, `bool`, `string` and
`shared` values (and `shared<U> | null`); the compiler knows which, so no type declares it. A
type parameter bounded by it (`T extends AtomicValue`) may be an `Atomic`'s `T` in generic
code, checked where the generic is instantiated.
exports.summary: The types an `Atomic` can hold: the integer types, `f32`, `f64`, `bool`, `string` and `shared` values (and `shared<U> | null`); the compiler knows which, so no type declares it.

exports.name: Frozen
exports.doc:
The types whose `shared` values are read in place, without a lock or a copy: what holds no
`Mutex`, weak reference, promise, function or interface value, and no class with subclasses
or a `clone()` of its own. The compiler knows which, so no type declares it (an `extends` or
`implements` of it is an error). With a type parameter bounded by it (`V extends Frozen`),
generic code reads a `shared<V>` as a `V`, checked where the generic is instantiated.
exports.summary: The types whose `shared` values are read in place, without a lock or a copy: what holds no `Mutex`, weak reference, promise, function or interface value, and no class with subclasses or a `clone()` of its own.

modules.doc:
Prelude: Node `Buffer`-style bulk operations on byte arrays (`u8[]`): short searches and XOR
masking sixteen bytes at a time with SIMD vectors (velt/lang/bytes/search, in Velt so that they
are compiled into their caller), text in bytes (velt/lang/bytes/text); long searches by memchr,
copying and filling by memmove and memset in the runtime.

A byte array is a plain `u8[]` (Velt has no separate `Uint8Array` type), so every array
method works on it too; the methods here replace the generic ones of the same name for `u8[]`.
`Buffer.alloc(n)` makes a zeroed array in one allocation (calloc: large arrays cost no
memset). Positions follow JS: negative ones count from the end.
modules.summary: Prelude: Node `Buffer`-style bulk operations on byte arrays (`u8[]`): short searches and XOR masking sixteen bytes at a time with SIMD vectors (velt/lang/bytes/search, in Velt so that they are compiled into their caller), text in bytes (velt/lang/bytes/text); long searches by memchr, copying and filling by memmove and memset in the runtime.

`base64` / `base64url` the decoded size. Names ignore case; an unknown one counts UTF-8, as

exports.name: structuredClone
exports.doc:
An independent deep copy of `value`, like JS's `structuredClone`: arrays, maps, sets, dates
and object types are copied all the way down (`value.clone()`), so changing the copy never
changes the original. What JS can't clone is a compile error: a function (JS throws a
`DataCloneError`) and an instance of a class of your own (JS copies it as a plain object,
without its class; write `value.clone()` for a copy that keeps it).
exports.summary: An independent deep copy of `value`, like JS's `structuredClone`: arrays, maps, sets, dates and object types are copied all the way down (`value.clone()`), so changing the copy never changes the original.

modules.doc:
Prelude: the builtin ordering interface.

`a.compareTo(b)` is < 0 when `a` sorts before `b`, > 0 when after, 0 when equivalent.
A generic `T extends Comparable<T>` can use `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` (they call `compareTo`).
Implemented here for every number type, `string` (UTF-16 code-unit order, as JS's `<`) and
`bool` (`false` first); an `extend` block defining `compareTo(other: X): i64` makes `X`
Comparable, and classes and structs can declare `implements Comparable<X>`. Floats order NaN
after every other value (and equal to itself), the total order `sort()` uses.
modules.summary: Prelude: the builtin ordering interface.

exports.name: Comparable
exports.doc:
A type with an order: `T extends Comparable<T>` lets generic code use `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`,
which call `compareTo`. Every number type, `string` and `bool` implement it; an `extend`
block or a class with `compareTo(other: X): i64` makes `X` one.
exports.summary: A type with an order: `T extends Comparable<T>` lets generic code use `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`, which call `compareTo`.

modules.doc:
Prelude: the JS `Date` object. An instant as milliseconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, held as a
number (NaN for an invalid date), with JS's conventions: months are 0-11, the plain getters and
setters are local time (the OS time zone, DST-aware) and the `UTC` ones are UTC, and strings
parse like `Date.parse` (a date alone is UTC, a date-time without an offset is local time).
The calendar arithmetic is velt/time/datetime's; prefer its `DateTime` (UTC-first, months 1-12) in
new code.

Differences from JS: `toString()` has no time zone name in parentheses, and the `toLocale…`
methods always use the `en-US` format.
modules.summary: Prelude: the JS `Date` object.

exports.name: Date
exports.doc:
Enables basic storage and retrieval of dates and times: an instant in milliseconds since
1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, NaN for an invalid date, with JS's conventions (months 0-11, local-time
and UTC getters and setters). Prefer `velt/time/datetime`'s `DateTime` in new code.
exports.summary: Enables basic storage and retrieval of dates and times: an instant in milliseconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, NaN for an invalid date, with JS's conventions (months 0-11, local-time and UTC getters and setters).

modules.doc:
Prelude: `any` and `unknown`, the dynamic value (issue #924, docs/reference/types.md "any
and unknown"), and `object` and `Function`, the dynamic value restricted to objects and to
functions (issue #926, docs/reference/types.md "object and Function").

Both are interfaces every type implements (the compiler adds the implementation): a value
converted to one is boxed with its type's descriptor, the interface table. They share one
representation; `unknown` must be narrowed before use, `any` converts to a typed value with
a check at run time (a `TypeError` when the value has another type).

The file name sorts last, so the prelude modules before it keep their indexes (and the
symbols of programs that use no `any` stay the same).
modules.summary: Prelude: `any` and `unknown`, the dynamic value (issue #924, docs/reference/types.md "any and unknown"), and `object` and `Function`, the dynamic value restricted to objects and to functions (issue #926, docs/reference/types.md "object and Function").

modules.doc:
Prelude: `Error`, the base class of every error thrown by std (`IoError`, `JsonError`).

A function's error type is the union of what it can throw, so a call that can fail in two ways
(e.g. `Response.json()` of a fetch: I/O, then JSON decoding) throws `IoError | JsonError`, and
`catch (e) { e.message }` works either way (every member has `message`). User error classes
extend it too.

exports.name: JSON
exports.doc:
Converts values to and from the JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) format. Unlike JS, it is
typed: `stringify` and `parse` are generated for the static type at compile time, `parse<T>`
checks the text against `T` and throws `JsonError` instead of returning `any`. There is no
`JSON.parse(text, reviver)` until #924; `JSON.parseValue(text).revive(reviver)` does what it
does. `stringify` takes JS's `replacer` (an array of
keys, `null`, or a `JsonReplacer` function) and its `space`. `parseValue` reads a document
of any shape.
exports.summary: Converts values to and from the JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) format.

members.name: stringify
members.doc: JS `JSON.stringify`: no whitespace, fields in declaration order, null optional fields omitted.
members.summary: JS `JSON.stringify`: no whitespace, fields in declaration order, null optional fields omitted.

members.signature: static parse<T>(text: string, options: JsonParseOptions | null = null): T
members.doc:
Decodes `text` into a `T` (throws `JsonError`); unknown object keys are skipped unless

members.summary: Decodes `text` into a `T` (throws `JsonError`); unknown object keys are skipped unless `options.unknownKeys` is "reject".

members.signature: static parseValue(text: string, options: JsonParseOptions | null = null): JsonValue
members.doc:
Parses any JSON document (throws `JsonError`); the options are `maxDepth`, `comments` and
`trailingCommas`.
members.summary: Parses any JSON document (throws `JsonError`); the options are `maxDepth`, `comments` and `trailingCommas`.

exports.summary: Invalid JSON, or JSON that does not match the type asked for: a `SyntaxError`, as in JS.

exports.name: JsonParseOptions
exports.signature: type JsonParseOptions = { unknownKeys?: "ignore" | "reject"; maxDepth?: i64; comments?: "error" | "skip"; trailingCommas?: bool }
exports.doc:
Options of `JSON.parse<T>(text, options)`; every field may be left out.
- `unknownKeys`: "reject" makes an object key the target type has no field for an error,
  `unknown field at $.key` (default "ignore": it is skipped).
- `maxDepth`: the deepest nesting of arrays and objects allowed (default 128, like serde_json:
  a typed decoder recurses per level, so a much higher limit can overflow the stack).
- `comments`: "skip" reads line (`//`) and block comments as whitespace (JSONC, as in
  `tsconfig.json`; default "error").
- `trailingCommas`: true accepts a comma before `]` and `}` (JSONC; default false).
exports.summary: Options of `JSON.parse<T>(text, options)`; every field may be left out.

exports.name: JsonReplacer
exports.signature: type JsonReplacer = (key: string, value: JsonValue) => JsonValue | undefined
exports.doc:
A replacer function of `JSON.stringify(value, replacer, space)`: called with each key and the
JSON form of its value (the value passed itself under the key `""` first), it returns the
value to write there, or `undefined` to leave a member out (an array element is then `null`).
exports.summary: A replacer function of `JSON.stringify(value, replacer, space)`: called with each key and the JSON form of its value (the value passed itself under the key `""` first), it returns the value to write there, or `undefined` to leave a member out (an array element is then `null`).

exports.name: JsonValue
exports.doc:
A JSON value of any shape, as `JSON.parseValue` returns it (`velt/encoding/json` calls it `Value`). It
has value semantics: an edit never shows through a clone, a parent or a child. Accessors on
the wrong kind return null / 0. `JSON.stringify` and `JSON.parse<T>` read and write it. Only
std makes one: the constructor is private, so no class can extend `JsonValue`.

Two forms (#1660). A parsed value is a position on a tape (velt/encoding/json/tape): reading it makes
nothing, and its children share the tape. A value built or edited here (`object()`, `set`, …)
or read from a database driver is a tree of reference-counted runtime nodes behind `#handle`
(which stays the first field: compiled glue writes it); an edit turns a tape value into such
a tree first, so it never shows through the tape.
exports.summary: A JSON value of any shape, as `JSON.parseValue` returns it (`velt/encoding/json` calls it `Value`).

members.summary: Parses any JSON document, like `JSON.parseValue` (throws `JsonError`).

members.name: revive
members.doc:
`JSON.parse(text, reviver)`'s second step, as JavaScript applies it: from the innermost
values out, `reviver(key, value)` gives each member's new value (`undefined`: the member is
deleted; an array element becomes `null`), and last the value itself, under the key `""`.
Returns the new value; this one is unchanged. `undefined` for the value itself throws a
`TypeError` (JavaScript returns `undefined`, which a `JsonValue` can't be). The reviver's
value parameter must be written `v: JsonValue` until #924.
members.summary: `JSON.parse(text, reviver)`'s second step, as JavaScript applies it: from the innermost values out, `reviver(key, value)` gives each member's new value (`undefined`: the member is deleted; an array element becomes `null`), and last the value itself, under the key `""`.

exports.name: PropertyKey
exports.doc:
A property key, as in TypeScript's lib: a string, a number (converted to its string) or a
symbol. `Record<PropertyKey, V>` is a `Record<string, V>`, whose symbol keys are in a table
of their own.
exports.summary: A property key, as in TypeScript's lib: a string, a number (converted to its string) or a symbol.

exports.name: PropertyDescriptor
exports.signature: type PropertyDescriptor = { value?: any; writable?: boolean; get?: any; set?: any; enumerable?: boolean; configurable?: boolean }
exports.doc:
A property's attributes (TypeScript's `PropertyDescriptor`), as a `getOwnPropertyDescriptor`
trap answers them and `Reflect.getOwnPropertyDescriptor` gives them. A data property has
`value` and `writable`, an accessor property `get` and `set`; an attribute left out is
`false` (`value`, `get` and `set`: `undefined`). The fields are in the order Node prints a
descriptor's.
exports.summary: A property's attributes (TypeScript's `PropertyDescriptor`), as a `getOwnPropertyDescriptor` trap answers them and `Reflect.getOwnPropertyDescriptor` gives them.

exports.name: Proxy
exports.doc:
A proxy for another object: the operations on it run the handler's traps. Create one with
`new Proxy(target, handler)`; the result is an `any`.
exports.summary: A proxy for another object: the operations on it run the handler's traps.

members.name: constructor
members.doc: A proxy of `target` whose operations run the traps of `handler`.
members.summary: A proxy of `target` whose operations run the traps of `handler`.

members.name: [PROXY_GET_GETTER]
members.doc:
`p.twice` of a class getter on a class instance brand that is this proxy (velt_sema
`proxy_getters.rs`): the `get` trap's answer, with the proxy as its receiver. While the trap
runs, the read is marked on the proxy, so a trap that forwards it with
`Reflect.get(target, key, receiver)` stops with a `TypeError` there (#1732): Node would run
the getter with `this` the proxy, Velt runs it on the target. Without a `get` trap nothing
forwards a receiver, and the read is the target's, as in Node.
members.summary: `p.twice` of a class getter on a class instance brand that is this proxy (velt_sema `proxy_getters.rs`): the `get` trap's answer, with the proxy as its receiver.

members.name: [PROXY_READS_GETTER]
members.doc: Whether this proxy's `get` trap is answering a brand's class getter read of `key`.
members.summary: Whether this proxy's `get` trap is answering a brand's class getter read of `key`.

members.name: [PROXY_VIEW]
members.doc:
A view of `target` as an object type (velt_vir `lower/any_view.rs`): an `any` holding an
object of another type converted to an object type. It has no traps, so every read and
write reaches the target, and converting the view back to `any` gives the target itself:
to the program the view is the target, as in Node. The conversion calls this only for an
object without a live view: it asks the runtime's table of views first (`any_view.rs`).
members.summary: A view of `target` as an object type (velt_vir `lower/any_view.rs`): an `any` holding an object of another type converted to an object type.

members.name: [PROXY_IS_VIEW]
members.doc: Whether this proxy is a view (`[PROXY_VIEW]`).
members.summary: Whether this proxy is a view (`[PROXY_VIEW]`).

members.name: [PROXY_PLAIN]
members.doc:
Whether the handler has no `get`, `set` or `has` trap: then a method call through this
proxy is the call on the target (`[PROXY_TARGET]`), since the method's reads and writes of `this`
could not tell the difference. (The key traps, `ownKeys`, `deleteProperty`, ..., don't run
for a method call.) An array target's methods run through the proxy (`[PROXY_ARRAY_CALL]`).
members.summary: Whether the handler has no `get`, `set` or `has` trap: then a method call through this proxy is the call on the target (`[PROXY_TARGET]`), since the method's reads and writes of `this` could not tell the difference.

members.name: [PROXY_HAS_GET]
members.doc:
Whether the handler has a `get` trap: a method called on a typed proxy needs it to read
the method (not supported yet, #823).
members.summary: Whether the handler has a `get` trap: a method called on a typed proxy needs it to read the method (not supported yet, #823).

`JSON.stringify` of this proxy: the value Node serializes in its place, read through the

exports.name: ArrayBufferView
exports.doc:
TypeScript's `ArrayBufferView`: a typed array or a `DataView` (`buffer`, `byteOffset`,
`byteLength`). A type only, as in JS.
exports.summary: TypeScript's `ArrayBufferView`: a typed array or a `DataView` (`buffer`, `byteOffset`, `byteLength`).

exports.name: DataView
exports.doc:
A view of a byte range of an `ArrayBuffer` for numbers of any size at any offset (JS
`DataView`): `getUint16(offset, littleEndian)`, `setFloat64(offset, value, littleEndian)`, ….
Multi-byte values are big-endian unless `littleEndian` is true, as in JS. An access outside
the view throws a `RangeError`.
exports.summary: A view of a byte range of an `ArrayBuffer` for numbers of any size at any offset (JS `DataView`): `getUint16(offset, littleEndian)`, `setFloat64(offset, value, littleEndian)`, ….

exports.name: Uint8Array
exports.signature: class Uint8Array extends TypedArray implements Iterable<number>
exports.doc:
An array of 8-bit unsigned integers (bytes) in an `ArrayBuffer` (JS `Uint8Array`): `new Uint8Array(n)` (`n` zeros),
`new Uint8Array([1, 2])` (a copy, converted), `new Uint8Array(buffer, byteOffset, length)` (a view of
`buffer`, sharing it), or a copy of another typed array.

modules.doc:
Prelude: the modules implicitly imported into every program, in the order the compiler loads
them (docs/internals/design/std-layout.md §4). The loader reads this list, not the folder: a
new prelude file is added here, and a test checks that every file is listed once. Only
side-effect imports of files in this folder (`import "./name";`) and comments may appear.

The core types and their methods come first, in name order. The dynamic types (`dynamic`:
`any`, `unknown`, `object`, `Function`) come next, and the compiler's hooks last (`hooks`:
velt/lang/hooks, with the interface adapters and the methods and operators of `any`).
modules.summary: Prelude: the modules implicitly imported into every program, in the order the compiler loads them (docs/internals/design/std-layout.md §4).

modules.doc:
Prelude: the iteration protocol (docs/reference/control-flow.md "for...of").

`for (const x of src)` works on arrays, on `Map`s and other classes with `entries()`, and on
any `Iterable<T, E>`: it calls `src[Symbol.iterator]()` once, then `next()` until a result
is `done`, and calls the iterator's `return()` when the loop is left early (`break`,
`return`, a thrown error). `E` is what `next()` throws (`never`: nothing); the loop throws
it too. Velt has no `undefined`, so a finished result has no `value` (reading `r.value`
without narrowing gives `T | null`).
modules.summary: Prelude: the iteration protocol (docs/reference/control-flow.md "for...of").

exports.signature: type IteratorResult<T> = { value: T; done: false } | { done: true }
exports.doc:
One step of an iterator: `{ value, done: false }` for the next value, `{ done: true }` once it
is finished (Velt has no `undefined`: a finished result has no `value`).
exports.summary: One step of an iterator: `{ value, done: false }` for the next value, `{ done: true }` once it is finished (Velt has no `undefined`: a finished result has no `value`).

exports.name: Generator
exports.signature: class Generator<T, E = never, N = never> implements Iterator<T, E>, Iterable<T, E>, IterableIterator<T, E>, IteratorObject<T, E>
exports.doc:
A generator (`function*`, docs/reference/functions.md "Generators"): what calling one creates.
The body runs lazily, one `next()` at a time, up to its next `yield`. `return()` (or dropping
the generator, or `using`) closes a generator suspended at a `yield`: its `finally` blocks run
and its `using` values are disposed, as if the `yield` were a `return`. After it finished,
threw, or was closed, `next()` reports `done` forever. `E` is what the body throws.

The compiler creates these objects: the generator's state follows the class's fields.
exports.summary: A generator (`function*`, docs/reference/functions.md "Generators"): what calling one creates.

members.name: next
members.doc: Runs the body up to its next `yield` and returns that value, or a `done` result.
members.summary: Runs the body up to its next `yield` and returns that value, or a `done` result.

members.name: throw
members.signature: throw(e: any): IteratorResult<T> throws E | any
members.doc:
Resumes the body with `e` thrown at the paused `yield`: a `try` around it catches it (and
the result is the body's next step), else the generator is closed (its `finally` blocks
run) and `throw()` throws `e`. A generator that has not started or is finished throws `e`
at once (and is done). `e` is an `any`, as in TypeScript.
members.summary: Resumes the body with `e` thrown at the paused `yield`: a `try` around it catches it (and the result is the body's next step), else the generator is closed (its `finally` blocks run) and `throw()` throws `e`.

members.name: return
members.doc:
Closes the generator: a body suspended at a `yield` runs its `finally` blocks and disposes
its `using` values. Returns a finished result.
members.summary: Closes the generator: a body suspended at a `yield` runs its `finally` blocks and disposes its `using` values.

modules.doc:
Prelude, loaded on use: `JSON`, `JsonError` and `JsonValue` (rt_abi_async.md §12.3–12.5; `JsonValue`
is in json_value.velt, `JsonError` in json_error.velt, the replacer and `space` of
`JSON.stringify` in layout.velt). A
program loads this module when one of its modules names one of them (the global
std/prelude/global/json.velt) or imports a std module that uses them.

`JSON.stringify<T>` / `JSON.parse<T>` are generated per type at compile time by the source
generators of velt/encoding/json (a string builder for stringify, a pull-reader decoder for
parse); parse failures throw a `SyntaxError` `JsonError` ("expected string at $.name"). The
generated code writes a `JsonValue` (at any depth) with its `[JSON_WRITE](b)`, decodes one with
`JsonValue[JSON_FROM_READER](r)`, and `console.log` prints one from the runtime tree
`[JSON_RUNTIME_HANDLE]()` makes for it (freed after); the keys are std/lang/hooks/keys.velt's,
which no program can name.

`JSON.parseValue` gives a `JsonValue` for data of unknown shape: a position on a tape (one
flat array per document, velt/encoding/json/tape), which its children share. A value built or edited
here is a tree of reference-counted runtime nodes behind an opaque `u64` handle
(rt_abi_async.md §3.2; 0 is the null handle, which a `JsonValue` holds for JSON null); an edit
turns a tape value into such a tree first.
Values have value semantics: `set`/`delete`/`push`/`setAt` copy a node another handle shares
before changing it (copy-on-write), so an edit never shows through a clone, a parent or a
child. Every `JsonValue` owns one reference to its tape or tree (`get`/`at`/`clone` return
new ones; children stay valid after their parent is released); a tree's is released by the
`[Symbol.dispose]()` drop hook. A value that contains a `JsonValue` has no automatic deep
`clone()` (sema rejects it: the generated copy could not take a new reference).
modules.summary: Prelude, loaded on use: `JSON`, `JsonError` and `JsonValue` (rt_abi_async.md §12.3–12.5; `JsonValue` is in json_value.velt, `JsonError` in json_error.velt, the replacer and `space` of `JSON.stringify` in layout.velt).

exports.name: JSON
exports.doc:
Converts values to and from the JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) format. Unlike JS, it is
typed: `stringify` and `parse` are generated for the static type at compile time, `parse<T>`
checks the text against `T` and throws `JsonError` instead of returning `any`. There is no
`JSON.parse(text, reviver)` until #924; `JSON.parseValue(text).revive(reviver)` does what it
does. `stringify` takes JS's `replacer` (an array of
keys, `null`, or a `JsonReplacer` function) and its `space`. `parseValue` reads a document
of any shape.
exports.summary: Converts values to and from the JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) format.

exports.name: JsonParseOptions
exports.signature: type JsonParseOptions = { unknownKeys?: "ignore" | "reject"; maxDepth?: i64; comments?: "error" | "skip"; trailingCommas?: bool }
exports.doc:
Options of `JSON.parse<T>(text, options)`; every field may be left out.
- `unknownKeys`: "reject" makes an object key the target type has no field for an error,
  `unknown field at $.key` (default "ignore": it is skipped).
- `maxDepth`: the deepest nesting of arrays and objects allowed (default 128, like serde_json:
  a typed decoder recurses per level, so a much higher limit can overflow the stack).
- `comments`: "skip" reads line (`//`) and block comments as whitespace (JSONC, as in
  `tsconfig.json`; default "error").
- `trailingCommas`: true accepts a comma before `]` and `}` (JSONC; default false).

exports.name: JsonValue
exports.doc:
A JSON value of any shape, as `JSON.parseValue` returns it (`velt/encoding/json` calls it `Value`). It
has value semantics: an edit never shows through a clone, a parent or a child. Accessors on
the wrong kind return null / 0. `JSON.stringify` and `JSON.parse<T>` read and write it. Only
std makes one: the constructor is private, so no class can extend `JsonValue`.

Two forms (#1660). A parsed value is a position on a tape (velt/encoding/json/tape): reading it makes
nothing, and its children share the tape. A value built or edited here (`object()`, `set`, …)
or read from a database driver is a tree of reference-counted runtime nodes behind `#handle`
(which stays the first field: compiled glue writes it); an edit turns a tape value into such
a tree first, so it never shows through the tape.
exports.summary: A JSON value of any shape, as `JSON.parseValue` returns it (`velt/encoding/json` calls it `Value`).

Prelude: `Map<K, V>`, an insertion-ordered hash map with JS `Map` semantics.
The layout, ownership and live iteration are described in std/lang/map/layout.velt.

exports.name: Map
exports.doc:
A collection of key/value pairs that remembers insertion order, with JS `Map` semantics:
re-setting a key keeps its position, and float keys compare like JS (`NaN` finds itself, `0`
and `-0` are one key). Numbers, `bool` and strings compare by value; objects (class instances,
object types, arrays, maps, records, interface and function values) by identity, as in JS, so
a key changed in place keeps its entry. Unlike JS, tuples compare part by part, as `===` does
(a tuple key is hashed when inserted: don't change it while it is in a map).
exports.summary: A collection of key/value pairs that remembers insertion order, with JS `Map` semantics: re-setting a key keeps its position, and float keys compare like JS (`NaN` finds itself, `0` and `-0` are one key).

members.name: constructor
members.doc:
A map holding `entries` (like JS `new Map(entries)`), in order; a later entry with the same
key replaces the value of an earlier one but keeps its position. Leaves `entries` as it is;
the map shares their keys and values, like JS. `new Map(iterable)` also takes any iterable
of pairs (a generator, another map), which the compiler collects into an array first.
members.summary: A map holding `entries` (like JS `new Map(entries)`), in order; a later entry with the same key replaces the value of an earlier one but keeps its position.

members.name: toFixed
members.doc:
`digits` (0 to 100) decimals, rounded like JS: to the nearest, and on an exact tie away from
zero (`(0.5).toFixed(0)` is "1", `(-1.25).toFixed(1)` is "-1.3"; `(1.005).toFixed(2)` is
"1.00" because 1.005 is really 1.00499…). From 1e21 up it is `String(x)`, as in JS.

members.name: toExponential
members.doc:
Exponential notation with `digits` (0 to 100) digits after the point, rounded like JS (to
the nearest, an exact tie away from zero): `(123.456).toExponential(2)` is "1.23e+2". Without
`digits`, as many as it takes to tell the value apart (`(123.456).toExponential()` is
"1.23456e+2"). `digits` is truncated as in JS (2.7 is 2, NaN is 0). `NaN` and ±Infinity are
`String(x)`, whatever `digits` is.
members.summary: Exponential notation with `digits` (0 to 100) digits after the point, rounded like JS (to the nearest, an exact tie away from zero): `(123.456).toExponential(2)` is "1.23e+2".

members.name: toPrecision
members.doc:
`precision` (1 to 100) significant digits, rounded like `toExponential`, in fixed notation
unless the exponent is below -6 or at least `precision`: `(123.456).toPrecision(4)` is
"123.5", `(123.456).toPrecision(2)` is "1.2e+2". `precision` is truncated as in JS (2.7 is
2). Without `precision`, `String(x)`.
members.summary: `precision` (1 to 100) significant digits, rounded like `toExponential`, in fixed notation unless the exponent is below -6 or at least `precision`: `(123.456).toPrecision(4)` is "123.5", `(123.456).toPrecision(2)` is "1.2e+2".

Returns the keys of a record as strings (a string enum key as its value): array-index keys
first, ascending, then the others in insertion order.
On other objects it lists their fields.

exports.signature: async function promiseAllSettled<T, E>(ps: Promise<T, E>[]): Promise<PromiseSettledResult<T, E>[]>
exports.doc:
`Promise.allSettled(ps)`: waits for every promise and reports each outcome, in order. The
promises already run concurrently (they started when created), so awaiting them one by one
settles when the last one does.
exports.summary: `Promise.allSettled(ps)`: waits for every promise and reports each outcome, in order.

exports.name: promiseAny
exports.signature: async function promiseAny<T, E>(ps: Promise<T, E>[]): Promise<T> throws AggregateError
exports.doc:
`Promise.any(ps)`: the first promise to fulfill; `AggregateError` when all of them reject
(or the array is empty).
exports.summary: `Promise.any(ps)`: the first promise to fulfill; `AggregateError` when all of them reject (or the array is empty).

exports.name: promiseNew
exports.signature: function promiseNew<T, E>(executor: (resolve: (value: T) => void, reject: (reason: E) => void) => void throws E): Promise<T, E>
exports.doc:
`new Promise<T, E>((resolve, reject) => ...)`: the compiler compiles the constructor to a call
of `promiseNew`. The executor runs at once and is released before anything waits, so
it can't keep the promise pending through a cycle; `resolve` and `reject` may be stored and
called later, from any task, and the first settlement wins. An error the executor throws
rejects the promise. A promise whose `resolve` and `reject` are all dropped without settling
never settles, like in JS: what awaits it waits until nothing else can happen, and the program
ends then.
exports.summary: `new Promise<T, E>((resolve, reject) => ...)`: the compiler compiles the constructor to a call of `promiseNew`.

exports.name: promiseNewResolveOnly
exports.signature: function promiseNewResolveOnly<T>(executor: (resolve: (value: T) => void) => void): Promise<T>
exports.doc: `new Promise<T>((resolve) => ...)`: an executor that only resolves.
exports.summary: `new Promise<T>((resolve) => ...)`: an executor that only resolves.

exports.name: PromiseWithResolvers
exports.signature: type PromiseWithResolvers<T, E> = { promise: Promise<T, E>; resolve: (value: T) => void; reject: (reason: E) => void }
exports.doc:
What `Promise.withResolvers<T, E>()` returns (ES2024): a pending promise and the functions
that settle it.
exports.summary: What `Promise.withResolvers<T, E>()` returns (ES2024): a pending promise and the functions that settle it.

exports.name: promiseWithResolvers
exports.doc:
`Promise.withResolvers<T, E>()`: the compiler compiles it to a call of `promiseWithResolvers`.
`resolve` and `reject` behave like a `new Promise` executor's: they may be stored, sent over
a channel or moved into a spawned task and called there, and the first settlement wins. A
promise whose `resolve` and `reject` are all dropped without settling never settles.
exports.summary: `Promise.withResolvers<T, E>()`: the compiler compiles it to a call of `promiseWithResolvers`.

exports.name: promiseResolve
exports.doc:
`Promise.resolve(value)`: a promise fulfilled with `value`. The compiler compiles
`Promise.resolve(v)` to a call of `promiseResolve`, and `Promise.resolve()` to one of
`promiseResolveVoid` (a `Promise<void>`).
exports.summary: `Promise.resolve(value)`: a promise fulfilled with `value`.

exports.name: promiseResolveVoid

exports.summary: `Promise.resolve()`: a fulfilled `Promise<void>`.

exports.summary: `Promise.reject(reason)`: a promise rejected with `reason`.

Prelude: `Record<K, V>` (docs/internals/design/record.md), a dictionary keyed by strings, a
union of string literal types or a string enum (the TypeScript `Object` helpers over it are in
object.velt).

A record has no members of its own: `r.name` reads the key "name". Sema turns `r[k]`, `r.name`,
`r[k] = v`, `delete r[k]` and object literals typed as a record into calls of the keyed
methods below (`[RECORD_GET]` for string keys, `[RECORD_AT]` for literal keys, which are always present).
Entries keep JavaScript's order: keys that are array indices (canonical `"0"` to
`"4294967294"`) first, ascending, then the others in insertion order. A key that is an array
index marks the record `unordered`; then the readers (`[RECORD_KEY_NAMES]`, `[RECORD_VALUES]`, `[RECORD_ENTRIES]`,
and the JSON and formatting glue through `[RECORD_POSITIONS]`) sort the entries they read, without
changing the record (they borrow it). A record without such keys pays one byte test per new
key (`Map[MAP_NEWEST_KEY_DIGIT]`, then `arrayIndex` for a key that starts with a digit). JSON reads
and writes a record as an object (a decoded record is checked for such keys once,
`[RECORD_DECODED]`), and `console.log` shows it like one.
modules.summary: Prelude: `Record<K, V>` (docs/internals/design/record.md), a dictionary keyed by strings, a union of string literal types or a string enum (the TypeScript `Object` helpers over it are in object.velt).

exports.name: Record
exports.doc:
A dictionary from keys of type `K` to values of type `V`, like TypeScript's `Record<K, V>`:
`K` is `string`, a union of string literal types or a string enum. `r.name` and `r[k]` read
a key, `r[k] = v` sets it, `delete r[k]` removes it; entries keep JavaScript's order
(array-index keys first, ascending, then insertion order).
exports.summary: A dictionary from keys of type `K` to values of type `V`, like TypeScript's `Record<K, V>`: `K` is `string`, a union of string literal types or a string enum.

Prelude: `RwLock<T>` for `shared(new RwLock<T>(x))` (docs/reference/async.md): many readers or
one writer. The compiler implements `new RwLock<T>(x)`, `rw.read(f)` and `rw.write(f)`; this
declaration only fixes the layout they use (the runtime's 19 words, rt_abi_async.md §9.2).
modules.summary: Prelude: `RwLock<T>` for `shared(new RwLock<T>(x))` (docs/reference/async.md): many readers or one writer.

exports.name: RwLock
exports.doc:
A lock around a value of type `T` that many readers may hold at once:
`shared(new RwLock<T>(x))`. `rw.read((v) => …)` runs the callback on the value while other
readers may run theirs; the callback cannot change the value. `rw.write((v) => …)` runs it
alone, like `Mutex.with`. A writer that has waited a while holds new readers back, so writers
don't starve. A `read` callback cannot run `with` or `write`, or start a promise or task.
exports.summary: A lock around a value of type `T` that many readers may hold at once: `shared(new RwLock<T>(x))`.

modules.doc:
Prelude: in-place array sorting (`sort`), and `toSorted`, which sorts a copy.

- `sort()` on arrays of numbers and strings: ascending, pattern-defeating quicksort
  (pdqsort, Orson Peters): median-of-3 / ninther pivots, branchless Lomuto partitioning
  (as in Rust's `sort_unstable`), a separate pass for runs of keys equal to the previous
  pivot, detection of already-sorted / reversed input, insertion sort for short ranges and
  heapsort once too many partitions come out unbalanced. O(n log n) worst case, no
  allocation. Not stable, which is unobservable for these types. Floats sort NaN last (a
  total order, so the algorithm's invariants hold).
- `sort(cmp)` for any element type (and on numbers and strings too): **stable** like JS
  `Array.prototype.sort(cmp)`.
  The shape of Rust's driftsort through a scratch buffer of the array's length: natural
  runs, stable quicksort between them, merges (std/lang/sort/stable.velt). O(n log n), O(n) on
  sorted or reversed input.
  `cmp(a, b)` returns < 0 when `a` goes first, > 0 when `b` goes first, 0 when equivalent
  (on `f64[]` a NaN result counts as 0). Any comparator, even an inconsistent one, gives
  some permutation of the elements.
Elements are never copied or cloned: pdqsort swaps them, the stable sort moves them between
the array and its buffer, so every algorithm here works for any `T`.
There is no generic ordering bound yet, so `sort()` is provided per element type. The
comparator returns a `number` as in JS, except on arrays of a declared integer type, where it
returns an `i64` (`(a, b) => a - b` on `i64[]`, or `a.compareTo(b)`).
modules.summary: Prelude: in-place array sorting (`sort`), and `toSorted`, which sorts a copy.

Prelude: JS string methods, `String.fromCharCode`, `String.fromCodePoint`, `parseInt`,
`parseFloat`, `Number(s)` (runtime string functions, rt_abi_async.md §12.2).

Positions and lengths count UTF-16 code units, as in JavaScript (`"😀".length` is 2): a
position may fall between the two halves of a surrogate pair, and slicing there keeps the
half as a lone surrogate (docs/reference/types.md "Strings"). Positions are `i64` so negative
arguments keep their JS meaning; "absent" is -1 (`indexOf`, `charCodeAt`) where JS would say
-1 or NaN. Inputs are borrowed; every returned string is owned by the caller (a substring of a
static string may itself be static, which is free to drop).
modules.summary: Prelude: JS string methods, `String.fromCharCode`, `String.fromCodePoint`, `parseInt`, `parseFloat`, `Number(s)` (runtime string functions, rt_abi_async.md §12.2).

options arguments.

rw_lock.velt, `Atomic<T>` in atomic.velt, `ThreadLocal<T>` in thread_local.velt).

The compiler implements `new Mutex<T>(x)` (initializes the lock word) and `m.with((v) => ...)`
(lock, run the callback on the value, unlock) on a `Mutex<T>` or `shared<Mutex<T>>`; this
declaration only fixes the layout they use: the runtime's 8-byte lock word, then the value.
It is never Copy (copying it would duplicate the lock). Its methods are the only way to reach
the value.

`shared(new Mutex<T>(x))`. `m.with((v) => …)` locks, runs the callback on the value, then

exports.name: ThreadLocal
exports.doc:
One value per thread, a number or `bool`: `const depth = new ThreadLocal<u32>(0)` at module
level (docs/std/sync.md). Each thread starts with the value given and changes its own with
`set`; `get` reads this thread's. A task moves to another thread only at an `await`, so it reads
its own writes until then. It is for code that keeps per-thread state, such as which reader
slot is this thread's: a value a task needs after an `await` belongs in a variable.

Only a module `const` can hold one, made with a literal: `get` and `set` are called on that
constant.
exports.summary: One value per thread, a number or `bool`: `const depth = new ThreadLocal<u32>(0)` at module level (docs/std/sync.md).

modules.doc:
Prelude: the global timer functions of TypeScript and Node, `setTimeout`, `clearTimeout`,
`setInterval`, `clearInterval`, `setImmediate` and `clearImmediate`, and the `Timer` handle they
return (docs/std/time/timers.md).
`velt/time/timers` re-exports them next to `delay` and `Ticker`.

A timer takes a callback returning the promise to run, like JS: `setTimeout(() => save(doc),
100)` or `setTimeout(async () => { ... }, 10)` (a promise can't be passed: promises start
when created). The callback runs on the task that created the timer, as a promise of that
task (never at the same time as its other code), so it shares what it captures with the code
around it, as in Node; it runs once the code that created it and the callbacks that code
queued are done. An error it throws is uncaught: it ends the process at the throw, as in Node,
so catch inside it.
A pending timer keeps the process alive after `main` returns, like a Node `Timeout` (a handle):
a timeout until its callback starts, an interval until it is cleared. `unref()` lets the
process exit without it. Spawned tasks and promises are not handles: what keeps them going is
what they wait for (a callback's promise too, once it started).
Timers are ordinary compiled Velt promises: no code pointer is cached anywhere, so `velt dev`
hot reload needs no special handling.
modules.summary: Prelude: the global timer functions of TypeScript and Node, `setTimeout`, `clearTimeout`, `setInterval`, `clearInterval`, `setImmediate` and `clearImmediate`, and the `Timer` handle they return (docs/std/time/timers.md).

modules.doc:
Prelude: `WeakMap<K, V>` (`WeakSet<T>` and `WeakRef<T>` are in weak_set.velt and weak_ref.velt)
(docs/std/prelude.md#weakmap-weakset-and-weakref), on velt_rt's weak-reference core
(docs/internals/design/weak-refs.md, rt_abi.md "Weak references").

A key (a `WeakSet` member, a `WeakRef` target) must be an object: a class instance, an object
type or an array (sema checks it). The compiler counts its type and makes it, and every type
reachable from a weak map's key and value types, weak-capable: their release tells a weakly
held object apart and removes it from every map and `WeakRef` as it is freed. A map whose
value refers back to its key (`raw -> proxy(raw)`) frees both once nothing else refers to
either (the ephemeron rule).

A map is created in the runtime on its first `set` (`#id` 0 until then): the intrinsic sees
the key and value types there and passes their glue. Maps and refs are bound to the thread
that made them: sema keeps them out of `spawn`, channels and `shared`.
modules.summary: Prelude: `WeakMap<K, V>` (`WeakSet<T>` and `WeakRef<T>` are in weak_set.velt and weak_ref.velt) (docs/std/prelude.md#weakmap-weakset-and-weakref), on velt_rt's weak-reference core (docs/internals/design/weak-refs.md, rt_abi.md "Weak references").

velt/process/child: run other programs (rt_abi_async.md §14.3).

`exec` / `execSync` run a program to completion and return its exit code and output;
`execShell` goes through the platform shell (`sh -c`, `cmd /C`). `spawn` starts a program
with configurable stdio and returns a `ChildProcess` whose pipes are read and written with
promises. Programs are found through `PATH`; arguments are passed as-is (no shell quoting).
A non-zero exit code is not an error (check `code`); failing to start the program throws
`IoError` (e.g. code "ENOENT", message "spawn <program>: …").

modules.doc:
velt/random/uuid: RFC 9562 UUIDs — random v4, time-ordered v7, parsing, formatting and
validation.

Text form is the canonical lowercase `xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx` (parsing accepts
either case); binary form is 16 bytes in network order. Randomness comes from the OS CSPRNG.
v7 puts the Unix time in milliseconds in the first 48 bits, so v7 ids sort by creation time
(ids created in the same millisecond are ordered randomly: no counter, no module state).
docs/std/random/uuid.md.

modules.doc:
velt/simd (internal): 128-bit SIMD, 8- and 16-bit lanes. Programs import the types from
`velt/simd`.

A vector is a value like a number: sixteen `u8` lanes in a `u8x16`, four `f32` in an
`f32x4`. Every method is one instruction, or a few, on x86-64 (SSE2), arm64 (NEON) and
WebAssembly (`simd128`), the same in debug and release builds; the `velt_simd_*` functions
below have no runtime implementation, the compiler emits them inline (rt_abi.md "SIMD").
Comparisons give a mask (`mask8x16`), which `any()`, `first()`, `bitmask()` and `select`
consume. In std the type names are built in; each `export type` below gives a module that
imports one the built-in type.

Generated by scripts/gen-simd-api.py: change the script, not this file.
modules.summary: velt/simd (internal): 128-bit SIMD, 8- and 16-bit lanes.

members.doc: A vector with every lane `x`.
members.summary: A vector with every lane `x`.

members.name: load
members.signature: static load(from: i8[], at: usize = 0): i8x16
members.doc:
The 16 elements of `from` starting at `at`. Panics with a RangeError unless all 16 are
inside the array.
members.summary: The 16 elements of `from` starting at `at`.

members.name: loadOptimistic
members.signature: static loadOptimistic(from: Atomic<i8>[], at: usize = 0): i8x16
members.doc:
The 16 words of `from` starting at `at`, read while other threads may be changing them:
an optimistic read (velt/sync `VersionLatch`). Each lane a word no thread wrote during the
read is that word; a lane a thread was writing is some value, never undefined behaviour,
so check the latch's version (`isUnchanged`) before trusting any lane. One vector load, as
`load` is, where reading the words one by one takes 16 atomic loads. Panics with a
RangeError unless all 16 are inside the array.
members.summary: The 16 words of `from` starting at `at`, read while other threads may be changing them: an optimistic read (velt/sync `VersionLatch`).

members.name: fits
members.signature: static fits(xs: i8[], at: usize = 0): bool
members.doc:
Whether the 16 elements of `xs` starting at `at` are inside the array: what `load` and
`store` check. As the condition of the loop that calls them (`while (i8x16.fits(xs, i))`),
it leaves them nothing to check.
members.summary: Whether the 16 elements of `xs` starting at `at` are inside the array: what `load` and `store` check.

members.doc:
The elements of `from` starting at `at` that exist, up to 16, in the low lanes; the other
lanes are 0. For the last elements of an array, after the steps that take 16 at a time.
`at` may be the length (no element left); past it, panics with a RangeError.
members.summary: The elements of `from` starting at `at` that exist, up to 16, in the low lanes; the other lanes are 0.

modules.doc:
velt/simd (internal): carry-less multiplication of 64-bit lanes as methods of `u64x2`
(docs/std/simd.md "Carry-less multiplication"): x86's PCLMULQDQ and ARM's PMULL, the instruction
behind CRC folding and GHASH. `a.clmulLow(b)` is the 128-bit product of the low lanes as
polynomials over GF(2) (XOR instead of addition, no carries), its low 64 bits in lane 0.

Every method always works: it is the instruction where the CPU has it (`u64x2.hasClmulX86()`,
`u64x2.hasClmulArm()`: the runtime's flags, rt_abi.md "SIMD") and otherwise an exact
emulation, a shift and XOR per bit. The checks are false on WebAssembly, in debug (Cranelift)
builds and with `VELT_SIMD_DISABLE=clmul`. Code that would be slower on the emulation than
without the instruction (a table-driven CRC) checks `u64x2.hasClmul()` first; in a function
gated on the extension (`targetFeature("clmul-x86")`, std only) the methods are the bare
instructions.
modules.summary: velt/simd (internal): carry-less multiplication of 64-bit lanes as methods of `u64x2` (docs/std/simd.md "Carry-less multiplication"): x86's PCLMULQDQ and ARM's PMULL, the instruction behind CRC folding and GHASH.

modules.doc:
velt/simd (internal): 128-bit SIMD, float lanes. Programs import the types from `velt/simd`.

A vector is a value like a number: sixteen `u8` lanes in a `u8x16`, four `f32` in an
`f32x4`. Every method is one instruction, or a few, on x86-64 (SSE2), arm64 (NEON) and
WebAssembly (`simd128`), the same in debug and release builds; the `velt_simd_*` functions
below have no runtime implementation, the compiler emits them inline (rt_abi.md "SIMD").
Comparisons give a mask (`mask8x16`), which `any()`, `first()`, `bitmask()` and `select`
consume. In std the type names are built in; each `export type` below gives a module that
imports one the built-in type.

Generated by scripts/gen-simd-api.py: change the script, not this file.

modules.doc:
velt/simd (internal): 128-bit SIMD, masks. Programs import the types from `velt/simd`.

A vector is a value like a number: sixteen `u8` lanes in a `u8x16`, four `f32` in an
`f32x4`. Every method is one instruction, or a few, on x86-64 (SSE2), arm64 (NEON) and
WebAssembly (`simd128`), the same in debug and release builds; the `velt_simd_*` functions
below have no runtime implementation, the compiler emits them inline (rt_abi.md "SIMD").
Comparisons give a mask (`mask8x16`), which `any()`, `first()`, `bitmask()` and `select`
consume. In std the type names are built in; each `export type` below gives a module that
imports one the built-in type.

Generated by scripts/gen-simd-api.py: change the script, not this file.

modules.doc:
velt/simd (internal): the CPU's SHA-1 and SHA-256 instructions as methods of `u32x4` (#1330,
docs/std/simd.md "SHA instructions"): the ARMv8 ones (ACLE `vsha256hq_u32` & co.) and the x86
ones (Intel's `_mm_sha256rnds2_epu32` & co.), named after the instruction, with the operands
in its order and lane 0 the low 32 bits.

Every method always works: it is the instruction where the CPU has it (`u32x4.hasShaArm()`,
`u32x4.hasShaX86()`: the runtime's flags, rt_abi.md "SIMD") and otherwise an exact emulation
(std/simd/sha_emulation.velt, from the ARM Architecture Reference Manual's and the Intel SDM's
pseudocode). The checks are false on another architecture, on WebAssembly and in debug
(Cranelift) builds, and with `VELT_SIMD_DISABLE=sha`, which runs the emulation on a CPU that has
the instructions.

The instructions are as fast as the checks around them allow: in a loop of them the flag is
read once, before the loop, and tested in every iteration. In a function gated on the
extension (`targetFeature`, std only, as std/crypto/index.velt's) the check is true and the
methods are the bare instructions.
modules.summary: velt/simd (internal): the CPU's SHA-1 and SHA-256 instructions as methods of `u32x4` (#1330, docs/std/simd.md "SHA instructions"): the ARMv8 ones (ACLE `vsha256hq_u32` & co.) and the x86 ones (Intel's `_mm_sha256rnds2_epu32` & co.), named after the instruction, with the operands in its order and lane 0 the low 32 bits.

exports.name: sha1Rounds
exports.signature: function sha1Rounds(abcd: u32x4, e: u32, wk: u32x4, f: u32): u32x4
exports.doc:
SHA1C / SHA1P / SHA1M (`f` 0, 1, 2): X = abcd, Y = e; per round
Y += ROL(X[0], 5) + f(X[1], X[2], X[3]) + W[e]; X[1] = ROL(X[1], 30); <Y, X> = ROL(Y:X, 32).
exports.summary: SHA1C / SHA1P / SHA1M (`f` 0, 1, 2): X = abcd, Y = e; per round Y += ROL(X[0], 5) + f(X[1], X[2], X[3]) + W[e]; X[1] = ROL(X[1], 30); <Y, X> = ROL(Y:X, 32).
