exports.name: emulSha1su1
exports.signature: function emulSha1su1(t: u32x4, w3: u32x4): u32x4
exports.doc: SHA1SU1: T = t EOR LSR(w3, 32); each lane ROL 1, lane 3 also EOR ROL(T[0], 2).
exports.summary: SHA1SU1: T = t EOR LSR(w3, 32); each lane ROL 1, lane 3 also EOR ROL(T[0], 2).

exports.name: sha256Hash
exports.signature: function sha256Hash(abcd: u32x4, efgh: u32x4, wk: u32x4, part1: bool): u32x4
exports.summary: SHA256hash(X = abcd, Y = efgh, W, part1): per round T1 = Y[3] + Σ1(Y[0]) + Ch(Y[0], Y[1], Y[2]) + W[e]; X[3] += T1; Y[3] = T1 + Σ0(X[0]) + Maj(X[0], X[1], X[2]); <Y, X> = ROL(Y:X, 32).

exports.name: emulSha256su0
exports.signature: function emulSha256su0(w0: u32x4, w1: u32x4): u32x4

exports.name: emulSha256su1
exports.signature: function emulSha256su1(t: u32x4, w2: u32x4, w3: u32x4): u32x4
exports.doc:
SHA256SU1: T0 = w3<31:0> : w2<127:32>, T1 = w3<127:64>; lanes 0, 1 from σ1(T1), lanes 2, 3
from σ1 of lanes 0, 1 of the result, each plus t[e] and T0[e].
exports.summary: SHA256SU1: T0 = w3<31:0> : w2<127:32>, T1 = w3<127:64>; lanes 0, 1 from σ1(T1), lanes 2, 3 from σ1 of lanes 0, 1 of the result, each plus t[e] and T0[e].

exports.name: emulSha256rnds2
exports.signature: function emulSha256rnds2(cdgh: u32x4, abef: u32x4, wk: u32x4): u32x4
exports.doc:
SHA256RNDS2: A, B, E, F from `abef` (lanes 3, 2, 1, 0), C, D, G, H from `cdgh`, two rounds
with WK0 = wk[0], WK1 = wk[1]; the result is A, B, E, F after them.
exports.summary: SHA256RNDS2: A, B, E, F from `abef` (lanes 3, 2, 1, 0), C, D, G, H from `cdgh`, two rounds with WK0 = wk[0], WK1 = wk[1]; the result is A, B, E, F after them.

exports.name: emulSha256msg1
exports.signature: function emulSha256msg1(a: u32x4, b: u32x4): u32x4
exports.doc: SHA256MSG1: lane i = SRC1[i] + σ0(next word), the word after SRC1[3] being SRC2[0].
exports.summary: SHA256MSG1: lane i = SRC1[i] + σ0(next word), the word after SRC1[3] being SRC2[0].

exports.name: emulSha256msg2
exports.signature: function emulSha256msg2(a: u32x4, b: u32x4): u32x4

exports.name: emulSha1rnds4
exports.signature: function emulSha1rnds4(abcd: u32x4, ewk: u32x4, func: u32): u32x4
exports.doc:
SHA1RNDS4: A, B, C, D = lanes 3, 2, 1, 0 of `abcd`; W0+E, W1, W2, W3 = lanes 3, 2, 1, 0 of
`ewk`; four rounds of function `func` with its constant (E is added only in round 0, through
W0+E; later rounds add the E the previous round left).
exports.summary: SHA1RNDS4: A, B, C, D = lanes 3, 2, 1, 0 of `abcd`; W0+E, W1, W2, W3 = lanes 3, 2, 1, 0 of `ewk`; four rounds of function `func` with its constant (E is added only in round 0, through W0+E; later rounds add the E the previous round left).

exports.name: emulSha1msg1
exports.signature: function emulSha1msg1(a: u32x4, b: u32x4): u32x4

modules.doc:
velt/simd (internal): 128-bit SIMD, 32- and 64-bit integer lanes. Programs import the types from
`velt/simd`.

A vector is a value like a number: sixteen `u8` lanes in a `u8x16`, four `f32` in an
`f32x4`. Every method is one instruction, or a few, on x86-64 (SSE2), arm64 (NEON) and
WebAssembly (`simd128`), the same in debug and release builds; the `velt_simd_*` functions
below have no runtime implementation, the compiler emits them inline (rt_abi.md "SIMD").
Comparisons give a mask (`mask8x16`), which `any()`, `first()`, `bitmask()` and `select`
consume. In std the type names are built in; each `export type` below gives a module that
imports one the built-in type.

members.name: load

The 4 elements of `from` starting at `at`. Panics with a RangeError unless all 4 are

members.name: loadOptimistic
members.signature: static loadOptimistic(from: Atomic<i32>[], at: usize = 0): i32x4
members.doc:
The 4 words of `from` starting at `at`, read while other threads may be changing them:
an optimistic read (velt/sync `VersionLatch`). Each lane a word no thread wrote during the
read is that word; a lane a thread was writing is some value, never undefined behaviour,
so check the latch's version (`isUnchanged`) before trusting any lane. One vector load, as
`load` is, where reading the words one by one takes 4 atomic loads. Panics with a
RangeError unless all 4 are inside the array.
members.summary: The 4 words of `from` starting at `at`, read while other threads may be changing them: an optimistic read (velt/sync `VersionLatch`).

members.name: fits
members.signature: static fits(xs: i32[], at: usize = 0): bool
members.doc:
Whether the 4 elements of `xs` starting at `at` are inside the array: what `load` and
`store` check. As the condition of the loop that calls them (`while (i32x4.fits(xs, i))`),
it leaves them nothing to check.
members.summary: Whether the 4 elements of `xs` starting at `at` are inside the array: what `load` and `store` check.

exports.name: Atom
exports.doc:
A `shared` value that threads read at once without a lock and replace whole, like Rust's
`arc-swap`: `Atom.create(shared(config))`. Readers never wait and never write; a value it
replaces is dropped once no thread can still be reading it (`velt/sync/epoch`).

- `read((v) => …)` runs the callback on the current value, borrowed: no count, the cheapest
  read. `load()` returns it as a reference of its own, to keep.
- `store(v)` and `swap(v)` replace it (`swap` returns the value before).
- `update((v) => …)` replaces it with what the callback makes of it. Updates take turns, so the
  callback runs once per update, unless a `store` or `swap` came in between (then it runs again
  on the newer value); if it throws, nothing changes. It must not `update` the same `Atom`.

Keep it in a `shared` object for threads to share it, or use an `Atomic<shared<T> | null>`
at module level.
exports.summary: A `shared` value that threads read at once without a lock and replace whole, like Rust's `arc-swap`: `Atom.create(shared(config))`.

members.summary: An `Atom` holding `value`.

The current value, borrowed by `f`: reading it there costs no count, and whatever `f`
keeps of it (returns, stores, captures) takes a reference of its own.
members.summary: The current value, borrowed by `f`: reading it there costs no count, and whatever `f` keeps of it (returns, stores, captures) takes a reference of its own.

exports.name: Backoff
exports.doc:
Waiting for another thread in a loop, twice as long each round: `snooze()` spins
`2^round` CPU spin hints up to `2^SPIN_ROUNDS`, then yields the thread to the OS each round.
Start a fresh one for each wait: `const b = Backoff.create(); while (!ready()) b.snooze();`.
It waits for another thread, never for a task: whatever it waits for must be taken and let go
between two `await`s (use a `Mutex` or a channel to wait for a task).
exports.summary: Waiting for another thread in a loop, twice as long each round: `snooze()` spins `2^round` CPU spin hints up to `2^SPIN_ROUNDS`, then yields the thread to the OS each round.

modules.doc:
velt/sync (internal): `Channel<T>`, a typed queue between tasks (docs/std/sync/channel.md). Any number
of tasks may send and receive through clones of one channel. A bounded channel makes `send` wait
while it is full (backpressure); an unbounded one never waits. `close()` ends the stream: sends
fail from then on, and receivers get what is queued, then `null`.

A sent value crosses to the receiver's task like a `spawn` argument: it moves when the sender
no longer uses it, and is deep-copied otherwise (objects are never shared between tasks).

`Channel<T>` is a handle struct, like `TcpStream` (docs/std/README.md "Handles"): copies share
one channel, so pass it to producers and consumers (also `spawn`ed tasks) freely. Close it
when done: a closed channel is freed once it is drained, and an unclosed one lives until the
program ends. Values nobody receives are dropped when the program ends.
modules.summary: velt/sync (internal): `Channel<T>`, a typed queue between tasks (docs/std/sync/channel.md).

exports.doc:

modules.doc:
velt/sync/epoch: epoch-based reclamation (Fraser's scheme, as crossbeam-epoch has it) for the
values an `Atomic` of a `shared` value replaces (docs/internals/design/atomics.md
"Reclamation"). Plain Velt on `Atomic`, `ThreadLocal` and `Mutex`.

A thread reads such values inside a *section* (`pin()` … `unpin()`), which announces the
global epoch it saw in its slot. A replaced value is *retired* with the epoch of its retiring:
kept until every thread that was in a section then has left it. The global epoch moves on
only when every thread in a section has seen the current one, so a value retired at epoch `g`
is unreachable once the epoch is `g + 2` steps on, and is dropped then.
docs/std/sync.md.
modules.summary: velt/sync/epoch: epoch-based reclamation (Fraser's scheme, as crossbeam-epoch has it) for the values an `Atomic` of a `shared` value replaces (docs/internals/design/atomics.md "Reclamation").

exports.name: collect
exports.doc:
Moves the epoch on if every thread in a section has seen the current one, then drops every
value retired 2 epochs or more before, on every thread's list. Returns how many it dropped.
exports.summary: Moves the epoch on if every thread in a section has seen the current one, then drops every value retired 2 epochs or more before, on every thread's list.

exports.summary: The values dropped so far, on every thread (by `collect`, and by `retire`'s own collects).

exports.summary: The values retired on every thread and not dropped yet.

exports.name: pin
exports.doc:
Enters a section: until the matching `unpin()`, no value retired from now on is dropped, and
neither is one retired before that this thread can still reach. Sections nest.
exports.summary: Enters a section: until the matching `unpin()`, no value retired from now on is dropped, and neither is one retired before that this thread can still reach.

Drops `value` once no thread can still be reading it: every thread in a section now has left

velt/sync: building blocks for lock-free code on the prelude's `Atomic<T>`
(docs/std/sync.md, docs/internals/design/atomics.md): `Backoff`, for a loop that waits for
another thread, and `VersionLatch`, the latch word of optimistic lock coupling, which a
concurrent tree keeps in every node (bbtree's `NodeLatch`). Both are plain Velt on the
public `Atomic` API: any package can write its own. `Atom<T>`, a shared value threads read,
replace and update, and `Channel<T>`, a typed queue between tasks (docs/std/sync/channel.md).

exports.name: VersionLatch
exports.doc:
A node's latch word for optimistic lock coupling (bbtree's `NodeLatch`), 8 bytes, kept in
place in a node or an array (`VersionLatch[]`). From the low bit: an exclusive bit, a count of
shared holders, and a version that only grows.

- **Optimistically:** a reader takes `readVersion()`, reads the node while writers may change
  it, then checks `isUnchanged(v)`; if that fails it reads again. A reader writes nothing.
- **Exclusively:** a writer takes the node at the version it read with `tryLockAt(v)` (never
  waiting; start over when it fails), or with `lockExclusive()`, and lets go with
  `unlockExclusive(v)`, which moves it to the next version so readers see it changed.
- **Shared:** `lockShared()` / `unlockShared()` keep writers out without changing the version.

Values read optimistically may be torn until `isUnchanged` says otherwise. Hold the latch only
between `await`s: its waits spin, so a task holding it across an `await` can hang the others.
exports.summary: A node's latch word for optimistic lock coupling (bbtree's `NodeLatch`), 8 bytes, kept in place in a node or an array (`VersionLatch[]`).

exports.name: VersionLatch
exports.doc:
A node's latch word for optimistic lock coupling (bbtree's `NodeLatch`), 8 bytes, kept in
place in a node or an array (`VersionLatch[]`). From the low bit: an exclusive bit, a count of
shared holders, and a version that only grows.

- **Optimistically:** a reader takes `readVersion()`, reads the node while writers may change
  it, then checks `isUnchanged(v)`; if that fails it reads again. A reader writes nothing.
- **Exclusively:** a writer takes the node at the version it read with `tryLockAt(v)` (never
  waiting; start over when it fails), or with `lockExclusive()`, and lets go with
  `unlockExclusive(v)`, which moves it to the next version so readers see it changed.
- **Shared:** `lockShared()` / `unlockShared()` keep writers out without changing the version.

Values read optimistically may be torn until `isUnchanged` says otherwise. Hold the latch only
between `await`s: its waits spin, so a task holding it across an `await` can hang the others.
exports.summary: A node's latch word for optimistic lock coupling (bbtree's `NodeLatch`), 8 bytes, kept in place in a node or an array (`VersionLatch[]`).

modules.doc:
velt/task: cancellation, timeouts, task scopes and task placement (docs/std/task.md).

`AbortController` / `AbortSignal` follow TypeScript's shapes. Cancellation is cooperative:
`abort()` sets the signal and wakes the tasks waiting on it; code that accepts a signal checks
it (`throwIfAborted()`) or races its work against `whenAborted()`. Nothing is dropped behind
the program's back, so `finally` blocks and `using` disposal run as usual. There is no
`addEventListener`: the runtime keeps no callbacks (they would break hot reload). Put
`signal.whenAborted()` itself in a `Promise.race` instead: a losing runtime wait is dropped,
whereas an async function wrapped around it would keep waiting.

A signal's runtime object is owned by a `shared` cell (atomic, so `spawn` shares it rather
than copying it) and released once, at the cell's last reference. No handle is public: a
signal is only made by an `AbortController` or the static constructors.
modules.summary: velt/task: cancellation, timeouts, task scopes and task placement (docs/std/task.md).

exports.name: taskScope
exports.signature: async function taskScope<T, E>(body: (scope: TaskScope<E>) => Promise<T> throws E, options: ScopeOptions = {}): Promise<T> throws E
exports.doc:
Structured concurrency: runs `body` with a `TaskScope` and settles only once the body and
every task it spawned with `scope.spawn` have finished, so no child outlives the scope. The
scope fails with the first error in time, of the body or of any child (even one nobody
awaited, or whose error the body caught), and otherwise returns the body's result. With
`cancelOnError` (the default), that first error aborts `scope.signal`, so the other children
can stop; their `AbortError`s come later and don't replace it.
exports.summary: Structured concurrency: runs `body` with a `TaskScope` and settles only once the body and every task it spawned with `scope.spawn` have finished, so no child outlives the scope.

exports.name: timeout
exports.signature: async function timeout<T, E>(p: Promise<T, E>, ms: i64): Promise<T> throws E | TimeoutError
exports.doc:
`p`, unless it does not settle within `ms` milliseconds: then `TimeoutError`. `p` is raced
directly, so after a timeout it is abandoned like a `Promise.race` loser: a runtime wait
(`signal.whenAborted()`, a timer) is dropped, and a started task keeps running, its
rejection handled (pass it a signal to stop it). When `p` wins, the timer is cancelled at
once, so nothing is left waiting.
exports.summary: `p`, unless it does not settle within `ms` milliseconds: then `TimeoutError`.

exports.name: TimeoutError
exports.doc:
Thrown by `timeout(p, ms)` when `p` does not settle in time, and by `throwIfAborted()` on a
signal that an `AbortSignal.timeout` aborted.
exports.summary: Thrown by `timeout(p, ms)` when `p` does not settle in time, and by `throwIfAborted()` on a signal that an `AbortSignal.timeout` aborted.

modules.doc:
velt/test: the test runner (docs/book/testing.md). `velt test` finds the test files, compiles
them with a generated `main` that registers their tests here (`registerFile`, `registerTest`,
`registerAsyncTest`) and calls `runRegistered`, and starts the program. Everything after that
is this module:

- Started by `velt test` (`$VELT_TEST_PLAN` names the plan, a JSON `Plan`), the program is the
  runner: it starts a process per test file, from the program the plan names for the file,
  several at once, and prints their reports in file order, then the summary; its exit code is
  the run's.
- Started for one file (`$VELT_TEST_FILE`, from the test `$VELT_TEST_FROM` on), it runs that
  file's tests one after another and reports each in marker lines for the runner. A failed
  test is an error it throws (a failed `assert` throws an `AssertionError`): it is caught and
  reported, and the next test runs. When a test ends the process (a panic, `process.exit`),
  the runner starts the file again from the test after it. After its last test the process
  exits, whatever timers or servers a failed test left behind.
- Started without either (a test program run by hand or under a debugger), it runs every file's
  tests in this process and prints the report itself.

modules.doc:
velt/text (internal): JavaScript-flavoured regular expressions over the runtime's Rust `regex`
engine (rt_abi_async.md §14). Matching is linear-time (no catastrophic backtracking); in exchange
lookaround and backreferences are not supported (compiling them throws `RegExpError`).

Offsets are UTF-16 code units, like every Velt string position (`slice`, `indexOf`).
`\d \w \b` are ASCII-only as in JS; `i m s` flags work as in JS; `g` makes `replace` replace
every match and `y` (sticky) makes `test`/`exec` match only at the start position. Called
without a start (`exec(s)`), a `g` or `y` regex starts at `lastIndex` and updates it, as in JS;
`exec(s, from)` takes the start explicitly and leaves `lastIndex` alone.

The string methods that take a regex (`s.replace(re, …)`, `match`, `matchAll`, `search`,
`split`, `replaceAll`) are the functions of velt/text/regex/string_methods, loaded with this
file: the compiler calls them when the first argument is a `RegExp` (velt_sema's
`regex_args`), and they call this class's methods keyed by velt/text/regex/keys.

A `RegExp` owns a runtime handle (released by `[Symbol.dispose]()`); the compiled program is
immutable and can be used from any task.
modules.summary: velt/text (internal): JavaScript-flavoured regular expressions over the runtime's Rust `regex` engine (rt_abi_async.md §14).

modules.doc:
velt/text (internal): `StringBuilder` (a global): builds a string in place, one buffer that
grows by doubling, so `n` appends cost O(total length) (#1677). Velt's own; JavaScript builds
with `+=` and `join`, which Velt compiles to the same builder.

The builder is the private string `buf`, which the runtime's builder functions append to in
place. `toString()` returns it shared, without a copy: the next append copies a shared buffer
before writing, as for any string, so the returned text never changes. `take()` hands the
buffer over and empties the builder, with no copy at all. Every call passes `buf` first, with no argument after
it that is a call: such an argument would make the compiler read `buf` into a copy first, to
keep its value, and the append would go to the copy.
modules.summary: velt/text (internal): `StringBuilder` (a global): builds a string in place, one buffer that grows by doubling, so `n` appends cost O(total length) (#1677).

Days are counted from 1970-01-01 (day 0) with Howard Hinnant's `days_from_civil` /
`civil_from_days` algorithms (http://howardhinnant.github.io/date_algorithms.html): exact for
every i64 day count a DateTime can hold, branch-light, and without tables.

modules.doc:
velt/time (internal): `DateTime`, a UTC-first instant (JS `Date` without its local-time
pitfalls) (`Duration` is velt/time/duration).

A DateTime is epoch milliseconds (i64, proleptic Gregorian, no leap seconds) in a Copy
struct, so it passes and stores like a number. Getters and `toISOString` are UTC; local time
(DST-aware, from the OS time zone) is opt-in: `localParts()`, `toLocalISOString()`,
`formatLocal()`. Months are 1-12 everywhere (unlike JS's 0-11). `parse` reads strings without
an offset as UTC (JS reads date-times without one as local time).
modules.summary: velt/time (internal): `DateTime`, a UTC-first instant (JS `Date` without its local-time pitfalls) (`Duration` is velt/time/duration).

exports.name: Ticker
exports.doc:
A drift-free periodic schedule: tick `k` is due `k * periodMs` after construction (measured
with `performance.now()`), independent of how long the loop body takes. Missed ticks are
skipped, not burst: a `tick()` that is already late resolves at once, and the next one is
the first schedule point after that. A stop wakes a pending tick at once: its sleep races the
stop signal (velt/task), and the losing sleep is cancelled.
exports.summary: A drift-free periodic schedule: tick `k` is due `k * periodMs` after construction (measured with `performance.now()`), independent of how long the loop body takes.

members.doc: Resolves when the next tick is due: true, or false once the ticker is stopped.
members.summary: Resolves when the next tick is due: true, or false once the ticker is stopped.

members.doc:
`for await (const n of ticker)`: each tick as `tick()` waits for it, numbered from 1,
until the ticker is stopped. Leaving the loop early does not stop the ticker.
members.summary: `for await (const n of ticker)`: each tick as `tick()` waits for it, numbered from 1, until the ticker is stopped.

timers created after it (like Node's `setImmediate`).

exports.name: setInterval
exports.signature: function setInterval<E>(task: () => Promise<void, E>, ms: i64): Timer
exports.doc:
Calls `task` every `ms` milliseconds (at least 1) until the returned timer is cleared, like
Node: on a fixed schedule, also while an earlier run's promise is still pending. Runs that
overlap interleave at their `await`s on the timer's task; they never run in parallel.
exports.summary: Calls `task` every `ms` milliseconds (at least 1) until the returned timer is cleared, like Node: on a fixed schedule, also while an earlier run's promise is still pending.

exports.name: setTimeout
exports.signature: function setTimeout<E>(task: () => Promise<void, E>, ms: i64): Timer
exports.doc:
Calls `task` after at least `ms` milliseconds (at least 1, like Node: `setTimeout(f, 0)` is
`setTimeout(f, 1)`) unless the returned timer is cleared first. An error it throws is uncaught,
as in Node.
exports.summary: Calls `task` after at least `ms` milliseconds (at least 1, like Node: `setTimeout(f, 0)` is `setTimeout(f, 1)`) unless the returned timer is cleared first.

members.doc:
Cancels the task if it has not started yet, and an interval's future runs at any time (a
no-op on a timeout that started, like JS `clearTimeout`). A cleared timer no longer keeps
the process alive. Dropping the handle does not cancel.
members.summary: Cancels the task if it has not started yet, and an interval's future runs at any time (a no-op on a timeout that started, like JS `clearTimeout`).

members.summary: Lets the process exit while this timer is pending, like Node's `timeout.unref()`.

members.summary: Keeps the process alive while this timer is pending again (the default), like Node's `timeout.ref()`.

exports.name: Ticker
exports.doc:
A drift-free periodic schedule: tick `k` is due `k * periodMs` after construction (measured
with `performance.now()`), independent of how long the loop body takes. Missed ticks are
skipped, not burst: a `tick()` that is already late resolves at once, and the next one is
the first schedule point after that. A stop wakes a pending tick at once: its sleep races the
stop signal (velt/task), and the losing sleep is cancelled.
exports.summary: A drift-free periodic schedule: tick `k` is due `k * periodMs` after construction (measured with `performance.now()`), independent of how long the loop body takes.

modules.doc:
velt/time (internal): timers that run a promise later: `delay`, and `setTimeout`,
`setInterval` and their `clear` functions, which are also globals (std/prelude/timers.velt), as
are `setImmediate` and `clearImmediate`.
modules.summary: velt/time (internal): timers that run a promise later: `delay`, and `setTimeout`, `setInterval` and their `clear` functions, which are also globals (std/prelude/timers.velt), as are `setImmediate` and `clearImmediate`.

exports.name: delay
exports.doc: Resolves after `ms` milliseconds (same as the built-in `sleep`).
exports.summary: Resolves after `ms` milliseconds (same as the built-in `sleep`).

exports.name: Timer
exports.doc: Handle of a pending `setTimeout` / `setImmediate` task or of a `setInterval` schedule.
exports.summary: Handle of a pending `setTimeout` / `setImmediate` task or of a `setInterval` schedule.

members.name: constructor
members.doc: Wraps the task's state (use `setTimeout` or `setInterval` to create timers).
members.summary: Wraps the task's state (use `setTimeout` or `setInterval` to create timers).

members.name: clear
members.doc:
Cancels the task if it has not started yet, and an interval's future runs at any time (a
no-op on a timeout that started, like JS `clearTimeout`). A cleared timer no longer keeps
the process alive. Dropping the handle does not cancel.
members.summary: Cancels the task if it has not started yet, and an interval's future runs at any time (a no-op on a timeout that started, like JS `clearTimeout`).

members.name: unref
members.doc:
Lets the process exit while this timer is pending, like Node's `timeout.unref()`.
Returns the timer.
members.summary: Lets the process exit while this timer is pending, like Node's `timeout.unref()`.

members.name: ref
members.doc:
Keeps the process alive while this timer is pending again (the default), like Node's
`timeout.ref()`. Returns the timer.
members.summary: Keeps the process alive while this timer is pending again (the default), like Node's `timeout.ref()`.

members.name: hasRef
members.doc:
Whether the timer is ref'd (`ref()`, the default) rather than `unref()`'d, like Node's
`timeout.hasRef()`.
members.summary: Whether the timer is ref'd (`ref()`, the default) rather than `unref()`'d, like Node's `timeout.hasRef()`.

members.name: cleared
members.doc:
Whether `clear()` cancelled the task before it started (an interval: whether it was
cleared).
members.summary: Whether `clear()` cancelled the task before it started (an interval: whether it was cleared).

members.name: started
members.doc: Whether the task has started (an interval: whether it ran at least once).
members.summary: Whether the task has started (an interval: whether it ran at least once).

exports.name: setTimeout
exports.signature: function setTimeout<E>(task: () => Promise<void, E>, ms: i64): Timer
exports.doc:
Calls `task` after at least `ms` milliseconds (at least 1, like Node: `setTimeout(f, 0)` is
`setTimeout(f, 1)`) unless the returned timer is cleared first. An error it throws is uncaught,
as in Node.
exports.summary: Calls `task` after at least `ms` milliseconds (at least 1, like Node: `setTimeout(f, 0)` is `setTimeout(f, 1)`) unless the returned timer is cleared first.

exports.name: clearTimeout
exports.doc: Cancels `t` if its task has not started (same as `t.clear()`).
exports.summary: Cancels `t` if its task has not started (same as `t.clear()`).

exports.name: setInterval
exports.signature: function setInterval<E>(task: () => Promise<void, E>, ms: i64): Timer
exports.doc:
Calls `task` every `ms` milliseconds (at least 1) until the returned timer is cleared, like
Node: on a fixed schedule, also while an earlier run's promise is still pending. Runs that
overlap interleave at their `await`s on the timer's task; they never run in parallel.
exports.summary: Calls `task` every `ms` milliseconds (at least 1) until the returned timer is cleared, like Node: on a fixed schedule, also while an earlier run's promise is still pending.

exports.name: clearInterval
exports.doc: Stops the interval `t` (same as `t.clear()`; also cancels a timeout, like JS).
exports.summary: Stops the interval `t` (same as `t.clear()`; also cancels a timeout, like JS).

exports.name: setImmediate
exports.doc:
Calls `task` once the code that is running and the callbacks it queued are done, before the
timers created after it (like Node's `setImmediate`).
exports.summary: Calls `task` once the code that is running and the callbacks it queued are done, before the timers created after it (like Node's `setImmediate`).

exports.name: clearImmediate
exports.doc: Cancels `t` if its task has not started (same as `t.clear()`).
exports.summary: Cancels `t` if its task has not started (same as `t.clear()`).
